title: Reverse engineering a Beyblade launch tracker - Simone's Blog
content:
Simone's Blog
Reverse engineering a Beyblade launch tracker
October 22, 2026 · 9814 views
At the beginning of June last summer, after resetting my Instagram algorithm for the 10th time that year, I started getting recommendations for something I hadn't heard of or seen since I was a kid: Beyblades. This new generation, called Beyblade X, was genuinely hypnotic to watch on reels, and I was instantly hooked. So, I decided to pay a visit to my local toy shop in Dublin, where I picked up a stadium and a bunch of beys. That same weekend, I called a few friends and organised a games night at my place. It didn't take long for us to understand what all the fuss was about!
Beyblade X battles are incredibly fun and fast paced compared to previous generations of the toy line. Thanks to the stadium's design, the bottom part of each top, known as the Bit, can latch onto a side rail and trigger a special "gimmick" called Xtreme Dash. The resulting collisions between the beys are absolutely epic! Everyone was ecstatic as we watched these tops fly left and right around the stadium in my living room.
Over the following months, I attended local tournaments, made new friends, and collected far too many Beyblades. Just like everyone else, I wanted to find the ultimate meta combos (Blades + Ratchets + Bits). During one of my procrastination-fuelled research sessions, I stumbled upon an interesting accessory called the Beybattle Pass (BX-09). From what I could gather online, it was developed by Takara Tomy and was (in theory) only available in Japan. When attached to a launcher, it could connect to an official mobile app via Bluetooth and transmit data from each launch, specifically the Shoot Power value, which is literally just the RPM (revolutions per minute) of the launch. Users could then accumulate points and use them to enter a Japan-exclusive lottery system for a chance to obtain rarer Beyblades.
I was fascinated by how this little gadget worked, and with a bit of patience, I managed to find one on eBay Japan, although at an unfortunate scalper price.
How does the Beybattle Pass work?
Here is a quick breakdown of how it works. Some of this is based on hands-on testing. Since this device was so expensive, I wasn't about to tear it apart and risk breaking it! Still, it was pretty straightforward to figure out how key parts operate.
Official Beyblade X launchers (such as the string launcher shown in the video) have two holes on the top. Inside the first hole is a small rotating disc that changes color from black to white depending on how quickly you pull the string.
Let's look at the bottom part now:
When you attach a Beyblade to the three hooks at the bottom you will also push a little white lever to the top, this little lever will come out from the second hole (blue arrow below):
We can now align the components shown in the picture above and work out how they interact. When the small white lever is pushed upwards, sliding into the Beybattle Pass, it signals that a Beyblade is attached to the launcher (see blue arrow). The white lever also acts as a button, turning on the Beybattle Pass and activating a sensor (purple arrow). This sensor detects how quickly the black-and-white disc spins as the launcher string is pulled.
From the video above, I was able to identify what appears to be an infrared sensor using my phone's front-facing camera. My theory is that the sensor tracks the rotating disc by detecting changes in the reflected infrared signal, allowing the Beybattle Pass to calculate the Shoot Power value. In the video, I'm simulating a Beyblade being attached to the launcher to demonstrate how the lever activates the sensor.
Analyzing the Bluetooth payloads
When the Beybattle Pass arrived, I immediately powered it on with a long press, then entered pairing mode by holding the button down again until the lights started blinking. The device BEYBLADE_TOOL01 popped up on my screen. Assuming it wasn't my neighbour's Bluetooth speaker, I connected to it and watched the blinking lights finally stop. I fired up LightBlue and PacketLogger and started sniffing the Bluetooth traffic. I was worried I'd need the official Beyblade X app, but it turned out I could capture launches without it.
After connecting to the device I got the following characteristics:
0x55c4f002f8eb11ecb9390242ac120002
Read and Notify

0x55c4f001f8eb11ecb9390242ac120002
Write without Response
At first, I thought, "Ok, this structure looks simple enough." I subscribed to the Read and Notify characteristics, but nothing happened. Then I wondered: what would happen if I connected the Beybattle Pass to the launcher and attached a Beyblade? Almost immediately, I noticed an orange LED lighting up.
Houston we got something!
a0 3a 00 04 ff 00 00 00 00 00 00 35 b4 04 51 c4 da
After receiving this initial, tiny payload, I had no idea what I was looking at. But when I launched the Beyblade, I received the following, much larger payload:
a0 3a 00 00 ff 00 00 a2 0c 01 00 35 b4 04 51 c4 da
b0 a2 0c 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b1 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b2 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b3 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b4 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b5 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b6 00 00 00 00 00 00 a2 0c 01 00 01 00 00 00 00 00
b7 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 5e
70 f2 28 ef 0c cc 09 0f 09 6e 0b 67 0b 73 29 35 13
71 34 0d e5 0a 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
72 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
73 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
After performing a few more launches, I noticed a consistent pattern: an initial 17-byte header was always followed by a much larger payload once a Beyblade was launched. Starting with the larger payload, I noticed that its first bytes always followed the same structure: a0, b0 through b7, and then 70 through 73. These looked like page tags to me, so I needed to carefully analyze the data that followed each one. Looking at the a0 page, I noticed that the tenth byte increased by one with every launch compared to the corresponding byte in the a0 page of the header payload. Easy enough! This was probably some kind of launch counter, incremented whenever a launch was successful. Next, the sequence 35 b4 04 51 c4 da remained constant across captures. This turned out to be the BLE device's address in reverse byte order. I was still trying to understand why bytes 8 and 9 (a2 0c) appeared to be copied into the b* pages.
Decoding the launches
After launching a few more times the chunky payload looked like this:
a0 3a 00 00 ff 00 00 62 10 03 00 35 b4 04 51 c4 da
b0 a2 0c 62 10 95 0d 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b1 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b2 ...
I noticed that, with each new launch, a few bytes were appearing in the b* pages: first a2 0c, then 62 10, and finally 95 0d. I tried converting each sequence into a decimal number, but the results were enormous. Like the value a2 0c, came out as 41,484. That couldn't possibly be an RPM value! :)
After searching online, I found that an average Beyblade launch could reach around 5,000 RPM. I decided to try swapping the two bytes in a2 0c, giving me 0c a2, which converted to 3,234.
That's more like it!
The reason I tried this was that Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) commonly uses little-endian byte order, where the least significant byte comes first. This made sense, so I had finally managed to decode the actual launch values. Now, back to the smaller header payload.
As I mentioned earlier, bytes 8 and 9 (e.g. 62 10) from the a0 page would occasionally appear in the b* pages, but their values seemed to change unpredictably. Whenever this happened, the Beybattle Pass would display a different light pattern after the launch. Instead of the usual blinking green  , it would flash orange → red → green  . Something was definitely different about these launches. But why?!
Decoding the numbers I would have:
0c a2 → 3,234
10 62 → 4,194 🔥
0d 95 → 3,477
AH, that looks like a high score to me, mystery solved!
Remaining bytes in the header
At this point, I had managed to decode the launch values, identify the launch counter, and figure out how the high score was stored. However, a few bytes in the header remained unexplained. During testing, I noticed that whenever I dropped or detached a Beyblade without launching it, the LED would blink red, and the device would return a different header payload:
Payload when attached:
a0 3a 00 04 ff 00 00 02 16 1d 00 35 b4 04 51 c4 da

Payload after being dropped (no launches): <---
a0 3a 00 00 ff 00 00 02 16 1d 00 35 b4 04 51 c4 da

Successfull launch (bulky payload):
a0 3a 00 00 ff 00 00 02 16 1e 00 35 b4 04 51 c4 da,
b0: d6 0f c1 03 88 13 02 16 f0 14 c7 14 4e 11 98 13,
b1: ...
The difference was easy to spot. The sequence 00 04 looked like some kind of status flag, possibly indicating that the device was ready for launch. When a launch failed, these bytes would revert to 00 00, and the launch counter (byte 10) would remain unchanged. However, when a launch was successful, the counter would increase, while the status bytes would read 00 00.
Over the following months, I also noticed that byte 5 (ff, or 255 in decimal, in the a0 page) was steadily decreasing. At the time of writing this post, for example, its value was da, or 218 in decimal. One possible theory is that this byte represents the battery level. However, I still can't explain why its value differs in the larger payload. One day, I'll figure it out...
Launchmaxxing
As the b* pages continued to fill up with data from new launches, my next question was: what happens when we reach the last page, b7? After performing a lot of launches, and by a lot, I mean 50 more, I noticed that the values in page b6 stopped at position 6 (counting from 1), leaving a gap filled with 00 00.
Here's what I mean:
50th launch bulky payload (32 hex):
a0 3a 00 00 ff 00 00 61 16 32 00 35 b4 04 51 c4 da
b0 d6 0f c1 03 88 13 02 16 f0 14 c7 14 4e 11 98 13
b1 18 12 59 0b 1b 10 b3 09 f8 0c 29 0d 88 06 a2 09
b2 a3 0d 3c 0a 22 0b c4 0a 04 01 67 0c 91 0d 4e 04
b3 09 0b 74 03 86 0d 35 0b a0 04 0e 0b e7 13 b3 15
b4 38 05 9e 04 c8 13 61 16 dd 10 2e 15 b5 0e b2 0b
b5 48 0c a6 0c a9 0c 2d 0d 20 0d cb 0d 55 0e 47 0d
b6 bc 0d 36 0d 00 00 61 16 32 00 32 00 00 00 00 00
b7 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 dc
70 ...

51st launch bulky payload (33 hex):
a0 3a 00 00 ff 00 00 61 16 33 00 35 b4 04 51 c4 da
b0 c1 03 88 13 02 16 f0 14 c7 14 4e 11 98 13 18 12
b1 59 0b 1b 10 b3 09 f8 0c 29 0d 88 06 a2 09 a3 0d
b2 3c 0a 22 0b c4 0a 04 01 67 0c 91 0d 4e 04 09 0b
b3 74 03 86 0d 35 0b a0 04 0e 0b e7 13 b3 15 38 05
b4 9e 04 c8 13 61 16 dd 10 2e 15 b5 0e b2 0b 48 0c
b5 a6 0c a9 0c 2d 0d 20 0d cb 0d 55 0e 47 0d bc 0d
b6 36 0d 2c 13 00 00 61 16 33 00 32 00 00 00 00 00
b7 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 37
70 ...
FIFO! I screamed while waking the neighbourhood!
It turned out that the maximum number of launches that can be recorded is 50. After that, the oldest entry at the beginning of b0 is discarded, and the new launch value is added to byte position 4 of page b6 (2c 13). After the padding bytes at positions 6 and 7, the same high score showed up again (61 16), followed by the total number of launches (33 00 → 51) and the number of stored entries (32 00 → 50, the maximum).
I couldn't wrap my head around the very last byte on page b7 at first, but it turned out to be a simple checksum. It was calculated by adding together every data byte across the b* pages, skipping each page's tag byte and the checksum byte itself, and then taking the result modulo 256.
Sending data to the Beybattle Pass
So far, I had managed to retrieve quite a lot of information simply by reading the initial characteristic (0x55c4f002). But then I started wondering: what was the other characteristic (0x55c4f001) used for?
Unfortunately, answering that question meant installing the official Beyblade X app and sniffing the Bluetooth traffic directly from my iPhone. The process was quite tedious, especially since I had to install an official Apple Bluetooth debugging profile on my iPhone and keep it connected to my Mac via cable. Once that was done, however, I could finally map out all the interactions.
After inspecting the payloads, I identified three distinct scenarios.
Sending the command 0x74 returned:
b0 a2 0c 71 0f 06 14 f4 13 55 11 88 13 bd 17 23 15
b1 46 13 c9 11 03 0c 1f 0f 46 0e 4d 1b 00 00 00 00
b2 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b3 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b4 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b5 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b6 00 00 00 00 00 00 4d 1b 0e 00 0e 00 00 00 00 00
b7 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 0c
That looks like the bulky payload without the 7* pages!
Then 0x51 returned:
a0 3a 00 00 d3 00 00 4d 1b 0e 00 35 b4 04 51 c4 da
And that's the the 17-byte header!
Finally 0x75 returned:
a1 00 00 00
a0 3a 00 00 d3 00 00 00 00 00 00 35 b4 04 51 c4 da
b0 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b1 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b2 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b3 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b4 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b5 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b6 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
b7 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
Damn, looks like I cleared the whole dataset lol
It was immediately clear what kind of operations were available. One returned the full list of launch values, another retrieved the initial metadata and the last one cleared the entire internal database. This final command was also easy to identify because the Beybattle Pass returned an extra a1 page that I hadn't encountered before.
The obscure 7* pages
If you've made it this far, you're probably wondering: what about the 7* pages? Sadly, I don't have much to say about those. To this day, I still haven't fully figured out what the values stored in these pages represent. After plotting them in a spreadsheet, nothing immediately jumped out at me.
Maybe you guys are smarter than me, but my theory is that these values represent some kind of physical data coming directly from the Beybattle Pass sensor. This would also explain why the 7* pages only appear when a Beyblade is actually launched, rather than when querying the Beybattle Pass using the Write Without Response commands.
Anyway the big part of this reverse job was finally over.
DiZZi 0.2
Of course, I couldn't just stop there. I now had a fully reverse engineered protocol for this nifty little device, which meant I could build my own Bluetooth app, bring it to tournaments, and compete with my friends to see who could achieve the highest spin score.
For my favourite part of any project, designing the UI, I already had something in mind. While watching the original anime from the early

title: Brazil elections: Lula secures fourth term after dramatic comeback
content:
Lula wins fourth term in Brazil but faces hostile Congress and divided country
3 hours ago
Share
Save
Add as preferred on Google
Marina Rossi,BBC News Brasil in São Paulo,Leandro Prazeres,BBC News Brasil in BrasíliaandVanessa Buschschlüter,Latin America online editor reporting from London
Reuters
Brazil's veteran left-wing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has been re-elected after a bitterly fought campaign, beating his right-wing rival Flávio Bolsonaro.
It is Lula's fourth win in a presidential election, having served two terms as president from January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.
But the road to his win in Sunday's run-off was not a smooth one.
Bolsonaro had beaten Lula in the first round on 4 October and many had not thought it possible for him to turn the result around in just three weeks.
He has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters have punished incumbents and turned to the right. Across the region, larger countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia all now have conservative leaders at their helm.
EPA/ Shutterstock
Lula greets supporters after casting his ballot on Sunday
Lula's campaign sprang back to life following his first-round defeat driven by street demonstrations and a massive social media push.
The former metalworker, who has been the dominant figure on Brazil's left since he first ran for president in 1989, nevertheless faces the most challenging political landscape since first taking office in 2003.
ADVERTISEMENT
His new term, set to begin on 5 January 2027, will start amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from US President Donald Trump.
While Trump did not endorse Lula's rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, directly – something he did with the right-wing candidates who went on to win presidential elections held in Colombia and Honduras – there is little doubt his administration would have preferred to see a conservative at the helm of this country of 213 million people.
The White House regards Latin America as an area of US influence with the Trump administration keen to have leaders in power who support its policies, including on defence, security and trade.
It is also keen to reduce China's influence in the Western Hemisphere.
Brazil, which is oil-rich and holds the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals, is the only big country in South America not governed by a right-wing leader, with Lula largely seen as China-friendly.
Flávio Bolsonaro had promised to align Brazil more closely with Washington while Lula had warned the US not to interfere in the election and insisted that Brazil would "never fit into anyone's backyard".
But while there may be disappointment in the White House, Lula's victory will be welcomed by environmentalists who had feared that a win by Bolsonaro would have given Brazil's influential agribusiness and mining sectors more power.
They had pointed to record levels of deforestation and forest fires in the Amazon during the presidency of his father, Jair, arguing that under the younger Bolsonaro laxer environmental policies could again lead to destruction in this key ecosystem.
Reuters
An aerial view from a Greenpeace flyover shows a fire burning in the Amazon rainforest during the UN Climate Change Conference (COP30), held near Centro Novo in the state of Maranhao, Brazil, in 2025
While Lula's supporters are ecstatic about his victory, the result shows that the country remains deeply divided, with more than 48% of voters choosing Bolsonaro.
In addition to the challenge of uniting such a deeply polarised country, Lula will have to govern alongside the most right-wing Congress in Brazil's democratic era.
Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) was the party that made the biggest gains in the election.
And yet, Lula's Workers' Party managed to organise huge rallies ahead of the run-off, showing the strong grassroots support it commands.
Before the election, Lula had described the poll as "a parting of the waters for Brazil".
He promised to bridge the gap between Brazil's opposing political poles with "a new way of governing", adding in a WhatsApp livestream before the election that "this country will never be the same again".
While he provided little detail as to what the new way of governing would entail, he insisted he would "remain firm in the fight for a more just country, with opportunities for all and policies directed at the needs of the population".
With a largely hostile Congress, this fight just may prove much harder for the veteran leadern - who will be 85 by the end of his fourth term - than in his three previous terms in office.

Hurston-1
Accented English text-to-speech built for the phone, steered by a plain-language voice description.
Hurston-1 introduces NB-TTS (Narrowband TTS): text-to-speech made for the phone line, where most customer service still happens, even when the other side is an AI agent. It learned in part from real phone calls between our contributors and AI voice agents, and its phone mode delivers what a caller actually hears: 8 kHz G.711 audio, ready for Twilio and other telephony systems. Full 24 kHz audio is still the default.
Hurston-1 is a fine-tune of Maya1 (Apache-2.0) built by Destined AI to speak English accents that most TTS systems handle poorly: Southern American, Nigerian, West African, East African, Southern African, alongside broader American English. It is the first open model in Destined AI's ClarityVoice family.
pip install torch transformers snac soundfile scipy speechbrain   # speechbrain is only needed for --check
python hurston.py --model . --check \
    --accent "Nigerian English accent" --gender Female \
    --text "Good afternoon. Please take one tablet twice a day after meals." --out hello.wav

# the same line as a caller hears it: 8 kHz G.711 mu-law WAV
python hurston.py --model . --check --phone \
    --accent "Southern American accent" --gender Male \
    --text "Thanks for calling, how can I help you today?" --out call.wav
from hurston import Hurston, describe
tts = Hurston('.', check=True)          # check=True retries takes that Whisper cannot follow or where the voice changes
wav = tts("Well hey there, thanks for calling.", describe('Male', 'adult', 'Southern American accent'))
The South got something to say
In 1995 André 3000 stood on stage at the Source Awards, in front of a crowd that booed OutKast, and said "the South got something to say." We think that line still fits.
Hurston-1 was built in Atlanta by a small, independent team. Since 2021 we've been recording consented, paid contributors from the American South and from across Africa. These are voices that most AI systems still flatten into generic American English. Nobody handed us a funding round to do this, so we built it ourselves. These voices belong in AI, and now they have an open model.
We named it for Zora Neale Hurston. She grew up in Eatonville, Florida, trained as an anthropologist, and traveled the South recording how Black Southerners actually talked: their stories, songs and speech, at a time when few institutions thought those voices were worth keeping. Our work is a small echo of hers. The name is a tribute; it does not imply any endorsement by her estate.
Hear the South
A few lines the way people actually talk around Atlanta. All synthetic; every voice is generated from a description.
Line Voice Listen
"The South got somethin to say." Male, Southern American accent, clear conversational
"Meet me on Peachtree. No, not that Peachtree, the other one." Female, Southern American accent, casual conversational
"I'm fixin' to head out, traffic on 285 is already backed up." Male, Southern American accent, casual conversational
"What part of Atlanta you from?" Female, Southern American accent, casual conversational
More samples for every accent are in demo/ (descriptions and text in demo/demos.csv).
Voice descriptions
The model was trained on descriptions of the form Gender, age, accent, style, pace:
Field Values
Gender Female, Male
Age adult, middle-aged, older
Accent American accent, Southern American accent, Nigerian English accent, Nigerian (Yoruba) English accent, Nigerian (Igbo) English accent, West African English accent, East African English accent, East African (Swahili) English accent, Southern African English accent
Style clear conversational voice, casual conversational voice, clear audiobook narration voice
Pace natural pacing, measured pacing, slow pacing, fast pacing
Pace labels are absolute speaking rates learned from the natural voices in training data: roughly slow is under 2 words per second, measured 2 to 2.6, natural 2.6 to 3.4, fast over 3.4. The model follows them approximately, not exactly. It still highly matches the behavior of the underlying dataset.
Each call samples a new voice that fits the description. Note: Hurston-1 does not clone voices and was not trained to reproduce any real person.
Built for the phone (NB-TTS)
Most voice AI is demoed in studio quality and then deployed over a phone line. Hurston-1 is built for where it will actually be heard:
Trained on real calls. About 10 hours of the training audio (7,600 turns from 250 contributors) is phone-quality speech from real calls with full-duplex AI voice agents, alongside studio-style reading and conversation.
Phone mode. --phone (or phone=True) filters the output to the 300 to 3,400 Hz telephone band, resamples it to 8 kHz and encodes it as G.711 mu-law (--codec alaw for A-law), the formats phone networks, SIP and Twilio use. It is a channel effect applied after synthesis, so --check still judges the full-quality take.
Ready to stream. ulaw_encode() returns raw mu-law bytes, the payload Twilio media streams expect.
from hurston import Hurston, describe, ulaw_encode
tts = Hurston('.', check=True)
call = tts("Hi, I'm calling about my appointment on Tuesday.", describe('Female', 'older', 'Nigerian English accent'), phone=True)
payload = ulaw_encode(call)   # 8 kHz mu-law bytes; base64 it for a Twilio media stream
What people build with it
Some places to start. At Destined AI we use accented TTS like this to build broad, high-quality test data, and that is still the use we would point to first.
Test data for speech recognition. Generate the same sentences in nine accents and see where your ASR, captioning or transcription system breaks. It makes a quick accent-coverage check or a regression set before a release.
Simulated callers for voice agents and IVR. Pair Hurston-1 with an LLM that writes caller scripts (customers, patients, applicants) and run hundreds of synthetic calls through your agent before real people do. Use phone mode so the agent hears what it will hear in production. Good for catching where an agent mishears accents, names or numbers.
Training data augmentation. Add accented synthetic speech to ASR, keyword-spotting or wake-word training sets where those accents are thin. Mix it with real speech instead of training on synthetic audio alone.
Voice prompts and announcements. Phone menus (phone mode output drops straight into an IVR), appointment reminders, store and transit announcements, app onboarding, in a voice that sounds like the community you serve.
Education and training. Listening practice across world Englishes for learners, and accent-familiarity practice for customer service, healthcare and call-center staff.
Accessibility and read-aloud. Read articles, forms or messages aloud in a voice closer to home.
Games, animation and media drafts. Background characters, temp voice tracks and podcast or audiobook drafts, labeled as synthetic.
Research. Accent-fairness audits of speech systems, listening and perception studies, and benchmarks that cover voices most datasets leave out.
Not a fit yet: one consistent brand voice across sessions (each call is a new voice; see Limitations), cloning a specific person, or anything safety-critical without a human listening first.
Evaluation
Two questions: does it sound like the accent, and does it say the words?
Accent strength vs base Maya1. Base Maya1 documents five accents (American, Indian, Middle Eastern, Asian American, British). For a fair comparison we prompted it in its own documented description style, naming each accent, and compared it with Hurston-1 on the same 10 sentences and 18 voices (180 clips per model). An accent classifier (African vs American English, trained on real speakers) scored each voice group:
Accent (probability judged African) Maya1 base Hurston-1
Southern African 0.60 0.95
West African 0.60 0.84
East African 0.81 0.98
East African (Swahili) 0.81 0.97
Nigerian 0.82 0.94
Nigerian (Igbo) 0.82 0.92
Nigerian (Yoruba) 0.87 0.93
American (should be low) 0.12 0.02
Southern American (should be low) n/a 0.01
The classifier cannot tell Southern American from general American English; that accent was checked by listening.
Intelligibility. Whisper large-v3-turbo word error rate (WER) against the input text, numbers normalized (lower is better).
Everyday sentences (the same 180 clips as the accent test above, natural pacing, single take):
Maya1 base Hurston-1
Mean WER 0.02 0.03
Harder sentences (30 unseen sentences × 17 voices, 510 clips):
Hurston-1, single take Hurston-1, with --check
Mean WER 0.145 0.062
Clips over 20% WER 17.1% 8.4%
The harder set covers reading, health, customer service, names and numbers, expressive and long sentences. Base Maya1 is very clear because it mostly stays in American English; Hurston-1 keeps nearly the same clarity while actually doing the accent.
Accent (510-clip set, WER with --check) Hurston-1
American 0.021
Southern American 0.070
Nigerian 0.070
Nigerian (Igbo) 0.016
Nigerian (Yoruba) 0.078
West African 0.059
East African 0.043
East African (Swahili) 0.019
Southern African 0.053
Names and numbers are the hardest category (WER 0.17 with --check). Part of that is the recognizer misspelling African names such as Adaeze Okafor rather than the model mispronouncing them.
Speaking rate. Median 2.84 words per second with natural pacing, against 3.76 for base Maya1. Hurston-1 speaks a little more deliberately; use fast pacing for quicker delivery.
Blind listening. Testers heard the same sentence from base Maya1 and Hurston-1 in random order, without knowing which was which, and chose the one that sounded more like a real person with the requested accent. Hurston-1 was chosen 78% of the time and base Maya1 6%; the rest were rated a tie or neither (54 comparisons). Base Maya1 was never chosen for an African or Southern American voice; its few wins were on plain American English.
Training data
LoRA (rank 64) fine-tune of Maya1, 2,000 steps, about 190 hours of speech:
Source Hours License
Destined AI accented English corpus: scripted reading, conversational speech and ~10 h of real phone calls with AI voice agents, from consented, paid contributors ~136 (a slice of our 1,800+ hour corpus) Owned by Destined AI
LibriTTS-R (audiobook style, keeps general quality) ~46 CC BY 4.0
Mozilla Common Voice English, African-accented speakers, quality-filtered ~10.5 CC0
Accent labels come from each contributor's self-reported background, checked against an audio accent classifier and human listening; speakers whose audio and labels disagreed were relabeled or removed. Pace labels come from each clip's measured speaking rate. All contributors were adults. The full Destined AI corpus (1,800+ hours, recorded since 2021) is not included in this release; contact us about licensing it.
Limitations
No voice consistency across calls. Each call is a fresh voice that fits the description. Long text is split at sentence ends into chunks of about 40 words, so the voice can change between chunks. Consistent named voices are planned for a later release.
Names, dates and amounts are the weakest content. Use --check and listen before you ship anything important.
The generic African English accent label is weaker (WER 0.26); use a specific region instead.
English only. No child voices.
Like other autoregressive TTS models it occasionally produces a garbled or overlong take, or the voice shifts mid-take; --check catches most of these.
Output is leveled to the same loudness for every voice, and pauses longer than half a second inside a take are shortened.
Phone mode changes the channel, not the speaking style: the model does not yet choose call-style delivery (turn-taking, backchannels) on request. See What's next.
What's next
Hurston-1 is the first step. What we are building toward:
Telephony-native TTS. A model that learns to talk like a person on a call, not just sound like the phone line: a call style distinct from reading style, with natural turn-taking, "mm-hm"s and call pacing, learned from our recordings of real people talking with full-duplex AI agents.
Consistent voices. The same named voice across every call and every sentence, for agents and brands.
Follow Destined AI on Hugging Face for the next release.
Responsible use
Do not use Hurston-1 to impersonate real people, deceive listeners, or commit fraud. Tell listeners when speech is synthetic. Audio in demo/ is synthetic.
Credits and licenses
Model weights: Apache-2.0, derived from Maya1 by Maya Research (Apache-2.0).
Audio codec: SNAC 24 kHz by Hubert Siuzdak (MIT), downloaded at run time. Phone mode uses ITU-T G.711 (public standard).
Optional checking: Whisper large-v3-turbo by OpenAI (MIT) and ECAPA speaker embeddings from SpeechBrain (Apache-2.0), downloaded at run time.
Training data: LibriTTS-R (Koizumi et al., 2023; CC BY 4.0), Mozilla Common Voice (CC0), and Destined AI's own corpus.

title: Learn or teach a language from TV shows, movies and podcasts with AI — RainbowSay
content:
LET ALL YOUR SENSES LIGHT UP
Learn
a language
from the
shows
you already love.
RainbowSay listens along with your favorite series, videos and podcasts. It pauses at the end of each sentence and shows you what was just said — translation, vocabulary, grammar. Real voices, real pace, one sentence at a time.
Download for macOS
macOS 14.2+ · Apple Silicon
See how it works
Free to start · no credit card
Listens to audio only — never records your screen
Animated demo of a Listening session. A Korean drama plays in a video player while the app’s overlay transcribes a line of dialogue: “있잖아, 행복은 가끔 그냥 햇살 아래 커피 한 잔이야.” At the end of the sentence the app pauses the video and shows a card with the translation — “You know, happiness is sometimes just a cup of coffee in the sun.” — a vocabulary list with romanized readings (있잖아, itjana, you know; 행복, haengbok, happiness; 가끔, gakkeum, sometimes; 그냥, geunyang, just; 햇살 아래, haetsal arae, in the sunshine; 커피 한 잔, keopi han jan, a cup of coffee) and a grammar note on the casual ending 이야. The original is replayed with a word-by-word highlight, the question “Why 행복은 and not 행복이?” is answered in a chat panel (은/는 marks the topic), and pressing Continue resumes the video.
The app’s real interface, animated: the video plays, the app hears a sentence end, pauses the player and unpacks the sentence.
THE IDEA
The world is filled with beautiful stories. Let them teach you.
Textbook dialogues don’t sound like anyone you know. The people in your favorite drama do. They mumble, joke, interrupt each other and fall in love — at their real pace. That is the language you actually want.
So why not use a large language model to learn or teach a language — literally? RainbowSay lets AI do the research on every sentence, automatically, while native speakers set the rhythm.

THREE WAYS TO PRACTICE, TEACH, CREATE
Let all your senses light up.
Ears, mouth, eyes. Each has its own kind of session — and its own color, in the app and on this page.
Listening
Speaking
Subtitles
LISTENING · EARS
Learn & teach from the infinite voices of humans, from all walks of life.
Play anything — a series, a vlog, a podcast, a lecture. RainbowSay hears it, pauses the player when a sentence ends, and hands you that sentence, unpacked. Press Continue and the story goes on.
It pauses for you. The video stops at the end of each sentence, so you’re never chasing the dialogue.
Every sentence, unpacked. Translation, vocabulary with readings, and the grammar that holds it together.
Hear it again. Replay the original or the spoken translation with a word-by-word highlight — and set the pace of the voice, from half speed up.
Ask anything. Open a chat about the sentence: why this tense, what that idiom really means.
Works with any app that plays sound on your Mac — all of it, or just the one you pick.
Read the Listening guide
Animated demo of the card the app shows when it pauses a video at the end of a sentence. The French sentence “Tu sais, le bonheur, c’est parfois juste un café au soleil.” is translated as “You know, happiness is sometimes just a coffee in the sun.” Vocabulary: Tu sais, you know (informal); le bonheur, happiness; parfois, sometimes; au soleil, in the sun. A grammar note explains that spoken French names the topic first (le bonheur) and picks it up again with c’est. The Original button is pressed and the French sentence is highlighted word by word as it plays; then the Translation button does the same for the English sentence. Pointing at the vocabulary entry “le bonheur” highlights it in the sentence, and “happiness” in the translation.
One sentence, unpacked — the app’s real card, replaying the original and the translation word by word.
SPEAKING · MOUTH
Your voice matters. Speak up.
Understanding is half of a language. The other half is you, out loud. Say a sentence in the language you’re learning, and a patient coach tells you how it came across: what it meant, every word you used, and the one thing worth fixing.
See that it came across. Your sentence is written out as it was heard, then translated back into your own language — aloud and on the card. Is that what you meant?
One gentle correction. Not a wall of red ink: the single most important fix, with the corrected phrase. Nothing to fix? It names the pattern you used best.
Every word you used. Your own sentence, glossed word by word. Replay yourself next to the translation, then ask the chat why — that preposition, that tense, how a native speaker would put it.
Push-to-talk or hands-free. Hold space or the mic button while you speak — or let the app hear where each sentence ends. Any microphone, with noise reduction for a laptop mic or a headset.
Read the Speaking guide
Animated demo of a Speaking session in push-to-talk mode: an English speaker practicing Spanish — drawn as a woman at her desk speaking into a microphone, next to the app. While the round microphone button is held, a level meter follows her voice and the learner’s Spanish sentence is written out as it was heard: “¿Podemos tener una mesa para dos cerca a la ventana?” On release the app speaks and shows what that meant in English — “Can we have a table for two near the window?” — so the learner can check it came across. The card then lists every word they used (Podemos, tener, una mesa, para dos, cerca, la ventana) and gives one correction: “cerca de la ventana” — “cerca” takes “de”, not “a” — with a more natural way to ask, “¿Nos da una mesa para dos?” The learner replays their own sentence with a word-by-word highlight, then asks in the chat, “Why «de» and not «a»?”, and gets a short explanation.
SUBTITLES · EYES + EARS
Read along, live.
Subtitles floats transparent, always-on-top captions over any video or call: the original words and their translation, streaming as they’re spoken. Nothing pauses.
Several languages at once. The original line plus up to three translations, side by side. The spoken language is detected for you.
A color for every language. Give each one its own text and background color, size and width.
Put them anywhere. Pop a language into its own window and drag it where you like on the screen.
Study it later. Sessions are saved as a timeline with audio — replay any line, in any language.
Read the Subtitles guide
Animated demo of a Subtitles session. A Japanese food vlog plays in a video player while a transparent caption window over the lower part of the video streams three lines word by word: the original Japanese, English and Spanish. The speaker says “今日は大阪の商店街に来ています。” (“Today we’re at a shopping street in Osaka.” / “Hoy estamos en una calle comercial de Osaka.”), then “このたこ焼き、外はカリカリで中はとろとろです。” (“These takoyaki are crispy outside and gooey inside.”), then “熱いうちに食べるのが一番ですね。” (“They’re best eaten while they’re still hot.”). Finished sentences move up to a dimmed line as the next one starts. The app’s overlay lists the two translated lanes, English and Spanish, as live; it is then closed with its close button and the subtitles keep running over the video.
SUBTITLES · FROM YOUR MICROPHONE
Translate for your audience, live.
Subtitles can listen to you instead of your Mac. Choose Microphone as the source, speak the way you always do, and everyone in the room — or on the stream — reads along in their own language.
Teach in your own words. Explain, give instructions, tell the story: what you say appears on the projector as you say it, with its translation underneath.
One room, several languages. Up to three translations at once, each in its own color — or its own window, on the screen that needs it.
Any microphone. Laptop, headset or lapel: pick it from the list, with noise reduction to match the room.
Captions for what you create. Record your screen with the captions on it, or export the saved session as an SRT file, timed to your voice.
How to caption your own voice
Animated demo of a Subtitles session that listens to the microphone instead of the computer’s sound. A teacher — drawn at a lectern with a microphone, beside a projected screen with a diagram of the water cycle, her class in front — speaks English. A transparent caption window over the lower part of the projected screen streams three lines word by word: what she says, Spanish and Chinese. She says “Good morning, everyone. Today we’re talking about the water cycle.” (“Buenos días a todos. Hoy vamos a hablar del ciclo del agua.” / “大家早上好。今天我们来讲水循环。”), then “The sun warms the sea, and water rises into the air as vapor.” (“El sol calienta el mar y el agua sube al aire en forma de vapor.”), then “High up, it cools into clouds and falls back down as rain.” (“En lo alto se enfría, forma nubes y vuelve a caer como lluvia.”). Finished sentences move up to a dimmed line as the next one starts, and a waveform on the lectern follows her voice. The app’s overlay reads “Listening to: System default microphone” and lists the two translated lanes, Spanish and Chinese, as live. She then closes the overlay with its close button: the panel disappears, and the subtitles keep running over her slide.
WHO IT’S FOR
Learn, teach, create — in real time.
RainbowSay is for people who spend real hours with a language, and would like those hours to be the fun ones.
STUDENTS
Turn tonight’s episode into homework you actually want to do.
Watch what you would watch anyway. Every sentence becomes a small lesson, with the vocabulary and grammar already looked up.
Say it out loud before the oral exam, the trip, the first date — and get one gentle correction each time.
A streak and a heatmap that show the hours quietly adding up.
TEACHERS
Bring the real language into the room.
Teach from authentic material — news, interviews, films — and pause on exactly the sentence you want to talk about.
Live subtitles in up to three languages at once — of what you play, or of what you say into the microphone — for a classroom that doesn’t share one.
Saved sessions become lesson material: the sentences, the vocabulary, the audio.
CREATORS
Create language content, without the editing marathon.
Play your footage and each sentence arrives unpacked — translation, vocabulary with readings, a grammar note. The word-by-word overlay your viewers pause for, ready to screen-record.
Live transcription and two-language captions over any video — or over your own voice, from the microphone — in your colors, size and position.
Every session is saved: copy the transcript into your script, or export subtitles as SRT, timed as spoken or aligned to the original.
Studying, teaching or creating? Write to support@rainbowsay.ai from your school address, or with a link to your public profile, and we’ll add extra free credit — so you can take your time before deciding on a plan.
STUDY HISTORY
Everything you learn, kept.
A sentence you understood at 11 pm shouldn’t be gone by morning. Every session is saved on your Mac, ready to replay — and the quiet evenings add up to something you can see.

Yours to keep — or delete

HOW IT WORKS
Three steps. Then just press play.
1
Download and sign in
Install RainbowSay on your Mac and sign in with Google. No API keys, no setup — free starter credit is already waiting.
2
Play anything — or speak
Start a series, a video, a podcast, a call. Pick Listening or Subtitles from the menu bar, or choose Speaking and use your microphone.
3
Learn sentence by sentence
The player pauses at the end of each sentence. Read it, hear it again, ask about it, press Continue. The story goes on, and so do you.
PRIVATE BY DESIGN, HONEST ABOUT THE REST
Audio only. Never your screen.
RainbowSay taps the sound your Mac is playing. macOS asks you for “System Audio Recording Only” — the app has no screen recording at all.
Your history stays on your Mac.
Sentences, audio clips, chats and subtitle timelines are saved locally. Our servers see how much you used — not what you watched or said.
The AI does hear the audio.
To transcribe and translate, the audio of a running session is sent to our AI provider, OpenAI. That is how the magic works, so we’d rather say it plainly.
Runs on Apple Silicon Macs with macOS 14.2 or later.
PRICING
Start free. Stay for the habit.
One allowance, shared by Listening, Speaking and Subtitles. Pay yearly and two months are on us.
FREE

Fair questions, plain answers.
Something else on your mind? Write to support@rainbowsay.ai — a person answers.

You have a right to know who's recording you when you leave home, especially when a private company controls the data and it's unclear how law enforcement uses that information. This map lets you search by ZIP code to see where Flock's license plate readers are located. Use it, make informed decisions about how you move through your own area and whether you need to reach out to your municipal leaders.
What a Flock camera records
A Flock camera photographs each vehicle that passes it, whether or not the driver is suspected of anything. It logs the plate, time, and location. Flock's Vehicle Fingerprint feature also records the make, model, and color, plus details like dents and bumper stickers, so a car can be found even without a readable plate.
Those records go into Flock's cloud, where police departments can search them and share them with other agencies across city and state lines. Flock says its network processes more than 20 billion vehicle reads a month across 49 states.
That kind of broad access leaves much room for misuse and abuse. A Washington Post review found at least 50 officers accused or charged with misusing license plate readers, often to follow people in their personal lives; Flock's system was involved in 46 of those cases. We asked Flock's CEO, Garrett Langley, how the company responds to misuse and who controls the data its devices collect.
Where the Flock map data comes from
The device locations on this Flock camera map come from independent research by cybersecurity researcher Joshua Michael
(new window)
. We don't host or distribute the underlying dataset.
In November 2025, Michael found that Flock's servers publicly exposed an access token anyone could obtain without logging in. He reported the issue to Flock, then published his findings and his own map in December. His inventory lists more than 170,000 cameras and over 130,000 other Flock devices. Flock has publicly cited around 120,000 cameras, so the actual camera count is about 40% higher.

title: Removing Next.js Got My Blog to 100 on Every Lighthouse Category
content:
Removing Next.js Got My Blog to 100 on Every Lighthouse Category
K
korindiehacker
Author
2026-10-26
8 min read
English
My blog just scored a perfect 100 on every Lighthouse category. I love blogging. I wanted to build a blog that’s light, fast, free of clutter, able to run multiple blogs, and fully accessible on top of that. And finally, at long last, I’ve more or less pulled it off. It was quite a tedious process. Ugh… and I even had to remove Next.js, the framework I’d been using most. It was far, far more painful than I expected. I’d like to share the journey of improving performance while building this blog.
Why did I decide to build my own blog?
When you think of blogs, a few names come to mind. Medium, Blogger, Ghost… But none of them satisfied me. Medium and Blogger are bloated with features, and their actual performance wasn’t satisfying either.
Blogger
Medium
Truly horrifying.
Hmm…… And there was another problem: it’s a hassle to work directly with the markup and raw code we all love (Markdown, HTML, CSS).
For the record, all performance measurements were taken with pagespeed.web.dev.
Of course, there are plenty of alternatives: WordPress, Ghost, Hugo. I didn’t like WordPress’s plugin hell. Ghost has to be self-hosted (there’s ghost.org too, but it’s way too expensive…), and every version upgrade broke something in the editor, so keeping it up to date was a chore. Hugo is the best of the bunch, but in the end, setting it up is still a hassle. Looking back, I guess what I really wanted was SaaS.
The one I liked most was Bear Blog. Great performance. I love its product philosophy, too. But its extreme minimalism was a downside for me. The editor UX didn’t work for me, either.
If it at least let me add AdSense and attach images for free, I probably would’ve just used Bear Blog.
As fast as Bear Blog, but with a bit more functionality and better usability. That’s the blog I wanted to build. Oh, and if you’re curious, you can check it out at bloffy.co.
Anyway. Enough about me. Let me share how I actually improved the performance.
Let’s hit 100 on Lighthouse Performance.
Obviously, caching is a must.
It goes without saying that caching is essential. Get caching right and performance improves dramatically. And Next.js makes caching really convenient. There’s ISR, and it also extends fetch with a next option for caching. Handy. Using these well alone gets you a long way on performance.
Unfortunately, though, our site can be reached from anywhere in the world. Why is that unfortunate? Within the same region, caching makes things fast, but visitors from other regions still end up eating the network latency.
No, silly. That’s what a CDN is for.
Yes. That’s why we use a CDN. And if you deploy a Next.js app to Vercel, you get a CDN out of the box. I don’t dislike Vercel; it’s incredibly convenient. But the Pro plan is pricey right from the start, there’s the serverless cold start problem, and the dependency on the Vercel ecosystem isn’t something you can ignore either.
So why not use a different CDN service? Cloudflare, for example. I honestly think Cloudflare is a genuinely nice company. You can run large-scale infrastructure and most apps on it for free. But then I figured I didn’t really need Next.js’s caching anymore. Having to invalidate two caches every time I publish a post makes things a pain to manage.
In short, for a static website, I figured a CDN alone is enough. And that’s reason number one why I didn’t need Next.js.
Image optimization.
Images these days run over 10MB. Serve those on the web as-is and your performance will go completely off the rails.
Optimizing images is quite a hassle. You have to resize per device, compress, and then handle the CDN on top of that. On a previous project, I had a serverless function (AWS Lambda) compress and resize images whenever one landed in storage (S3), and I put CloudFront in front as the CDN. It was a pretty reasonable setup for tailoring things exactly the way I wanted. But it’s also a setup that needs a fair amount of upkeep.
So this time I went with Cloudflare’s Image Transformations. Even on the free tier you get 5,000 images, so I use it without a second thought.
At this point I sound like a Cloudflare sales rep. I’m just an ordinary solo developer.
Ta-da. Here’s the Next.js blog’s performance after all that caching and image optimization.
For reference, this was Next.js 16.1.6.
Pretty high scores. But this isn’t enough. We want 100. A clean, no-asterisks 100. So I dug into what the problem was.
It said a substantial amount of legacy JavaScript was found, and it wasn’t code I wrote. It came from the framework runtime that Next.js ships in its bundle.
But this page is a static page with zero interaction. Every page is pre-rendered with ISR, and I thought I’d followed the Next.js guidelines well. So as an experiment, I ripped out every client component the app had, left only server components, and measured again. The score didn’t budge.
At first I suspected hydration, but once I dug in, the problem wasn’t hydration alone. The cause was the client runtime that Next.js always ships, even for static pages. Even with only server components, the runtime chunks, hydration, and the RSC payload for the router all stay. That’s because next/link and next/image are themselves client components ('use client'), so having just those two is enough to pull in the runtime and trigger hydration.
So what if I strip out next/link and next/image too? The App Router’s own runtime, the router and error boundaries, still remains. There’s no official way to get it down to zero; the only option was a hack: stripping the scripts out of the rendered HTML. That’s when it hit me: “If I’m going to do that, why am I even using Next.js?”
And then, the unused code.
You can see that the bulk of the JavaScript is code that isn’t needed. Unused code alone comes to 230,460 bytes. That’s not good. Most static websites don’t need JavaScript at all. Unused JavaScript is needed even less.
This is where I really agonized. Is dropping Next.js for the sake of 100 points the right call? I’d spent a lot of time building the public-facing web app.
Let’s remove Next.js.
In the end, for the quality of the blog (even if it’s just 5 points), I decided to rip Next.js out entirely. My judgment was that I wouldn’t need Next.js’s excess features in the long run either. I considered going fully vanilla, but I didn’t want to give up the productivity and infrastructure benefits of a framework. I needed to find the right one.
I chose Hono. I liked its technical philosophy. “Fast and simple” was exactly the solution I needed most, and JSX support was a bonus. The migration cost didn’t look too big, either.
Ta-da. Finally, 100.
Tada. And just like that, 100 across the board. Go ahead and run the very page you’re reading right now through pagespeed.web.dev.
There’s no JavaScript, and unused code dropped sharply to 407 bytes. As a bonus, build time went down by about 40% too.
Oh, why is SEO at 69? That site was built for testing, and it deliberately blocks search indexing. That’s why it’s 69.
By the way, if you score 100 on everything in DevTools, Lighthouse actually sets off fireworks for you. 🎉🎉
Hono vs. Next.js Performance
Next.js Performance (server components only)
Hono Performance
The long task that runs before anything is rendered on screen took 309.3ms on Next.js, and when I built the same page with Hono, it took 68.01ms. That’s roughly a 78% improvement.
Does your static site really need Next.js?
Is a JS payload, hydration included, really doing a static site any good? I don’t think so. It leaves behind unnecessary JavaScript, so in most cases I think it’s simply not needed.
That said, for an interaction-heavy app, I think Next.js can be a great framework. In fact, the management app for this very blog is built with Next.js!

title: G-Diffuser on 3DS
content:
01 · OVERVIEW
F-ZERO X ON 3DS — OLD AND NEW, NATIVE, WITH THE 64DD EXPANSION KIT
A post-mortem of porting G-Diffuser, the F-Zero X decompilation, to the Nintendo 3DS — v1.0.0, covering both the original 24-day sprint that put it on a New 3DS at 60 fps in 3D (2026-08-11 to 09-03) and the 43-day second phase that added Old 3DS support, a native renderer, and the Expansion Kit (2026-09-07 to 10-19). One person directed throughout; one long-lived Claude session orchestrated; 147 subagents built the first phase and many more carried the second.
The console went from a black screen to a native-60 stereoscopic racer, then from a New-3DS-only build to a four-way release covering both consoles with and without the 64DD expansion.
59.6fps
median on hardware, full Grand Prix, New 3DS, end of the first phase (from 12–20 fps in the first emulator race)
51.4fps
tenth-percentile floor in 30-machine crowds, first phase (from 25–35)
53%
of frames at the 60 cap, first phase (from 14% one week earlier)
15
active days across the first phase's 24 calendar days, three pauses when the weekly plan allowance ran out
3.17 B
tokens across all sessions and agents, first phase only; see Cost
$4,974
at published API list prices (Fable $10/$50 per MTok, 1-hour cache writes), first phase only; see Cost
250
commits touching the 3DS port in the first phase, frozen 2026-10-08 from the v0.9.0 docs — not re-verified against final history
15,039
lines under port/3ds plus 48 pure-delta patches, first-phase count
WHAT V1.0.0 ADDED
3
released console builds from one source tree: Old 3DS, New 3DS, and New 3DS with the Expansion Kit
199
internal progress notes written during the second phase
43days
calendar span of the second phase, 2026-09-07 to 10-19 inclusive
The tiles above are dated. The first phase's hardware numbers and token/cost figures were measured through 2026-09-03 and have not been re-run for v1.0.0; the Agentic workflow page describes how the second phase was run, and the Cost page is explicit about what it does and does not price.
ON HARDWARE
v1.0, New 3DS: the Expansion Kit's Select Mode (COURSE EDIT, CREATE MACHINE); the bottom screen is DASH's idle view.
v1.0, New 3DS, mid-race: DASH on the bottom screen with energy, position, lap times and the course map.
The clips and photos below are from v0.9 (2026-09), before DASH replaced the debug console on the bottom screen.
open clip
v0.9: Grand Prix on a New 3DS. The bottom screen is the port's debug menu: 59.8 fps, heap, build id.
open clip
v0.9: handheld, mid-race. Native 60 Hz pacing; no interpolation.
Title screen, launched from the Homebrew Launcher (.3dsx).
Select Mode.
Select Machine.
Blue Falcon.
WHAT WAS BUILT
Three released console builds from one source tree, all booting from the HOME menu (.cia) or the homebrew launcher (.3dsx): the base game for Old 3DS / 2DS and for New 3DS / New 2DS XL, and a New 3DS build with the 64DD Expansion Kit (course editor and machine creator, playable with a user-supplied disk image). Every build reads prebaked asset archives from the SD card — no ROM or disk image ever ships with the game.
They play the whole game: Grand Prix, Time Trial, Practice, Death Race, and the machine editor screens, with music and effects on the real DSP, stereoscopic 3D on the slider, a bottom-screen dashboard with three HUD layouts and an idle view outside races, and clean HOME suspend, resume, close, lid sleep and power-off. The New 3DS build keeps the native-60 frame pacing the first phase reached; the Old 3DS build gets to a comparable result by a different route. At v1.0.0, with no ini, both builds default to that same route: the native renderer ([perf] preset = auto). The New 3DS's first-phase render-thread/per-draw-stereo path is still built in and reachable with an explicit ini, but is no longer the default — see Frontier and Pushing the boundaries for the two builds compared side by side.
The stack
decomp: the F-Zero X decompilation (inspectredc/fzerox), untouched upstream, plus a patch stack.
libultraship: the N64 runtime (Kenix3), untouched upstream, including a 13-line newlib fix that lets it build on devkitARM; it still draws every menu and non-race screen.
port/3ds: 15,039 lines as of the first phase, since grown: a citro3d rendering backend, stereo, audio, input, menu, lifecycle, render thread, profilers, packaging.
the native renderer (added in the second phase): an owned interpreter that skips the per-frame display-list walk for race geometry, and is the v1.0.0 default on both consoles — see Frontier for how, and why it is what lets the Old 3DS keep up.
The headline numbers on hardware, first phase (New 3DS)
WHEN MEDIAN P10 AT CAP
08-14 first race (emulator) 12–20 – –
08-21 first hardware run 48–50 – –
08-28 release-grade build ~51 ~40 (crowds, MINIMAL) –
09-02 Round 1: Mainline before the campaign 51.3 39.2 9%
09-02 Round 2: Bridge memos (brfast) 57.2 46.6 29%
09-02 Round 3: HUD atlas · triangle memo · TMEM · audio 56.0 48.0 32%
09-02 Round 4: Render thread on core 2 (pipe) 57.6 44.6 14%
09-03 Round 5: Ahead mode · bridge on main · auto rival detail 59.6 51.4 53%
THE FIRST PHASE IN FIVE LINES
08-11 → 08-14: from research to a race. Feasibility dossier, plan for a team of agents, five parallel foundation streams, six boot bugs, first race at 12–20 fps in the emulator.
08-20 → 08-22: from pink to playable, then to a real console. Fog, HUD, livery, shadow, sky fixed; the loadblock discovery took menus from 27 to 60 fps; first hardware run 08-21 ("wow it runs amazing"); audio the same evening.
08-27 → 08-28: product grade. Five-agent fleet drop, stereo armed, touch menu, rival detail, GPU vertex-transform moonshot built and shelved, README with legal notice, release package.
09-01 → 09-02: lifecycle and the last big lever. HOME crash and close-from-HOME hang fixed; a bridge output cache proven a NO-GO and replaced by memoizing each sub-display-list's classification instead of re-scanning it every frame; LOCKED-60 campaign launched with four parallel levers.
09-02 → 09-03: multi-core. Render thread on core 2, one-frame-ahead mode, bridge on main, auto LOD; median 59.6 with 53% of frames at cap; crash fixed; viewport placement fixed; stereo markers anchored.
THE SECOND PHASE IN SIX LINES
Not originally planned; it ran 09-07 to 10-19, 43 calendar days.
09-07 → 09-29: scoping, then making it fit. The Old 3DS milestone, previously written off, was restarted; parallel agents fit the build into its 64 MB app region (the RDRAM arena halved, audio streamed instead of resident, texture uploads capped); on 2026-09-29, in the first hardware session on a real Old 3DS, the shipped (New-3DS-era, 16 MiB RDRAM) build died at boot while the -DGDX_3DS_O3DS=ON profile, built to fit the console's memory grant, booted and raced the same session at about 10 fps.
09-29 → 09-30: finding the real costs. A narrowed audio lock cut the race-wall wait on the Old 3DS by about 20 ms a frame; frame skipping ended the game's accidental slow motion; a first retained-mode renderer won big in the emulator and barely moved the number on hardware.
09-30 → 10-01: the probe that changed the plan. Hardware performance counters showed the real limit was instruction-cache misses, not instruction count. A pose-replay fallback was built and worked, then was set aside on the user's call: "we should go for a real 60! i still believe it has to be possible."
10-01 → 10-02: the native renderer. Rebuilt around the cache instead of around instruction counts, one small loop per race category, sized to fit the 16 KB instruction cache. Median frame time on a 2D Grand Prix race reached 16.5 ms.
10-03 → 10-08: 3D at 60, on the Old 3DS too. A per-eye resubmit with its own swap-pacing mode reached 59–60 fps in 3D on most Grand Prix courses; the heaviest courses (Silence, Sand Ocean) can still trip the frame-skip safety net to a steady 30 fps mid-race.
10-08 → 10-19: the Expansion Kit, a dashboard, and release. The 64DD Expansion Kit verified tick-for-tick identical under the native renderer and booted on the Old 3DS, which then proved too slow to release it on; the bottom-screen DASH shipped; a standing adversarial review audited the merged result before the v1.0.0 release.
See Agentic workflow for how the second phase was run and Old 3DS for the full campaign, card by card.
READ ON

title: Overgrown, when plants invade your abandoned tabs | Charlie Gerard | Senior research engineer & Creative Technologist Charlie Gerard | Senior research engineer & Creative Technologist
content:
Charlie Gerard
Projects
Speaking
Blog
Overgrown, when plants invade your abandoned tabs
20/10/2026
I was doing a little creative exercise the other day around the word "Overgrowth". The first thing that came to mind was an apocalyptic scene, something like The Walking Dead or The Last of Us, where plants tend to overgrow abandoned buildings.
I then wanted to apply this idea to the digital world, and the word "abandoned" made me think of my browser tabs... What if my tabs were slowly taken over by plants the longer I left them unread? What if I had to clear away these invasive plants to access my tabs again? A bit like trying to open a door that's been overgrown...
So I built this fun little Chrome extension that does just that. It won't necessarily make me read my tabs more but it's ok.
Demo
Link to the repository
The idea
Every tab has a neglect clock. It runs while the tab is out of view and stops while you're looking at it.
The longer a tab is neglected, the more plants grow over it, from the edges towards the middle.
Once a tab is more than 5% overgrown, the page behind the vines is walled off: you can scroll, but you can't click, select or drag anything.
To free it, you have to slash through the vines by dragging your mouse across them. Get it down to 5% and the last bits fall off. If you abandon your tab once more, the jungle starts growing again.
Just for fun, you can pick your weapon of choice between the rusty machete, the chainsaw and the flamethrower.
You can also change how long it takes for your tabs to be fully overgrown.
Originally, I was thinking about blocking users from closing their overgrown tabs until they slash all plants, but I thought it would be too annoying... 😅
The extension
The code is organised in 3 main parts: the background logic, the content script to display the plants and animation on the tabs and the popup folder that handles the UI of the extension itself.
Background worker
The background.js file starts the jungle on each open tab and forgets it when it closes.
The popup
This folder handles the UI for the extension with some small components for the time setting, the weapon choice, the list of tabs and their current stat.
The overlay
The content folder contains the SVGs for the plants and the weapons, the logic to position and grow the clusters, the neglect clock and the sounds.
I've been wanting to get back into building things for a while now and this project felt like a small, fun way to start. I'm writing this on a new computer so I currently "only" have 22 tabs open but 14 of them are already completely overgrown... 😂 It might not make me read them more but slashing through the vines makes coming back to them more fun! 🪚🌿

title: [2512.19428] Attention Is Not What You Need
content:
Computer Science > Machine Learning
[Submitted on 22 Dec 2025]
Attention Is Not What You Need
Zhang Chong
We revisit a basic question in sequence modeling: is explicit self-attention actually necessary for strong performance and reasoning? We argue that standard multi-head attention is best seen as a form of tensor lifting: hidden vectors are mapped into a high-dimensional space of pairwise interactions, and learning proceeds by constraining this lifted tensor through gradient descent. This mechanism is extremely expressive but mathematically opaque, because after many layers it becomes very hard to describe the model with a small family of explicit invariants.
To explore an alternative, we propose an attention-free architecture based on Grassmann flows. Instead of forming an L by L attention matrix, our Causal Grassmann layer (i) linearly reduces token states, (ii) encodes local token pairs as two-dimensional subspaces on a Grassmann manifold via Plucker coordinates, and (iii) fuses these geometric features back into the hidden states through gated mixing. Information therefore propagates by controlled deformations of low-rank subspaces over multi-scale local windows, so the core computation lives on a finite-dimensional manifold rather than in an unstructured tensor space.
On the Wikitext-2 language modeling benchmark, purely Grassmann-based models with 13 to 18 million parameters achieve validation perplexities within about 10 to 15 percent of size-matched Transformers. On the SNLI natural language inference task, a Grassmann-Plucker head on top of DistilBERT slightly outperforms a Transformer head, with best validation and test accuracies of 0.8550 and 0.8538 compared to 0.8545 and 0.8511. We analyze the complexity of Grassmann mixing, show linear scaling in sequence length for fixed rank, and argue that such manifold-based designs offer a more structured route toward geometric and invariant-based interpretations of neural reasoning.
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Algebraic Geometry (math.AG)

title: Alfie John > Why I am a programmer
content:
Why I am a programmer
There they sit, the preschooler class encircling their mentor, the substitute teacher.
"Now class, today we will talk about what you want to be when you grow up. Isn't that fun?"
The teacher looks around and spots the child, silent, apart from the others and deep in thought.
"Jonny, why don't you start?"
she encourages him. Jonny looks around, confused, his train of thought disrupted. He collects himself, and stares at the teacher with a steady eye.
"I want to code demos,"
he says, his words becoming stronger and more confidant as he speaks.
"I want to write something that will change peoples perception of reality. I want them to walk away from the computer dazed, unsure of their footing and eyesight. I want to write something that will reach out of the screen and grab them, making heartbeats and breathing slow to almost a halt. I want to write something that, when it is finished, they are reluctant to leave, knowing that nothing they experience that day will be quite as real, as insightful, as good. I want to write demos."
Silence. The class and the teacher stare at Jonny, stunned. It is the teachers turn to be confused. Jonny blushes, feeling that something more is required.
"Either that or I want to be a fireman."
  -- Denthor of ASPHYXIA (aka Grant Smith), TUT7.TXT (1993)
In the Beginning...
I grew up in a pre-mainstream Internet world. A time when only a handful of kids at my primary school had a computer. We lived in a rough neighbourhood and so having a computer meant that you were a target for robbery. As we all knew somebody who had their computer stolen at least once, having a computer was kept on the low down. But we still found each other. Each time word got out that some kid got a new computer, they was suspiciously quizzed before being let into our digital posse.
A lot of my childhood was spend living indoors behind a buzzing 14" CRT, pirating games with other kids via 3.5" single-density floppies with their corners drilled out, and once in a while even playing them. But I was more of a collector than gamer. Like Ash from Pokemon - got to catch them all. And the people who created computer games were my idols. I was always in awe of what they could do with that big, heavy, beige box under the table.
One day word spread that there was a way to edit saved game files via XTreeGold's Hex View that gave you unlimited lives and allowed you to skip stages. With each new game that came out, the race was on to see who could be the first to flip the right bits to get the powerups. It was seriously heart pumping. Although only tinkering, it felt like we were our own gods.
We bought a modem a few years later and soon after got a copy of The Australian BBS Listing - a textfile containing most of the publically accessible BBSes online. I dialed every one of them (but that's for another blog post). It opened up a whole new world to explore. Instead of just a handful of kids pirating games via Sneakernet, I was connected to the digital underground - a world where anything digital was within reach (some even had Internet gateways). Even the newest blockbusters that I had only read about in PC Zone magazine were all there for me to leech. All of them, soon slowly trickling down the wire via ZMODEM.
But there was something different with these BBS downloaded games. Not something bad, but something exciting. Each time these games were run, it was like a short commercial was played before the title screen. Now I'm not talking about commercials selling steak knives. Instead, these were brazen posters screaming fuck you by the people who had managed to crack the game's copy protection code and were now distributing the game illegally for free. I later found out that these commercials were called cracktros. The precursor to demos and what started the whole demoscene. But simply calling them demos just doesn't give them justice. They were more of an out of body experience. Sensory overload. Like what you would feel at 2am, half tipsy, half asleep and being woken up stunned as you stare at a late 90s acid hard trance film clip, feeling it inject directly into your cerebral cortex. Once it finished playing, you were frozen. Still unsure whether you saw something real or just imagined it all. The only thing you were sure of, was that it was awesome.
Then one day while browsing the file section of some random BBS, I stumbed onto a file innocently called TUT1-9.ZIP. It's FILE_ID.DIZ caught my attention:
    +----------------------------+
    |     The ASPHYXIA VGA       |
    |   DEMO TRAINER SERIES!     |
    |                            |
    |   By Denthor of ASPHYXIA   |
    |                            |
    |    Documentation on how    |
    |  to code demo like effects |
    |         in TP6/7!          |
    |                            |
    |Full Pascal source included!|
    |                            |
    |    From putting a pixel    |
    |  to sprites and animation  |
    |  to wireframe 3D to solid  |
    |            3D!             |
    |                            |
    |       Get it now!          |
    +----------------------------+
How to code demo like effects? You mean I too could be one of those sorcerers that had the computer under their complete control!? My heart raced as I added it to the download queue, fired up the aging Epsom LQ-300, then covered me ears as its loud ink needles hit the blue and white computer paper.
I didn't know anything about programming but I was completely estatic with the potential. I followed along with Denthor's tutorials as much as I could, typed everything out and hoped that Borland's Turbo Pascal 6.0 wouldn't laugh at me too much. It only gave me a basic understanding of how all the pieces to the puzzle fit together, but it was enough to whet my appetite and crave for more. I wasn't even into my teens yet but I definitely knew at the time that I didn't want to watch demos or play computer games anymore. I wanted to make them. I wanted to be elite. I wanted to be a programmer.

SYSTEMS
IBM CEO says open weight models are now irresistibly good and cheap on-prem
90 percent of the performance at ten percent of the price, in just two or three racks, is hard to beat
Simon Sharwood
APAC EDITOR
33
Published Thu 22 Oct 2026 // 04:26 UTC
Make us preferred on Google
READ MORE
After threatening AI export bans, China allows DeepSeek to keep selling
now
Autonomous attack agent in 'Skynet mode' hijacks other models to carry out its evil deeds
1 day ago
OpenAI disables internet access during model training while Anthropic issues another mea culpa
2 days ago
Red-team report found OpenAI utterly failed to monitor its agents during Hugging Face attack
2 days ago
AI models describe humans as a bunch of amoral sheep
2 days ago
IBM CEO Arvind Krishna has told investors that open weight models now make brilliant sense for on-prem enterprise use.
Speaking on the company’s Q3 earnings call, Krishna said that in 2024 closed frontier models were plainly superior to open alternatives.
“If you ran some assessment, some benchmark, and it was broad-based, not narrow, the top model might score a 70, and the open model might score a 20 or a 30.”
“In late 2025, we began to see that gap shrink, where maybe the gap was not 70 to 20 or 30, it was 70 to 50,” he continued.
The CEO said open weight models currently deliver “anywhere from 25 percent to 10 percent of the token cost of the frontier models. That is very attractive given that they’re now 90 percent as effective.”
“It’s a simple question for any enterprise. Would you like something that’s 10 percent of the cost if it’s 90 percent as good as the best, or do you want to pay that 10 times higher cost?”
Krishna thinks businesses will most often choose not to incur the higher costs.
“Then the question is: how many tasks require that? I would tell you some do, but the vast majority, summarizing an email, examining a contract, answering a customer call, composing an email, all of those can be done as well with the much cheaper answer.”
The CEO said those numbers mean IBM is seeing booming interest in on-prem AI infrastructure. While he thinks most businesses can build useful AI infrastructure in just two or three racks, he feels many will struggle to get it running.
“The question becomes: how do you do that?” he said. “The question that the enterprise struggles with is: ‘Where are my kernel engineers? Where are the people who worry about the underlying network? Who can make sure that the model is clustered on GPUs that are close to each other in network proximity? Who can make sure that you’re doing the right caching of results so you get an incredible response?’”
He didn’t have answers, other than to say IBM will produce software that eases AI deployments. Krishna also predicted demand for on-prem AI will spur sales of Big Blue’s Spyre mainframe accelerator cards.
The CEO said current-gen z17 mainframes have delivered $1bn more revenue than any previous model, and said Big Blue’s new rackable models delivered “the strongest midrange launch in IBM Z in nearly two decades.” Mainframe revenue, however, fell 20 percent – as IBM expects given it’s now 18 months since it launched the z17.
IBM’s infrastructure revenue grew five percent year-over-year to $3.7 billion, much slower improvement than recorded by rivals Dell, HPE, and Lenovo.
Software did rather better, scoring nine percent growth to reach $7.8 billion for the quarter. Red Hat was the star, growing eleven percent and increasing annual recurring revenue by 30 percent. Some of that future revenue is for Red Hat’s virtualization products, which have now won $800 million of deals, with a pipeline of a further $750 million. That’s a solid result for a product line launched in 2024, and IBM believes there’s more to come given the possibility some VMware users are on the move.
Total quarterly revenue hit $17.1 billion, up five percent. IBM’s share price wobbled in after-hours trading and ended down a point or two.
‘Emergency maintenance’ for IBM Cloud
Another IBM matter The Register is watching today is a severity one incident in the Big Blue cloud, caused by “emergency maintenance” that meant users could not provision new resources or virtual private clouds for 90 minutes. Users of IBM’s Classic Cloud, the service it acquired from SoftLayer in 2013, have been told Big Blue will “restore new provisioning and resource management in our Classic environment” by 08:00 UTC on Thursday – meaning the incident will last at least 16 hours.
IBM commenced that work a handful of hours after the announcement of critical bugs in PHP. We’ve asked if fixing that flaw is the reason for the incident and will update this story if we get a response. ®
