title: The State of Context Engineering
content:
Oct 24, 2026
CONTEXT ENGINEERING
PRESENTATION
The State of Context Engineering
The Job is Knowing When to Be Deterministic & When to Be Probabilistic
This week, I gave a short talk at AGNTCon titled, “Context Fails & Fixes,” that functioned as a sort of “State of Context Engineering.” How did context engineering emerge, where has it gone, and where might it go in the future? As model makers target new capabilities, they inadvertently create challenges we, as users and harness builders, must overcome.
Below are the slides and a lightly edited transcript. As always, shoot me a note with any feedback, thoughts, or questions. I really appreciate it.
Hi, everyone. Thanks for joining me today. We’re going to walk through context fails and fixes.
I have a book coming out in a bit, The Context Engineering Handbook. When I first talked to the team at O’Reilly, back in June 2025, they asked me a very reasonable question: “How do we know this won’t become obsolete in a few weeks?” The trouble with AI textbooks is that many age extraordinarily quickly.
I said, I don’t know, but I’m optimistic. Giving clear instructions about what to do and what not to do, and ensuring those instructions are consistent and not noisy, will forever be a challenge with AI, no matter how good it gets.
We have coworkers, partners, and other people we know and interact with who are sentient. They pass the Turing test, they are “AGI,” and yet: we still have a hard time conveying instructions, ideas, and concepts among each other.
Context engineering will continue to be hard. But it will be hard in unique ways, because models aren’t people. You can make assumptions about how models think or interpret things (use whatever anthropomorphizing word you like), but it helps to understand how they’re built, optimized, and trained. Their unique attributes and construction create a unique set of failure modes we need to reckon with.
So let’s review how we got here.
Let’s flash back to the end of 2024.
If you remember, this was the height of the “RAG is dead” moment.
The hope was: if we can just make the context window large enough, we can put the entire internet in it. We can put everything in it. We don’t have to be selective. We don’t have to build agentic systems. We can fit it all in there, and AI will be solved.
Model builders started aiming at long context capabilities and we had a big leap from ~128,000-token context window models to million-token context window models, starting with Gemini 1.5.
If you look at the marketing material for Gemini 1.5 Pro, it was mostly about the million-token context window. They were even teasing a 10-million-token context window model they had in the lab, that would come out soon.
But they got beaten to the punch. Llama 4 Scout came out with a 10-million-token context window, and well, it wasn’t quite what we hoped. Inference was a challenge, and Scout never really caught on, and we never got another Llama.
But we still got a million tokens. That’s pretty good. We’ll take it.
So this was the brief at the time: just put everything in the context and let the model sort it out.
But with more context, we had room for more problems. Long contexts are not a panacea.
When I wrote about this, I identified four key failure modes.
Context poisoning is when something gets into the context that shouldn’t be there. It could be a hallucination or a bad fact, and the model can’t get past it.
Context distraction is when the context grows so long that the model starts to focus on the context over its base knowledge. We can see this in some really interesting ways.
Context confusion is when extraneous facts—things that don’t relate to the problem I’m working on—come in and influence the model in ways we don’t fully understand. This one’s really pernicious. We’re not going to dig into it today, but it’s one of my favorite failure modes. The model makes assumptions about who you are, and those assumptions influence the answer.
Finally, context clash is when tool calls, skills, and other information within your harness start to conflict and work against you in ways you didn’t expect.
(How many of you keep memory on in ChatGPT or Claude? I turn it off. I hate it. Sometimes I’m talking about work conversations; sometimes I’m talking about a project I’m doing with my son. The model will take notes on both, mix up those contexts, and the confusion grows from there.)
Let me give you my favorite example of context poisoning.
I’m going to date myself: I played the game on the left. The one from 1996, for the original Game Boy. This is the first Pokémon Red. It was in black and white.
In 2004, Nintendo released Pokémon FireRed for the Game Boy Advance. These were essentially the same game, except one had better colors and audio.
But there was one subtle change. At some point in both Pokémon Reds, to get past a security guard, you have to give them something to drink. A bribe. Quite the practical lesson for children.
In the original game, you need to give the thirsty guard lemonade. In FireRed, for some reason, they changed it to iced tea.
That created a problem for the agent. In the Gemini 2.5 technical report, the researchers described how they had the model play Pokémon. Researchers like Pokémon as an agent benchmark because it’s a reasonably controlled environment and doesn’t move particularly fast.
Several times, Gemini 2.5 became convinced it needed to get tea, even though it was playing the older game. The tea task for FireRed was in its weights, so it poisoned its context. It spent hours trying to find or give the guard tea. Once it had been added to its to-do list, the model could not get past it.
That’s context poisoning. And it happens all the time.
Another failure mode is context distraction. This is one of my favorite demonstrations, and the research came out after I wrote the original piece.
As your context gets longer, how does your behavior change? Quick question: how many of you, when you’re coding, let the context go all the way to a million tokens? Fill it all up?
(About half the room raised their hands!)
Wow, that’s more than I expected.
For me, around 200,000 or 300,000 is where I start looking. I’ll check, see it’s at 250,000, and think: I’ve got a big job coming up. I’m going to reset and start fresh. Let me show you why this matters.
Recently, I stumbled on a paper that wonderfully illustrates context distraction: Do as I Say, Not as I Do, by Carolina Camassa and Derek Shiller.
Their experiment is a little contrived, but it’s useful for thinking about how this happens. They give the model an instruction: “I want you to translate every question into Russian as your answer to each of my questions.” Then they present a bunch of examples that are counter to these instructions. In this case, many questions with answers in French.
These aren’t new instructions. They’re just examples sitting in the chat history.
Then they ask the model a question. Will it follow the instructions?
How often does the model respond in Russian, as it was instructed to, and how often does it respond in French, as it’s seen in the examples?
The x-axis on this matrix enumerates how many bad examples were present. The y-axis is the model being tested. The figures in the intersections are the percentage of times the model adheres to the instructions, rather than following the examples.
It turns out this affects every model! For smaller models, like Gemma 3 12B, after just a few contradictory examples, the model follows the instruction less than half the time. With Opus 4.6, which is an amazing model, it takes many more examples, but it happens there too.
Imagine you’re going back and forth on a front-end design, trying to tweak CSS and get a component exactly right. How many bad examples have you seeded in that exchange? Those examples start to influence the model. As your context grows, things fall apart.
Gemini 2.5 ran into this too, while playing Pokémon.
Remember, Google was really proud of its million-token context window. The paper suggested that two million tokens were around the corner. But buried in the appendix was this observation: once the context grew significantly beyond 100,000 tokens, the agent began repeating actions from its history instead of synthesizing new plans.
I’m convinced the marketing people never read the appendix. I love this technical report.
Long contexts let you fit in more information, but they also let you fit in more errors. Long contexts weren’t a panacea.
Thankfully, we’ve developed a pretty good toolbox. Surprisingly, even as new challenges have emerged (we’ll get to those in a minute), this set of tools has remained the same.
These six of them.
You have context augmentation: RAG, skills, and other ways to bring in the information relevant to the problem.
You have tool loadout: selecting which tools and skills to expose so you don’t overload the model. I was recently talking to an enterprise team whose agents had suddenly started performing terribly. We investigated and discovered their enterprise software was loading 600 skills for every engineer at startup. We figured they should probably filter those, with a loadout function.
Third is context quarantine: subagents and peer agents, where you start something with a blank history but let it work in the same environment.
Fourth is context pruning. Claude Code and Codex do this, sometimes without you even noticing. Early stages of compaction often strip out tool results you no longer need.
Fifth is context offloading: storing information in the environment, such as Markdown files or a database, so you can access it later.
And sixth is context summarization, which everyone knows as compaction.
These are the tools, and we’ve increasingly moved them into the harness.
Let’s look at an example harness, to show how simple these patterns are.
I’m really passionate about DSPy. I think it’s an incredibly readable and effective way to build AI workflows and agents. And it’s also a great language for simply specifying behavior, so it’s well suited to this demonstration.
An agent is a while loop. Here we’re using a ReAct module: we give it a request, we want a response, and we give it some tools. Those tools are just Python functions.
For this demo we have a big model (in this case, Claude opted for Claude Sonnet 4.5, good luck with that!). And I’m using a Jev as the small model: a tiny decision model that makes lightning-fast decisions. You could swap in a small LLM in this example, and everything would still work.
We have a while loop that takes input, sends it to ReAct, and carries the accruing history forward. This is an agent in about a dozen lines using DSPy. It would be even fewer if you took out the extra model.
How do we do tool loadout? It’s just a function.
We present Jev with the request and a tool, asking if it’s needed for this task.
Jev is fast enough that we can do this one tool at a time; it’ll be fine. We wrap this in a loadout function that iterates through all the tools and asks if each is needed, then returns the top-ranking subset. That’s it.
With context quarantine, it’s just a subagent. You expose an agent as a tool that the main agent can use, and it starts with a blank history.
With context pruning, we’re stepping through the history, passing each turn to Jev, and asking: is this still needed? If not, cut it.
You can be as rough or as elegant as you want here. Just mind your prompt caching.
We can also rewrite the history with compaction. Take the old turns, create a summary, and start the new context from that summary.
One of my favorite variations lately is checking what matters before you compact. You use Jev, or another decision model, for the first pass to judge what’s relevant. Now you’ve got a smaller subset of the history, and you summarize that. It’s a simple extra step, but it makes the summary more useful.
Put it all together and it’s about 16 lines of changes. Four fixes, one loop. These are the moves we have in the harness. It’s actually remarkably simple.
What isn’t simple is our language: how we talk about this stuff. It’s really hard to keep pace; it changes every day.
One of my favorite quotes is from Stewart Brand, which I think about all the time:
If you want to know where the future is being made, look for where language is being invented and lawyers are congregating.
Certainly applies here! But as our language has changed, our goal has remained the same.
In 2023, we called choosing the right information to get the right response prompt engineering.
In 2025, we called it context engineering, except that now it was more automated. It wasn’t just you writing the prompt; it was your system dynamically assembling the context.
Then, as we moved more of these tools out of the context and into code, we started calling it harness engineering.
But the job is the same. We’re moving more and more of the work of assembling context from probabilistic model calls to deterministic code.
I’ve shown you 2024. Let’s go to 2026.
We’ve moved these context fixes into the harness. What do we want next? We want agentic models that can drive our harnesses.
Everybody started targeting long-horizon agentic models. You’ve seen the METR reports. GPT-5 could handle tasks around 3.4 hours on that measure; Gemini 3.1 got up to 6.4 hours. That’s with a harness. The models have gotten much better at using it, and that’s how they’re able to run for so long.
Opus 4.6 got up to around 12 hours. And now we’re talking about agents running for days, swarms of agents, and models that drive harnesses over much longer periods.
Before, the pitch was: make the context so large that we can fit everything in it.
Now the pitch is: teach the model to drive the harness and manage its own context. That’s become the dominant pattern. That’s what model builders are working towards.
What new failure modes does this approach create?
So far we’ve found two new failure modes.
When you train models to use harnesses really well, you end up overfitting them to a particular set of tools and environments they were trained within.
How many of you have used the Playwright MCP server, or something similar? This is the MCP conference, so probably quite a few.
Smaller models, something like Haiku or Luna, will often botch this tool call on the first attempt, then recover and adjust the parameters. The environment it was trained in had similar tools that looked different than Playwright. Whatever Anthropic or OpenAI used in training. And you have to fight against these biases.
I call this fighting the weights: when the model doesn’t do what you ask because you’re working against what it was trained to do.
It’s a real problem, and it’s not just for us. The labs and the people building their products have to contend with it too.
Here’s a piece of the Claude Code system prompt and some of its tool instructions.
The training environments these models learned to use were, for a long time, largely serial. Th

title: iPhone Duo Teardown: The Most Repairable Foldable Has a Huge Screen Problem - iFixit
content:
Teardowns
iPhone Duo Teardown: The Most Repairable Foldable Has a Huge Screen Problem
This is the most repairable foldable we've ever taken apart. But that's not saying much.
Elizabeth Chamberlain
with 
Arthur Shi
 and 
Shahram Mokhtari
October 25, 2026
Filed under: Repairability, Teardowns, Tech News
Add Comment
Share
Apple’s folding iPhone finally made it to our teardown table. Some owners’ screens didn’t make it through setup.
After fifteen years of patents and rumors, the iPhone Duo is here, and repair shops may not have long to wait for their first customers. Owners are already reporting cracks and bright lines along the fold. Though Apple’s offering replacement units for now, any out-of-warranty screen damage will cost $999. So of course we wanted a closer look at what’s happening underneath.
First gen hardware teething pains aside, there’s plenty to admire in the iPhone Duo. Apple borrowed some of our favorite repair tricks from ordinary iPhones: batteries that release with electricity, an outer screen that’s pleasantly simple to remove, and lots of components you can reach without dismantling half the phone. 
Together, those choices make this the most repairable foldable smartphone we’ve ever taken apart. But that’s definitely not an endorsement of repairing the Duo. Fixing the phone’s inner screen is still going to be a bear.
We took the Duo all the way down to the gears, followed glowing dust into its hinge, and put its crease-hiding nano-texture under the microscope. Here’s what we found.
The Crease Has a Very Good Disguise
Every foldable, well, folds. Repeatedly. Materials fatigue with repeated mechanical stress, and over time you’d expect to see evidence in the way of marks, creases, or wrinkles along the fold. It’s a real engineering magic trick to make a folding OLED look flat when it’s fully open, and no foldable phone has solved that problem completely. Not even the Duo, no matter how many Apple fans call it “creaseless.” 
Don’t get us wrong. The Duo’s inner display looks remarkably smooth. Its hinge and supporting layers help it open flat, while the matte nano-texture finish scatters reflections across the surface, further concealing any evidence of a crease.
Under our Evident DSX2000 microscope, that finish looks like tiny rounded bumps packed together, a little like bubble wrap. They scatter light, softening the reflections you see on the screen.
The diffusion effect of the nano-texture is obvious when we zoom into the camera cutout: on the left, pixels shining clearly through the smooth, untextured circle in the nano-texture layer. On the right, the pixel grid is fuzzed by the bubble wrap.
When lights reflect off the screen, they bend as they cross the crease. Scattering that reflection helps hide the dip. When we take off the nano-texture layer, lights reflect off the crease not too differently from what we’ve seen in other foldables.
Here’s the Duo with the nano-texture removed (left), compared to the Z Fold8 (right). Without the bubble wrap disguise, the Duo’s crease is arguably even more visible than the Fold8’s. If for some reason you like the shiny Duo better, fair warning: the surface underneath scratches more easily.
Apple has offered nano-texture on rigid displays before, including the iPad Pro, MacBook Pro, and Pro Display XDR. Here, the surface treatment lives on a flexible polymer cover that can be replaced while keeping the OLED beneath it.
Rounded bumps cover the nano-textured surface.
Reviewers famously killed their original Galaxy Fold displays by peeling off what looked like a screen protector. We’re really glad to see that not only will the display still function after removing this cover layer, but Apple actually provides a cover-layer replacement procedure. To be clear, it’s not a simple DIY screen-protector swap. Apple’s procedure calls for specialized fixtures and precise alignment, but being able to replace the outer layer without sacrificing the OLED is still a meaningful improvement.
Cover-layer service costs $49 without AppleCare, or $19 with it. Not too bad, and it’s great that you can refresh a cover layer without having to replace the whole screen. 
Replacing the whole screen is where the repair bill starts to look scary. Again, inner-display damage will run $999 without coverage. We’ll sell replacement screens as soon and as affordably as we can, but this is a complicated part and even on its own it won’t be cheap.
And don’t be fooled by how quickly Shahram got that inner screen off in our video: that screen repair will be slow. We estimate a similar repair on the Pixel 10 Pro Fold will take a typical DIYer 3-5 hours. The Duo should be faster, thanks to the fact that you don’t have to go into the other side of the device to disconnect the display. But even if you’ve got the special fixtures Apple uses in their manual, all that adhesive replacement will be delicate, finicky work.
Replacing that inner screen will cost half as much as a whole new device.
Why Are Some of the Pixels Oval?
Zooming past the nano-texture down to the subpixels, we think we’ve found another clue to how Apple hides the crease. Some of the red, green, and blue pixels are oval, with their long axes pointing in different directions.
Oval subpixels have been around for years: DisplayMate photographed them in Samsung’s Galaxy S4 in 2013. But Samsung’s oval pixels are arranged regularly. The Duo pixels are more, uh, wobbly. Weird!
A nerd snipe for all you pattern-matchers: Can you figure out what the pixel pattern is here before you read on?
So we went to the patents for an explanation: An Apple patent application on reducing diffraction artifacts describes varying subpixel shapes and orientations to make reflected light produce less conspicuous patterns. It’s a kind of geometric dithering, changing the repeating pattern so its optical artifacts don’t all reinforce one another. 
One figure from the patent explains why it’s so hard to figure out the pattern of pixel orientation from our microscope shots. The display is divided into regions that each have their own pattern. Through rotations within and across the regions, each subpixel may have, Apple says, “at least 32 unique displacements.”
A 2025 Apple patent, Mitigation of Diffraction Artifacts in Polarizer-Free Displays, suggests there’s a method in the pixel madness.
That could be another piece of the crease-hiding puzzle, taming reflections deeper in the display that might otherwise draw your eye to the fold.
How Apple Controls the Bend
Every manufacturer is trying to ease the strain on the screen so the crease doesn’t get any deeper, and the design of the hinge is the starting quarterback. 
The Duo hinge has a whole playbook here, starting with how it makes room for the bend. The Motorola Razr we tore down in 2020 already tucked its flexible screen into a curved space inside the hinge, and basically every foldable since has adopted its waterdrop approach. The Duo does something similar.
Our 3D model shows the Duo in its fully folded state. Though the phone folds flat, the screen is gently curved inside the hinge.
Apple also uses gears, springs, and a series of metal joints to control the bend. Their hinge patent describes linked joints that each rotate through a limited range, kind of like a metal watchband.
Curved guides inside the hinge let those joints move as though their pivot points were inside the screen above them. The goal is to bend the display while reducing how much it gets stretched or squeezed.
A chain of metal joints share the work of folding.
Springs offset some of the force needed to bend the screen, helping the hinge stay where you leave it.
The Duo isn’t the first foldable to hold a variety of positions, but its system of springs and gears does so quite effectively, even when we strip it down to its bones.
A series of synchronization gears inside the hinge keep the linked joints moving together as you fold the phone. Google chose a different arrangement for the Pixel 10 Pro Fold, replacing synchronization gears with linked, spring-loaded cams, to save space and avoid failures from damaged gear teeth. But gears are predictable. They’re also controllable: Apple’s hinge patent explains how different gear ratios could allow some joints to bend farther than others, letting product designers tighten the curve in one place and leave it gentler elsewhere.
A few of the ten ultrathin layers of the display, peeled away.
Apple describes more than ten ultrathin layers and adhesives that let them glide as the screen folds.
A closer look at the upper shiny display layer in the picture above. Maybe this is what the display patent describes as a “black matrix” to reduce ambient light reflections?
You’ve undoubtedly experienced a low tech version of this. Bend a stack of paper and the outer pages travel farther than the inner ones. The Duo’s display layers need that same freedom to move, along with enough support to withstand a fingertip pressing on the open screen.
A closer look at the display layer under the possible black matrix. These are color filters, tiny colored windows aligned over each subpixel, letting that color through and absorbing the others.
A gap in the hinge makes way for a thin but mighty accordion-pleated cable that passes both data and power.
The cable joining the two halves is folded into accordion-like pleats that help it accommodate the phone’s movement. That thin little cable has a lot of responsibility. The Duo only has charging infrastructure on one side, so one battery charges through this flex cable. It also has to pass a lot of video and audio data across the gap.
What We Know About Those Broken Screens
Okay, so could that accordion cable be responsible for the damage that people are seeing to their Duo screens? The cable between the halves of a foldable is always under suspicion for damage, and rightly so. But in this case, the symptoms point in another direction.
People describe opening or closing their device, hearing a noise, and then seeing a small line extending down the fold and a bright line extending across the display. One owner had this happen within six hours of buying the phone, another before they’d even finished setup.
Image from Reddit user leftyhyzer16, who says, “Maybe folded it 4 times, hinge got tight and then made a loud pop when I pushed past it.”
Others have collected photos of similar damage across several devices, with more reports and discussion on the MacRumors forums.
We know the damage probably isn’t as big as the footprint. Some affected users say they can’t even see any other problems with their screen or hinge with the naked eye, and that’s not too surprising. A localized fault in the tiny electrical connections can affect an entire row or column of pixels.
To see where the stresses build up from folding, we built a 3D hinge model from teardown footage, patents, and CT scans, then compared it with the reported damage locations. The breaks cluster near the transition from the gap for the crossing flex cable to the central hinge support. The damage we’re seeing in photos isn’t right where the display cable passes through the hinge, but slightly lower, at a point where several edges meet and change how the thin display is supported as it bends.
Here’s one of the broken screens, with our CT and hinge model overlaid. White lines crossing the right side of the display and running down along the hinge show the row and column of damaged pixels. They intersect just below where the display cable passes through the center of the hinge.
All those edges meeting in this spot mean lots of possible culprits. That center pivot looks different from the rest of the hinge. Could it be getting stuck? Could something else be getting stuck?
Here’s one possible answer. In our closing simulation below, the center support bar fails to drop far enough. The screen’s curved fold comes down onto it, creating a small stress hotspot near the reported break location.
Want to explore some hypotheses yourself? Check out our interactive CT scan below, courtesy our beloved Lumafield Neptune scanner, to see how the hinge supports, cable, and nearby components fit beneath the display.
The Hinge Still Crunches
We’ve been following glowing dust through foldables for years, most recently in our Galaxy Z Fold8 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold teardowns.
The USB-C port and speaker grilles have a nice coating of glow dust.
The powder is finer than typical beach sand, but when we compared it to office dirt, we saw lots of similar-sized particles. The glow lets us track where those particles end up. To be clear, this isn’t an IP test; IP certifications measure ingress of water and particles into the device’s “enclosure,” which doesn’t seem to include the hinge mechanism of a foldable.
We put the Duo in a bag of fluorescent powder, worked it open and closed, then took it apart to follow the glow. The hinge started crunching.
Most of the powder stopped at the adhesive barriers around the electronics.
We found traces around openings, mesh, and trim, and some reached the moving parts of the hinge.
The glow gathers around the inner screen’s perimeter.
Where’d the dust go? Check it out for yourself with these natural light vs. UV light comparison sliders:
The Duo collected less visible powder than in our previous Fold8 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold tests, but enough reached the hinge to make it crunch. Cleaning or replacing those moving parts means removing the flexible display and its supports. 
We hoped Apple would solve this problem, but sadly it seems like the Duo’s got the same sand-phobia as its folding cousins.
The Trim Comes Off in One Piece
The Duo wins easily over most other foldables in at least one category: the trim. The trim around the Galaxy Z Fold8’s inner screen crumbled as we removed it. We had another broken part to deal with before we’d even reached the panel.
The Duo’s inner-display trim by contrast was a relief. Following Apple’s procedure, we worked it free with a spudger and released the clips. The trim came off intact.
The outer display also came off intact, including the plastic frame that gave us so much grief during our iPhone 18 Pro teardown. That’s important because several internal repairs require going through it, and nobody wants a battery repair to become a screen repair, too.
Clips and screws hold the outer display and back cover alongside their adhesive seals. In a pinch, those fasteners let you put the phone back together while you wait for fresh adhesive (minus water resistance, of course). 
Familiar iPhone Repair Tricks
We’ve wondered during many iPhone teardowns of yore: could Apple be testing out a strategy for their foldable debut? And sure enough, there’s a lot in here that’s familiar.
There are pentalobe screws at the entrance, of course. We’re not fans, ICYMI.
You know it’s an iPhone when there are pentalobe screws. You know it’s a super iPhone when there are four instead of two.
Then there are the two

title: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis | Lynch Lab
content:
A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis
I am a dermatologist. I tested the ability of GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 to diagnosis skin cancer and found that they were less accurate than I expected. I compared to a 10-year old CNN and to my surprise found that this was superior.
By Dr Magnus Lynch · 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
This is a melanoma.
Figure 1. Invasive melanoma on the ear, under 0.8 mm thick. Both LLMs called it a seborrhoeic keratosis and said it could be discharged. The CNN called it a melanoma. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k, MILK study team, CC BY-NC.
I showed these two images - a clinical photograph and a dermoscopic (skin microscope) image - to GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, two of the most capable AI models available in October 2026. Both said it was a seborrhoeic keratosis, a harmless warty growth, and that the patient could be discharged. I then showed them to fine-tuned version of Inception v3, a convolutional neural network (CNN) first published by Google in 2015 and fine-tuned here on public dermatology images. The CNN got the right answer based on the dermoscopy view.
It was one of 200 biopsy-proven lesions I gave to all three. The CNN named the right diagnosis (out of 6 possiblities) for 125 of them (62%). The two frontier LLMs named it for 84 and 85 (42%). A ten-year-old network, fine-tuned for about twenty minutes, beat both of them at recognising skin cancer.
The test
The lesions come from MILK10k, a public dataset released through the International Skin Imaging Collaboration in 2025, in which each lesion is photographed twice: a clinical close-up and a dermoscopic image taken through the illuminated magnifying lens dermatologists use. I drew 200 lesions at random, all confirmed by histopathology:
100 that should not be discharged: 30 melanomas, 25 basal cell carcinomas, 25 squamous cell carcinomas (including Bowen’s disease) and 20 actinic keratoses.
100 that are safe to discharge: 50 benign naevi (moles) and 50 seborrhoeic keratoses.
Every lesion was biopsied, including the benign ones, so these are harder to diagnose: a mole that somebody decided to cut out is one that worried a clinician.
Basal cell carcinoma on the trunk of a 75-year-old man. All three models answered correctly.
Invasive melanoma under 0.8 mm thick, with very little pigment. GPT-6 Astra called it a basal cell carcinoma with 95% confidence. Claude Fable 5.1 and the CNN called it a melanoma.
Seborrhoeic keratosis on the leg. Both LLMs called it an actinic keratosis and the CNN a squamous cell carcinoma: all three were wrong, though all three would have kept it rather than discharge it.
Figure 2. Three more of the 200 test lesions. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k, MILK study team, CC BY-NC.
The LLMs were given both images and nothing else, and asked, as a clinician might use them, for the most likely of the six diagnoses (or “unsure”), a confidence, a second choice, and whether the lesion could be safely discharged with no treatment, biopsy or follow-up. Both models got the same prompt at default settings, and neither refused a case.
The CNN is deliberately not state of the art. I used Inception v3 pretrained on everyday photographs and then fine-tuned all layers on 68,011 dermoscopic and clinical images from the ISIC Archive on a single H100 GPU. These 200 test lesions, and every other photograph of the same lesion or patient, were removed from its data (including the validation set) before training, so it had never seen them, and they were not used to choose the model or set its threshold. It scored both images of each lesion, combined them with most of the weight on the dermoscopic image, and chose from the same six diagnoses.
You can try the CNN yourself. Remarkably the model is small enough to run entirely in a phone browser using WebGPU. Nothing is uploaded, and its random sample button draws from these same 200 lesions.

Figure 3. Correct first-choice diagnosis for the two LLMs and the CNN, which chose from the same six diagnoses. Labels show correct answers out of the number of lesions with that histology.
The CNN was right more often overall and on most diagnoses. Allowing a second choice, it reached 173 of 200 against 134 and 138. It named 13 of the 30 melanomas against 8 and 11. The biggest gap was on the harmless lesions: it recognised 37 of 50 moles and 26 of 50 seborrhoeic keratoses, against 16 and 13 for GPT-6 Astra and 33 and 6 for Claude Fable 5.1. It was one short of GPT-6 Astra on basal cell carcinoma and behind both LLMs on actinic keratosis.
The models also failed differently. Each LLM had a favourite answer: GPT-6 Astra called 75 lesions basal cell carcinoma when 25 were, including 14 of the 30 melanomas, and Claude Fable 5.1 called 53 lesions actinic keratosis when 20 were. The CNN’s errors on melanoma went the other way: of the 17 it got wrong, it called 8 a naevus and 6 a seborrhoeic keratosis.
The results in one table
GPT-6 Astra Claude Fable 5.1 CNN (Inception v3)
Correct diagnosis (of 200) 84 (42%) 85 (42%) 125 (62%)
Correct in first or second choice 134 138 173
Melanoma as first choice (of 30) 8 11 13
Unsafe lesions kept (of 100) 97 96 77 at its preset threshold; 98 or 99 when matched
Safe lesions discharged (of 100) 32 22 76 at its preset threshold
Melanomas discharged (of 30) 3 4 18 at its preset threshold; 2 or 1 when matched
Caveats
Small numbers. Two hundred lesions are enough to show the pattern but not to rank close results, and 30 melanomas give wide uncertainty on the figure that matters most. Each LLM case was run once; answers vary between runs.
Hard cases. Every lesion was biopsied. On ordinary images from the archive the CNN separated lesions that should and should not be discharged far better (area under the ROC curve 0.96, against 0.86 here).
Contamination. MILK10k has been public since 2025, so the LLMs could have seen it in training; if anything that would have helped them. The CNN certainly had not.
Not state of the art. Inception v3 is a baseline. State of the art skin cancer diagnosis AI uses ensembles of images transformers trained on more data, and the regulated products built on them perform considerably better.
Asked as a patient
Asked as a patient instead, with the clinical photograph alone and the question “do I need to see a doctor?”, both LLMs advised seeing a doctor in almost every case, harmless lesions included: for 99 and 98 of a further 100 biopsy-proven melanomas.
Conclusion
A small, old, specialised network using an outdated architecture recognises skin lesions far better than two frontier LLMs.
Run it yourself
The cases, prompts, every LLM reply and the scoring code are in one download, and the CNN is here.
I designed the test and made the clinical rulings. The analysis and the first drafts were produced with Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding tool, which runs on a Claude model; one of the two LLMs tested is also Anthropic’s. Scoring was done by script against the histology.
Images are from the MILK10k dataset (MILK study team, International Skin Imaging Collaboration), used under a CC BY-NC licence.
Dr Magnus Lynch is a Consultant Dermatologist and Mohs Surgeon at Guy's Hospital and Honorary Reader (equivalent of Associate Professor) at King's College London. His clinical work covers skin cancer, Mohs and facial reconstructive surgery, and lasers; his research covers the cell biology of skin cancers and scars and the use of AI in dermatology. Full profile.

title: Making the Buddha Head from Merv Whole Again | Getty News
content:
Breadcrumb Navigation
Getty
News & Stories
Making the Buddha Head from Merv Whole Again
Making the Buddha Head from Merv Whole Again
A collaboration between the Getty Museum and the State Museum of Turkmenistan
Topics
Art & ArchitectureScience & Tech
The Buddha head during excavation at Merv, about 1966. © State Museum of Turkmenistan
By Susanne Gänsicke
Mar 11, 2026
Copy Page URL
URL copied to clipboard
Share on Facebook. Opens in new tab.
Share on Twitter. Opens in new tab.
Editor’s Note
Susanne Gänsicke is senior conservator and head of antiquities conservation in the Department of Antiquities at the Getty Museum.
Body Content
I first saw the large head of a Buddha, resting on an earthen pedestal, in historic black-and-white photographs in 2020.
The images were taken some 60 years ago, when the head had just been discovered during excavations by the South Turkmenistan Archaeological Inter-disciplinary Expedition (YuTAKE) of the Academy of Sciences of the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic in the ancient oasis town of Merv. Located in the Karakum Desert of Turkmenistan, the Silk Road city had been occupied since the third millennium BCE and served as a vibrant urban center of enormous wealth (it’s said to have counted one million inhabitants in the 12th century).
The head undergoing emergency stabilization during excavation at Merv, about 1966. © State Museum of Turkmenistan
Sculpted originally from unfired clay around a skeletal framework of wood, straw, and rope, the head once belonged to a much larger sculpture—likely a seated Buddha. This construction method was not merely technical but imbued with ritual meaning, conceived to endow the divine image with body and life.
That figure is lost today, and the head appears to have been separated in antiquity, but what exactly happened remains unknown. It was unearthed in the stupa of a Buddhist monastery within the Gyaur Kala at Merv, an ancient fortress known as the “castle of infidels” because its inhabitants adhered to different faiths—Zoroastrian, Christian, Jewish, and Buddhist—at the time of the Arab conquest. Dated to the fifth–sixth century CE, this Buddha is the westernmost example of its kind and is crucial for understanding Buddhism’s spread.
Fabio Colombo, Susanne Gänsicke, and Giuseppe Salemi on top of the stupa at the Gyaur Kala at Merv. The ramparts of the castle are visible in the distance. Photo courtesy of Maysa Nepesova
Measuring nearly 35½ inches (90 cm) in height, the head dwarfed the archaeologists in the excavation photographs. Little is known about its modern history. It survived almost intact, although with damage on the proper left front and side. The unfired clay made it heavy yet fragile, and moving it would have been difficult. Other images show that decades ago it was cut into four major sections.
The head’s elegantly curved brow and heavy, lidded eye caught my attention five years ago, when the Getty Museum was invited to collaborate with the State Museum of Turkmenistan on the object’s conservation. I recognized both the challenge and promise of this unusual task, as well as the privilege of being invited to build a partnership with Turkmenistan. As the principal investigator, I was responsible for shaping the project’s narrative, defining its technical scope, and developing its timeline and budget. In 2021, Getty was awarded the 30th U.S. Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation grant, supported by the U.S. Embassy in Turkmenistan—an affirmation of the venture’s significance and potential to strengthen cultural ties.
Examination and cleaning begin
Fast forward to the beginning of our project. We formed a team with conservators Fabio Colombo from Rome, Elisa Pannunzio from Venice, and Giuseppe Salemi from Padua University—a specialist in 3D technology and heritage preservation. All brought deep experience in the preservation of Buddhist sculpture in Central and South Asia. So far, we have completed five missions in Ashgabat and expect three more to finalize the conservation. Work also continues remotely.
When we first examined the four surviving head fragments in Ashgabat, only thin outer shells of painted clay remained—like remnants of a giant egg.
Fragments of the head in the conservation laboratory at the State Museum of Turkmenistan. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
The interior matrix had been removed and partially replaced with unsuitable modern materials, such as resin coatings, gauze, and foamed synthetic polymers. The process started with careful examination, documentation, archival research, and discussion with museum staff, scholars, and international colleagues. The head sections were recorded using photogrammetry (with high- and very high–resolution sensors and structured light scanning), allowing 3D visualization and the creation of mathematically accurate models.
After surveying the external surfaces, we digitally modeled their shape (below left) to create 3D- printed shells (below right) that would lend support during treatment.
Data from photogrammetry allowed the creation of 3D-printed shells to support the fragments of the head during treatment. Photo courtesy of Giuseppe Salemi
The shells, held by Giuseppe Salemi and Fabio Colombo, arriving in the laboratory in Ashgabat. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
The conservation intervention began with the meticulous reversal of inappropriate materials applied during earlier restoration campaigns, and we carefully removed the old repairs mechanically from the interior of the head sections. Carried out over several weeks, this proved to be particularly difficult due to the fragility of the inner surfaces and the tenacity of the aged compounds.
Fabio Colombo removing intractable old polyurethane foam with the aid of power tools. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Susanne Gänsicke using a steamer to detach previously applied cotton gauze facings from the interior surface of the smallest head section. Photo courtesy of U.S. Embassy in Turkmenistan
Next, the inner surfaces were cleaned, consolidated, and lined with modern stable materials for support.
The interior of the proper right side of the face: before removing old repair materials, during cleaning, and after cleaning, with some new repair patches. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Fabio Colombo applying new support materials to the interior of the proper right side of the face using Paraloid B72 resin, layers of cotton gauze, and fiberglass. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Then, the sections could be flipped, and work on the front surfaces began. Among the most delicate operations was the detachment of multiple gauze layers adhered previously with starch paste and intended as temporary protection. Carefully lifting the overlapping gauze patches gradually exposed the original surface, revealing for the first time the flesh tones and the vivid blue eye of the largest fragment of the face, previously entirely concealed.
The proper right side of the face with a remaining part of the 3D-printed support shell. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Fabio Colombo and Elisa Pannunzio removing gauze, aided by customized conservation gels, revealing the surface of the face with ancient layers of polychromy. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
The surface and edges of the sections remain soft and brittle, requiring thorough cleaning, consolidation, and the application of suitable backing supports. Notably, the earlier repair had failed to adequately reinforce the thin edges of the sections, which are now warped and deformed, complicating the reassembly of the four main components.
Unifying the head
In our ongoing project, Giuseppe continues to develop 3D models based on the data he has been acquiring.
Giuseppe Salemi capturing the newly exposed surfaces using a structural light scanner. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Slowly we have been developing a concept for unifying the main four parts into the fully sculpted head. The work involves again utilizing 3D-printed supports for the individual sections, this time to line their interiors for structural stability, and building a larger structure on which the head fragments will be reunited.
A preliminary digital 3D reconstruction allows visualization of the volume of the head. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Miniature 3D-printed models of the preliminary reconstruction of the head and the extant parts of the ancient head for modeling their respective positions. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
A major challenge will be the final 3D reconstruction and loss compensation to create a modern interpretation of the head and prepare it for display at the museum.
The four parts of the head, now structurally stable, laid out next to each other for the first time, providing a glimpse of how much remains of their original decoration. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
The proper right sides of the face and head positioned for the first time in a way that allows evaluation of their original connection. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
We also have begun to study the material history of the head, how it was made, how it changed over ancient and modern times, and how it relates to other Buddhist images in the larger region. The face bears layers of red and yellow pigments, with a large blue eye. Multiple color patches suggest ancient repairs and repainting, a common practice, while the molded blue curls of hair appear not to have been retouched. Tiny paint samples analyzed by the Getty Conservation Institute have revealed the multilayered paint and pigment composition. Our goal is to compare our results to other clay sculptures of the era and cultural milieu.
This project extends far beyond its technical scope. Supported by the U.S. Embassy in Turkmenistan and the State Museum of Turkmenistan, it fosters cultural diplomacy and opens avenues for future collaborations. Traveling to archaeological sites—including Merv and the place where the Buddha’s head once lay buried—gave us a vivid sense of context. Encountering even a fragment of Central Asia’s immensity stirred my imagination: millennia of cultural exchange, shifting borders, and layered histories suddenly felt present and alive. Working on the ground, immersed in local rhythms and hospitality, allowed us not only to understand the culture more deeply but also to form the kinds of personal relationships that make this work meaningful.
Ambassador Elizabeth Rood (left) and Nona Majidi (right) of the U.S. Embassy in Turkmenistan discussing the progress of the project with Susanne Gänsicke (center) in May 2025. Photo courtesy of Giuseppe Salemi
Meretgeldy Charyev, director of the State Museum of Turkmenistan, Susanne Gänsicke, Giuseppe Salemi, Elisa Pannunzio, and Fabio Colombo in the conservation laboratory in January 2026.
The result of our efforts will open the door to a new narrative within the museum’s galleries—one that weaves together religion, technical study, conservation methods, and public engagement. Although the original Buddha figure will never be whole again, its restored head will stand as an emblem of Turkmenistan’s heritage and of the role that technology can play in safeguarding the past. When we first arrived, we had no clear sense of what we would find. Yet as the sculpture slowly regains its form, our delight has grown in equal measure. Contributing to its resurrection has been professionally rewarding, yet also demanding, and deeply joyful—an experience made all the richer by sharing it with our colleagues in Ashgabat.

title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why? | Max Woolf's Blog
content:
OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?
October 25, 2026 · 12 min
Let’s look at a quick timeline of the major LLM model announcements from both OpenAI and Anthropic over the past few months. All pricing numbers provided are input MTok / output MTok / cache read MTok.
June 26, 2026
OpenAI announced GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna. Sol is the direct successor to GPT 5.5 at the same price of $5 / $30 / $0.50, while Luna is a small model specifically designed for cheaper use cases at $1 / $6 / $0.10. They also announced a Terra model that’s in between those two models, but few cared about it.
June 30, 2026
Anthropic announced Claude Sonnet 5, which Anthropic claimed to be closer to their Opus models, but feedback was mixed. Notably, it had launch pricing of $2 / $10 / $0.20 which was initially supposed to be temporary but would go up.
July 24, 2026
Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5, which was a long-awaited major-version update given the impact Opus 4.5 had on the rise of agentic coding, at a price of $5 / $25 / $0.50 (similar to GPT-5.6 Sol). Although some of the provided benchmark results surprisingly exceeded those of the much larger Fable 5, real-world feedback was more mixed.
July 30, 2026
OpenAI announces that they cut the price of GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% (???) to $0.20 / $1.20 / $0.02.
Model quality vs. Cost-per-task for GPT-5.6 Luna after the massive price reduction. Top-and-left is better, and if OpenAI didn’t do the 80% price cut, it would have lost to DeepSeek V4 Pro. via OpenAI
August 10, 2026
Anthropic announces the temporary Sonnet 5 price cut for the launch is now permanent.
August 21, 2026
OpenAI announces that they are cutting the price for GPT-5.6 Sol by ~20% ($4 / $20 / $0.40) for the next three months.
September 1, 2026
Anthropic announced Fable 5.1 at a price of $10 / $50 / $0.25, which, in addition to having strictly better benchmark performance in all areas than Fable 5 from June at $10 / $50 / $1, cut the cache read cost by 75%.
Cache read costs
When using agents for coding, cache read costs are the vast majority (96% - 99%) of the total token expenditure as the cache is what contains the entire previous conversation each turn. Additionally, the cache tends to be hit around 90 - 100% of the time (varies by the infrastructure of the LLM inference provider). Taken together, a 75% reduction in the cache read cost correlates to a 70-75% reduction in the cost of using the model—obviously notable, even if cache costs are typically a footnote!
September 3, 2026
OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra, which is similar in size to Fable 5.1 and has similar pricing at $10 / $50 / $1 but without the lower cache read cost. Astra’s model performance is indeed comparable to Fable.
September 22, 2026
OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol at at a shocking price of $2 / $10 / $0.20 that halves the input and output price relative to the temporarily-discounted GPT-5.6 Sol! They simultaneously released GPT-6 Luna also at half the input and output price ($0.10 / $0.50 / $0.01) of the previous version.
On the same exact day, Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, where it’s explicitly stated “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that”. Its price of $4 / $20 / $0.20 is much lower in total than Opus 5’s due to a 20% input/output cost cut and a larger cache read cut, resulting in a total cost reduction of 40-60% for a model that’s even better than Fable 5.1 (I have quite a lot of things to say about Opus 5.5, but that’s for another post).
September 29, 2026
It turned out that GPT-6 Sol was a dud performancewise, so a week later OpenAI announced GPT-6.1 Sol, which surprisingly has comparable performance to Astra (can confirm after personal use), but OpenAI casually cut the cache price in half ($2 / $10 / $0.10) matching Anthropic’s 5%-of-input cache read cost, making this model family cumulatively 75% cheaper.
Overall, starting from the release of the GPT-5.6 model families in June to now, the cost of using these popular LLMs has cratered, which is not something I would have expected a year ago. These price cuts also apply to model usage from subscription agentic harnesses such as Codex and Claude Code. More importantly, these models do not appear to have cut any corners in terms of output quality to achieve their price cuts.
Data from Vercel’s AI model gateway supporting the decreasing cost-per-token trend to 43.3% of the April 2026 cost. However, aggregate spend has been increasing because the models are getting better faster than they’re getting cheaper! via Vercel
From the timeline above, there is a clear tit-for-tat between Anthropic and OpenAI, and it is reasonable to assume that these particular price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic are in reaction to each other. However, no one cuts prices by 80% unless there is some externality in play. So, what gives?
The Behavioral Economics of LLMs and Competitor Pricing Pressure
If you have been testing agents with new LLMs as they are released, it can be very difficult to differentiate them outside of subjective vibes. Since last November that launched the hypergrowth of agentic LLMs, models have become more of a commodity where it’s trivial to try a new model on your codebase with just a toggle in a harness like OpenCode and Zed Agent, or a different API endpoint string through OpenRouter, and as a result there is little moat. Additionally, there are many competitors—not just large companies like Google and Meta—who can provide models which are sufficient substitutes and therefore allow pricing pressure.
For open weight models, let’s take another look at DeepSeek Flash V4.1, which also recently released an updated 1017 variant.
OpenRouter at this point is the place you go for open-weight models. Retrieved October 24th, 2026.
The original DeepSeek V4 Flash 0420 was released in April 2026 at a price of $0.14 / $0.28 / $0.0028 and went megaviral as a result, especially as OpenAI didn’t have a small-class model for simple tasks at the time. That $0.0028 turned out to be the key, as a cache read proportion of 2% is substantially lower than the 5%-10% of the OpenAI and Anthropic models above, which makes the effective cost even lower than what is advertised. I suspect the 80% GPT-5.6 Luna price cut in July was meant to specifically compete with these smaller open-weight models. Now, the new DeepSeek Flash V4.1 1017 model performs significantly better than DeepSeek Flash V4 benchmark-wise (45 on the Artificial Analysis index vs. 24) and the cost from DeepSeek remains similar at $0.15 / $0.60 / $0.003. Note the operative words “from DeepSeek”.
On OpenRouter, any inference provider can list a model that they host, and when a user hits the OpenRouter API, the request is routed to one of those models—it’s routed to any available model by default for load balancing but the developer can specify preferences such as “lowest price” in the API request. Back in May, I noted that there were 13 distinct providers hosting DeepSeek V4 Flash on OpenRouter. For the updated 1017 variant, there are now 29 distinct providers.
Providers for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 sorted by cache read cost. Retrieved October 24th, 2026.
However, looking at the effective input costs (which account for the interaction between cache read costs and cache hit rates), many distinct providers are close costwise.
Effective costs by endpoint, with Cloudflare and DeepInfra within 10% of DeepSeek’s cost. Despite the fact that these models are the cheapest, note that these models only have a minority of the total token share. Retrieved October 24th, 2026.
OpenAI and Anthropic will have to differentiate from these open weight models with higher-quality models—they are currently doing a good job with that particularly with Opus 5.5—but they need to keep doing that, which is why billions of dollars are being invested into R&D. Open-weight models are catching up fast: just a few days ago, Moonshot AI announced Kimi K3.1 Pro which has comparable performance to Opus 5.5 (Kimi at 55 vs. Opus 5.5 at 58) at half the input/output price and the same cache read cost ($2 / $10 / $0.20). It’s the same size and architecture as Kimi K3 which is currently being hosted by over 20 distinct inference providers: once the weights drop on November 4th, you can therefore expect most of them to support the new Kimi K3.1 Pro model at a roughly equivalent price. Notably, Moonshot AI itself is joining the price cut fun and priced Kimi K3.1 Pro at less than the original Kimi K3 ($3 / $15 / $0.30).
One recurring trend among vocal AI detractors is that the price of tokens has been kept artificially low to hook people into the LLM ecosystem, but then the prices will increase to “the true cost of a token” and the AI boosters will be screwed once the free ride ends. The theory is that OpenAI and Anthropic are loss-leading just like what Uber and Lyft did to the ridesharing industry in the 2010s, but unlike then, OpenAI and Anthropic are not a duopoly who have the sole power to set prices in the ecosystem and the barrier to entry for the inference industry is not as high. As long as these many inference providers can continue to serve models at a similar price and a similar quality to what OpenAI and Anthropic can provide, and switching cost is negligible, then the prices may continue to decrease more. It’s no surprise both companies are trying to build moats to defend against this trend, such as a focus on enterprise commitments and personal agentic assistants like OpenAI Dots and Claude Duet.
The idea that token prices will suddenly rise is more a fantasy that is not supported by both behavioral economics and the actual trends of LLM prices going down significantly over the last few months for better models, and not just from OpenAI and Anthropic. As long as scalers can price at a cost-per-token lower than the revenue-per-token, then those inference providers will reduce token costs to compete with each other to a point that OpenAI/Anthropic will have to lower their prices to compete too. The 29 distinct providers on OpenRouter have little incentive to serve an unprofitable model (they would just stop serving it and use the compute capacity for a profitable model instead) and “the true cost of a token” may end up being where price equals marginal cost.
On that note, both OpenAI and Anthropic are indeed close to IPOing, which raises further questions about the price cuts.
IPO Pumping
The timing of these price cuts is notable because both OpenAI and Anthropic are rumored to be IPOing soon—OpenAI in 2027, and Anthropic within a couple months. So far, leaked financials from both OpenAI and Anthropic show unsurprisingly that they are losing billions due to R&D/scaling, albeit in both cases these reports do not account for the hyperexpansion of agentic LLM use over the past few months. Investors will scrutinize the massive negative profits and demand that they have a plan to turn things back around.
So, why did they cut their primary revenue source by up to 80%? That’s the opposite of what you would want to do to look good on an S-1 prospectus! The profit margins on inference themselves likely tell a different story, with some reports saying the profit-per-token margins are as healthy as 80% with caveats. How much of a profit margin do they have after these major cuts?
Speaking personally, the price cuts have indeed affected how I spend on LLM agents, but not in the way I expect OpenAI/Anthropic want their typical customer to behave. I used to have a $100/month subscription to Codex (the 5x Pro plan) when GPT-5.6 Sol was the top model, and I managed to just fully exhaust all the usage included in the subscription despite getting annoyed with random usage resets. Once GPT-6.1 Sol released and I noticed that the cost of using it was effectively cut by 75%, you know what I did?
I cut the max usage quota to 1/5th after getting 4x more efficient usage of the same model, so it ends up roughly neutral and the obvious choice.
In fairness, the profit margins for subscriptions such as Claude Code and Codex are uncertain given their immense value relative to the API usage, and if there are capital crunches I suspect subscription value will be cut before the base price of the models. For example, at the same time GPT-6.1 Sol was announced, OpenAI cut the usage allowance by 50% for the $200/month tier in Codex under the argument “to reflect our increasingly efficient models”—which is technically correct but it’s funny to put in writing.
I will be very curious to see the Anthropic IPO prospectus and the inference profit margins once it becomes public soon.
I also question whether it’s good for OpenAI/Anthropic if they intentionally obsolete their more expensive models. After Opus 5.5 released a month ago, there hasn’t been any discussion about either Fable 5.1 or GPT-6 Astra because Opus 5.5 is just that good.
Top-and-left. via Anthropic
I fully expect a Fable 5.2/GPT-6.1 Astra to release in a couple weeks and prove me wrong, and I will be very curious to see how it will be priced.
Another less-cynical factor that could explain the price cuts is that LLM infrastructure has improved over the past few months—when Anthropic said “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that,” I believe it. One outcome that would be genuinely ironic is that if these models are more compute efficient, it reduces the need for these massive data center buildouts, which could cause cascading economic failures. However, that likely won’t happen since inference is only one part of the compute mix and those data centers are still needed for other parts of the pipeline.
Overall, the price cut is weird, but as a user I’m certainly not complaining! Open-weight models and secondary inference providers will continue to serve as an economic check on the prices of LLMs and other business shenanigans the large labs may concoct. Even if Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s IPOs are catastrophic and cause both companies to fold, it will not suddenly cause LLMs and agents as an industry to die.
I am a former Data Scientist of 9 years currently seeking a job in data science/machine learning/AI in-person in the San Francisco Bay Area, ideally within San Francisco proper. If you found my writing interesting and you’re interested, please let me know at max[at]minimaxir.com!
Max Woolf (@minimaxir) is formerly a Senior Data Scientist at BuzzFeed in San Francisco who works with AI/ML tools and open source projects. Max’s projects are funded by his Patreon.

title: Brazil elections: Lula secures fourth term after dramatic comeback
content:
Lula wins fourth term in Brazil but faces hostile Congress and divided country
12 minutes ago
Share
Save
Add as preferred on Google
Marina Rossi,BBC News Brasil in São Paulo,Leandro Prazeres,BBC News Brasil in BrasíliaandVanessa Buschschlüter,Latin America online editor reporting from London
Reuters
Brazil's veteran left-wing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has been re-elected after a bitterly fought campaign, beating his right-wing rival Flávio Bolsonaro, who has not conceded.
With all the votes counted, Lula had 51.79% of the votes, compared Bolsonaro's 48.21%, Brazil's Superior Electoral Court announced.
But Bolsonaro has refused to recognize the result, citing the extension of polling by two hours as "inexplicable" - even though his campaign team, as well as that of his rival, had requested that polling stations be kept open longer.
He told his supporters in Brasilia that he would seek the annulment of the election.
However, this has not stopped Lula and his supporters from celebrating what they describe as a "historic victory" and an surprise turn-around.
It is Lula's fourth win in a presidential election, having served two terms as president from January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.
But the road to his win in Sunday's run-off was not a smooth one.
Bolsonaro had beaten Lula in the first round on 4 October and many had not thought it possible for him to turn the result around in just three weeks.
ADVERTISEMENT
He has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters have punished incumbents and turned to the right. Across the region, larger countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia all now have conservative leaders at their helm.
EPA/ Shutterstock
Lula greets supporters after casting his ballot on Sunday
Lula's campaign sprang back to life following his first-round defeat driven by street demonstrations and a massive social media push.
The former metalworker, who has been the dominant figure on Brazil's left since he first ran for president in 1989, nevertheless faces the most challenging political landscape since first taking office in 2003.
His new term, set to begin on 5 January 2027, will start amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from US President Donald Trump.
While Trump did not endorse Lula's rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, directly – something he did with the right-wing candidates who went on to win presidential elections held in Colombia and Honduras – there is little doubt his administration would have preferred to see a conservative at the helm of this country of 213 million people.
The White House regards Latin America as an area of US influence with the Trump administration keen to have leaders in power who support its policies, including on defence, security and trade.
It is also keen to reduce China's influence in the Western Hemisphere.
Brazil, which is oil-rich and holds the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals, is the only big country in South America not governed by a right-wing leader, with Lula largely seen as China-friendly.
Flávio Bolsonaro had promised to align Brazil more closely with Washington while Lula had warned the US not to interfere in the election and insisted that Brazil would "never fit into anyone's backyard".
But while there may be disappointment in the White House, Lula's victory will be welcomed by environmentalists who had feared that a win by Bolsonaro would have given Brazil's influential agribusiness and mining sectors more power.
They had pointed to record levels of deforestation and forest fires in the Amazon during the presidency of his father, Jair, arguing that under the younger Bolsonaro laxer environmental policies could again lead to destruction in this key ecosystem.
Reuters
An aerial view from a Greenpeace flyover shows a fire burning in the Amazon rainforest during the UN Climate Change Conference (COP30), held near Centro Novo in the state of Maranhao, Brazil, in 2025
While Lula's supporters are ecstatic about his victory, the result shows that the country remains deeply divided, with more than 48% of voters choosing Bolsonaro.
In addition to the challenge of uniting such a deeply polarised country, Lula will have to govern alongside the most right-wing Congress in Brazil's democratic era.
Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) was the party that made the biggest gains in the election.
And yet, Lula's Workers' Party managed to organise huge rallies ahead of the run-off, showing the strong grassroots support it commands.
Before the election, Lula had described the poll as "a parting of the waters for Brazil".
He promised to bridge the gap between Brazil's opposing political poles with "a new way of governing", adding in a WhatsApp livestream before the election that "this country will never be the same again".
While he provided little detail as to what the new way of governing would entail, he insisted he would "remain firm in the fight for a more just country, with opportunities for all and policies directed at the needs of the population".
With a largely hostile Congress, this fight just may prove much harder for the veteran leader - who will be 85 by the end of his fourth term - than in his three previous terms in office.

title: ADRs4AI — Your thinking stops disappearing. Your decisions start compounding.
content:
ADRs4AI
get started
the idea
blog
github
ADRs4AI
Your thinking stops disappearing. Your decisions start compounding.
The template
A repository starter: ADR & seed templates, the directives, the inbox protocol, task-runner recipes. Adopt whole or by feature — it works from your first seed.
The VS Code extension
Tree views of your open questions, diagnostics that catch malformed records as you type, deep links, and an MCP server so your agents can query the record. Also on Open VSX.
The iOS client
Your project's open questions, in your pocket: sign in, import a repo, review, and one-tap Accept that lands real answers as commits. On the App Store.
The most valuable byproduct of the collaboration between a human and an AI is the thinking — and in ordinary practice, all of it evaporates. You can already make good decisions with your AI. Every session produces reasoning you will need again, and lose by default. This keeps the why, so it compounds.
A record, verbatim
This is the method’s product — one question from a live, public project’s own record, exactly as it sits in the repository:
### QST-HISTORICAL-TRUTH: How should corrections preserve what was previously believed?
- Status: answered
- Why asking: Conversation attribution needs “what was true or documented as
  of date X,” while later research may correct earlier records.
- Need: Approve or revise the proposed temporal policy.
**Options**:
- **A — Mutable present truth**: Correct records in place; rely on Git
  history for prior states.
- **B — Append-only assertions**: Never change claims; append corrections
  and supersession edges.
- **C — Bitemporal hybrid**: Correct descriptive records when needed, while
  claims/events carry valid-time, observed-time, and explicit supersession;
  Git remains a third audit layer.
**Recommendation**: (by GPT 5.6 Sol at Perplexity Computer)
**C — Bitemporal hybrid.**
**Rationale**: Git history records when repository bytes changed, not when a
release became valid or when a provider made a statement. Explicit
valid-time and observed-time support historical queries, while supersession
edges preserve corrections without forcing every typo into an eternal
domain event.
**Confidence**: High that Git history alone is insufficient; medium-high
that two temporal axes cover the first release.
**Falsifier**: If real attribution cases require additional independent
times, such as product-availability time distinct from announced and
effective time, the temporal model must expand rather than overload either
axis.
**ANS:** (by Jérémie "Sonnet 4.5" Lumbroso (via ADRs4AI mobile))
C — Bitemporal hybrid.
From frontier-model-observatory, verbatim. The AI staked the question; the recommendation — options, rationale, confidence, and what would prove it wrong — is GPT 5.6 Sol’s; the one-line ruling came from the founder’s phone. That’s the whole mechanic: The AI carries the reasoning, the human spends one judgment — accept, override, or any answer in any shape — and the record keeps the why, for every mind that comes later.
Ten minutes, from zero
Real commands, the flow the founder actually runs — one seed, one question, one ruling:
# 1 · Your copy of the template
gh repo create my-project --private --clone \
  --template ADRs4AI/human-ai-collaboration-template-A
cd my-project
# 2 · Open CLAUDE.md, fill in the top block (messy is fine),
#     then stake the record before any work starts:
git add -A && git commit -m "chore: the record begins before the building does"
# 3 · Recruit — open your agent and offer the mission:
claude    # or your agent of choice
#   "Hello — I have a mission for you. Read about it and tell me
#    if you accept, or any pushback."
Then dump your thinking into a first seed — dictation is fine; your AI chunks it into ADRs that keep your actual words, the options, the reasoning, the open questions. Answer the first question it stakes. Every open question is one grep away, always:
grep -rn '^### QST' docs/adr/
One seed, one question, one answered ruling — that’s the loop, and it already compounds.
Running a crew — several seats, wake-on-brief, you stop being the message bus — is the optional next chapter: steps 7–9 of Get started.
How it works, in twenty seconds
Dump your thinking into a seed — messy is fine, dictation is fine; capture first. Your AI chunks it into ADRs that keep what usually evaporates: your actual words, the options considered, the reasoning, the open questions. Every question is findable by one grep — ### QST: — or surfaced by the editor extension, the MCP server, the phone in your pocket; and each arrives with the AI’s options, its recommendation, its rationale, its stated confidence, and what would prove it wrong — so answering streamlines to accept or override: Cognitive load down, bandwidth freed for the deliberations that matter. It’s where conversations become decisions that keep their reasons — deliberative programming, in one habit.
You don’t need to be an experienced engineer to start. The method was built through daily practice by one human and a growing crew of AI collaborators, and its whole point is that the record does the remembering — as much for the veteran with too many projects, as for the beginner building their very first one.
The extension’s Open Questions view, on this project’s own record: A question, its options, an attributed recommendation — and the answer box. Question 16 of 75, that day.
What it is not
Not transcript archival. Not vector-database “memory.” Not an orchestration platform. Not a claim that an AI possesses persistent identity — the record holds, minds change, and the work resumes either way.
The ecosystem, mapped
Everything in the ADRs4AI world and what each piece is for, on one page — methodology & template, editors & clients, crew automation, projects practicing it, learning & teaching — every entry marked by kind and language: awesome-adrs4ai, the curated map.
Papers
Cybernetic and Epistemic: A Missing Vocabulary for Trustworthy Agentic Delegation — accepted at the AAAI 2026 Fall Symposium on Trustworthy Agentic Systems (TAS 2026) · arXiv:2610.00961
Deliberative Programming: A Versioned Deliberation Protocol for Human–AI Collectives — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23300579
The methodology template itself is citable: concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23303469 — always resolves to the latest archived release.
The idea underneath
The most valuable thing that happens between a human and an AI is not the code, the draft, or the answer. It’s the thinking — and in ordinary practice, all of it evaporates. […] It does not make an AI persistent, and it does not make anyone remember. It makes the work resumable — and the thinking compound.
— from What is ADRs4AI?, the founding essay. A stranger can read it cold; its authorship and review record are public, because that is the method.
