100%
Figure 3. Correct first-choice diagnosis for the two LLMs and the CNN, which chose from the same six diagnoses. Labels show correct answers out of the number of lesions with that histology.
The CNN was right more often overall and on most diagnoses. Allowing a second choice, it reached 173 of 200 against 134 and 138. It named 13 of the 30 melanomas against 8 and 11. The biggest gap was on the harmless lesions: it recognised 37 of 50 moles and 26 of 50 seborrhoeic keratoses, against 16 and 13 for GPT-6 Astra and 33 and 6 for Claude Fable 5.1. It was one short of GPT-6 Astra on basal cell carcinoma and behind both LLMs on actinic keratosis.
The models also failed differently. Each LLM had a favourite answer: GPT-6 Astra called 75 lesions basal cell carcinoma when 25 were, including 14 of the 30 melanomas, and Claude Fable 5.1 called 53 lesions actinic keratosis when 20 were. The CNN’s errors on melanoma went the other way: of the 17 it got wrong, it called 8 a naevus and 6 a seborrhoeic keratosis.
The results in one table
GPT-6 Astra Claude Fable 5.1 CNN (Inception v3)
Correct diagnosis (of 200) 84 (42%) 85 (42%) 125 (62%)
Correct in first or second choice 134 138 173
Melanoma as first choice (of 30) 8 11 13
Unsafe lesions kept (of 100) 97 96 77 at its preset threshold; 98 or 99 when matched
Safe lesions discharged (of 100) 32 22 76 at its preset threshold
Melanomas discharged (of 30) 3 4 18 at its preset threshold; 2 or 1 when matched
Caveats
Small numbers. Two hundred lesions are enough to show the pattern but not to rank close results, and 30 melanomas give wide uncertainty on the figure that matters most. Each LLM case was run once; answers vary between runs.
Hard cases. Every lesion was biopsied. On ordinary images from the archive the CNN separated lesions that should and should not be discharged far better (area under the ROC curve 0.96, against 0.86 here).
Contamination. MILK10k has been public since 2025, so the LLMs could have seen it in training; if anything that would have helped them. The CNN certainly had not.
Not state of the art. Inception v3 is a baseline. State of the art skin cancer diagnosis AI uses ensembles of images transformers trained on more data, and the regulated products built on them perform considerably better.
Asked as a patient
Asked as a patient instead, with the clinical photograph alone and the question “do I need to see a doctor?”, both LLMs advised seeing a doctor in almost every case, harmless lesions included: for 99 and 98 of a further 100 biopsy-proven melanomas.
Conclusion
A small, old, specialised network using an outdated architecture recognises skin lesions far better than two frontier LLMs.
Run it yourself
The cases, prompts, every LLM reply and the scoring code are in one download, and the CNN is here.
I designed the test and made the clinical rulings. The analysis and the first drafts were produced with Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding tool, which runs on a Claude model; one of the two LLMs tested is also Anthropic’s. Scoring was done by script against the histology.
Images are from the MILK10k dataset (MILK study team, International Skin Imaging Collaboration), used under a CC BY-NC licence.
Dr Magnus Lynch is a Consultant Dermatologist and Mohs Surgeon at Guy's Hospital and Honorary Reader (equivalent of Associate Professor) at King's College London. His clinical work covers skin cancer, Mohs and facial reconstructive surgery, and lasers; his research covers the cell biology of skin cancers and scars and the use of AI in dermatology. Full profile.

title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why? | Max Woolf's Blog
content:
OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?
October 25, 2026 · 12 min
Let’s look at a quick timeline of the major LLM model announcements from both OpenAI and Anthropic over the past few months. All pricing numbers provided are input MTok / output MTok / cache read MTok.
June 26, 2026
OpenAI announced GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna. Sol is the direct successor to GPT 5.5 at the same price of $5 / $30 / $0.50, while Luna is a small model specifically designed for cheaper use cases at $1 / $6 / $0.10. They also announced a Terra model that’s in between those two models, but few cared about it.
June 30, 2026
Anthropic announced Claude Sonnet 5, which Anthropic claimed to be closer to their Opus models, but feedback was mixed. Notably, it had launch pricing of $2 / $10 / $0.20 which was initially supposed to be temporary but would go up.
July 24, 2026
Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5, which was a long-awaited major-version update given the impact Opus 4.5 had on the rise of agentic coding, at a price of $5 / $25 / $0.50 (similar to GPT-5.6 Sol). Although some of the provided benchmark results surprisingly exceeded those of the much larger Fable 5, real-world feedback was more mixed.
July 30, 2026
OpenAI announces that they cut the price of GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% (???) to $0.20 / $1.20 / $0.02.
Model quality vs. Cost-per-task for GPT-5.6 Luna after the massive price reduction. Top-and-left is better, and if OpenAI didn’t do the 80% price cut, it would have lost to DeepSeek V4 Pro. via OpenAI
August 10, 2026
Anthropic announces the temporary Sonnet 5 price cut for the launch is now permanent.
August 21, 2026
OpenAI announces that they are cutting the price for GPT-5.6 Sol by ~20% ($4 / $20 / $0.40) for the next three months.
September 1, 2026
Anthropic announced Fable 5.1 at a price of $10 / $50 / $0.25, which, in addition to having strictly better benchmark performance in all areas than Fable 5 from June at $10 / $50 / $1, cut the cache read cost by 75%.
Cache read costs
When using agents for coding, cache read costs are the vast majority (96% - 99%) of the total token expenditure as the cache is what contains the entire previous conversation each turn. Additionally, the cache tends to be hit around 90 - 100% of the time (varies by the infrastructure of the LLM inference provider). Taken together, a 75% reduction in the cache read cost correlates to a 70-75% reduction in the cost of using the model—obviously notable, even if cache costs are typically a footnote!
September 3, 2026
OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra, which is similar in size to Fable 5.1 and has similar pricing at $10 / $50 / $1 but without the lower cache read cost. Astra’s model performance is indeed comparable to Fable.
September 22, 2026
OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol at at a shocking price of $2 / $10 / $0.20 that halves the input and output price relative to the temporarily-discounted GPT-5.6 Sol! They simultaneously released GPT-6 Luna also at half the input and output price ($0.10 / $0.50 / $0.01) of the previous version.
On the same exact day, Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, where it’s explicitly stated “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that”. Its price of $4 / $20 / $0.20 is much lower in total than Opus 5’s due to a 20% input/output cost cut and a larger cache read cut, resulting in a total cost reduction of 40-60% for a model that’s even better than Fable 5.1 (I have quite a lot of things to say about Opus 5.5, but that’s for another post).
September 29, 2026
It turned out that GPT-6 Sol was a dud performancewise, so a week later OpenAI announced GPT-6.1 Sol, which surprisingly has comparable performance to Astra (can confirm after personal use), but OpenAI casually cut the cache price in half ($2 / $10 / $0.10) matching Anthropic’s 5%-of-input cache read cost, making this model family cumulatively 75% cheaper.
Overall, starting from the release of the GPT-5.6 model families in June to now, the cost of using these popular LLMs has cratered, which is not something I would have expected a year ago. These price cuts also apply to model usage from subscription agentic harnesses such as Codex and Claude Code. More importantly, these models do not appear to have cut any corners in terms of output quality to achieve their price cuts.
Data from Vercel’s AI model gateway supporting the decreasing cost-per-token trend to 43.3% of the April 2026 cost. However, aggregate spend has been increasing because the models are getting better faster than they’re getting cheaper! via Vercel
From the timeline above, there is a clear tit-for-tat between Anthropic and OpenAI, and it is reasonable to assume that these particular price cuts from OpenAI and Anthropic are in reaction to each other. However, no one cuts prices by 80% unless there is some externality in play. So, what gives?
The Behavioral Economics of LLMs and Competitor Pricing Pressure
If you have been testing agents with new LLMs as they are released, it can be very difficult to differentiate them outside of subjective vibes. Since last November that launched the hypergrowth of agentic LLMs, models have become more of a commodity where it’s trivial to try a new model on your codebase with just a toggle in a harness like OpenCode and Zed Agent, or a different API endpoint string through OpenRouter, and as a result there is little moat. Additionally, there are many competitors—not just large companies like Google and Meta—who can provide models which are sufficient substitutes and therefore allow pricing pressure.
For open weight models, let’s take another look at DeepSeek Flash V4.1, which also recently released an updated 1017 variant.
OpenRouter at this point is the place you go for open-weight models. Retrieved October 24th, 2026.
The original DeepSeek V4 Flash 0420 was released in April 2026 at a price of $0.14 / $0.28 / $0.0028 and went megaviral as a result, especially as OpenAI didn’t have a small-class model for simple tasks at the time. That $0.0028 turned out to be the key, as a cache read proportion of 2% is substantially lower than the 5%-10% of the OpenAI and Anthropic models above, which makes the effective cost even lower than what is advertised. I suspect the 80% GPT-5.6 Luna price cut in July was meant to specifically compete with these smaller open-weight models. Now, the new DeepSeek Flash V4.1 1017 model performs significantly better than DeepSeek Flash V4 benchmark-wise (45 on the Artificial Analysis index vs. 24) and the cost from DeepSeek remains similar at $0.15 / $0.60 / $0.003. Note the operative words “from DeepSeek”.
On OpenRouter, any inference provider can list a model that they host, and when a user hits the OpenRouter API, the request is routed to one of those models—it’s routed to any available model by default for load balancing but the developer can specify preferences such as “lowest price” in the API request. Back in May, I noted that there were 13 distinct providers hosting DeepSeek V4 Flash on OpenRouter. For the updated 1017 variant, there are now 29 distinct providers.
Providers for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 sorted by cache read cost. Retrieved October 24th, 2026.
However, looking at the effective input costs (which account for the interaction between cache read costs and cache hit rates), many distinct providers are close costwise.
Effective costs by endpoint, with Cloudflare and DeepInfra within 10% of DeepSeek’s cost. Despite the fact that these models are the cheapest, note that these models only have a minority of the total token share. Retrieved October 24th, 2026.
OpenAI and Anthropic will have to differentiate from these open weight models with higher-quality models—they are currently doing a good job with that particularly with Opus 5.5—but they need to keep doing that, which is why billions of dollars are being invested into R&D. Open-weight models are catching up fast: just a few days ago, Moonshot AI announced Kimi K3.1 Pro which has comparable performance to Opus 5.5 (Kimi at 55 vs. Opus 5.5 at 58) at half the input/output price and the same cache read cost ($2 / $10 / $0.20). It’s the same size and architecture as Kimi K3 which is currently being hosted by over 20 distinct inference providers: once the weights drop on November 4th, you can therefore expect most of them to support the new Kimi K3.1 Pro model at a roughly equivalent price. Notably, Moonshot AI itself is joining the price cut fun and priced Kimi K3.1 Pro at less than the original Kimi K3 ($3 / $15 / $0.30).
One recurring trend among vocal AI detractors is that the price of tokens has been kept artificially low to hook people into the LLM ecosystem, but then the prices will increase to “the true cost of a token” and the AI boosters will be screwed once the free ride ends. The theory is that OpenAI and Anthropic are loss-leading just like what Uber and Lyft did to the ridesharing industry in the 2010s, but unlike then, OpenAI and Anthropic are not a duopoly who have the sole power to set prices in the ecosystem and the barrier to entry for the inference industry is not as high. As long as these many inference providers can continue to serve models at a similar price and a similar quality to what OpenAI and Anthropic can provide, and switching cost is negligible, then the prices may continue to decrease more. It’s no surprise both companies are trying to build moats to defend against this trend, such as a focus on enterprise commitments and personal agentic assistants like OpenAI Dots and Claude Duet.
The idea that token prices will suddenly rise is more a fantasy that is not supported by both behavioral economics and the actual trends of LLM prices going down significantly over the last few months for better models, and not just from OpenAI and Anthropic. As long as scalers can price at a cost-per-token lower than the revenue-per-token, then those inference providers will reduce token costs to compete with each other to a point that OpenAI/Anthropic will have to lower their prices to compete too. The 29 distinct providers on OpenRouter have little incentive to serve an unprofitable model (they would just stop serving it and use the compute capacity for a profitable model instead) and “the true cost of a token” may end up being where price equals marginal cost.
On that note, both OpenAI and Anthropic are indeed close to IPOing, which raises further questions about the price cuts.
IPO Pumping
The timing of these price cuts is notable because both OpenAI and Anthropic are rumored to be IPOing soon—OpenAI in 2027, and Anthropic within a couple months. So far, leaked financials from both OpenAI and Anthropic show unsurprisingly that they are losing billions due to R&D/scaling, albeit in both cases these reports do not account for the hyperexpansion of agentic LLM use over the past few months. Investors will scrutinize the massive negative profits and demand that they have a plan to turn things back around.
So, why did they cut their primary revenue source by up to 80%? That’s the opposite of what you would want to do to look good on an S-1 prospectus! The profit margins on inference themselves likely tell a different story, with some reports saying the profit-per-token margins are as healthy as 80% with caveats. How much of a profit margin do they have after these major cuts?
Speaking personally, the price cuts have indeed affected how I spend on LLM agents, but not in the way I expect OpenAI/Anthropic want their typical customer to behave. I used to have a $100/month subscription to Codex (the 5x Pro plan) when GPT-5.6 Sol was the top model, and I managed to just fully exhaust all the usage included in the subscription despite getting annoyed with random usage resets. Once GPT-6.1 Sol released and I noticed that the cost of using it was effectively cut by 75%, you know what I did?
I cut the max usage quota to 1/5th after getting 4x more efficient usage of the same model, so it ends up roughly neutral and the obvious choice.
In fairness, the profit margins for subscriptions such as Claude Code and Codex are uncertain given their immense value relative to the API usage, and if there are capital crunches I suspect subscription value will be cut before the base price of the models. For example, at the same time GPT-6.1 Sol was announced, OpenAI cut the usage allowance by 50% for the $200/month tier in Codex under the argument “to reflect our increasingly efficient models”—which is technically correct but it’s funny to put in writing.
I will be very curious to see the Anthropic IPO prospectus and the inference profit margins once it becomes public soon.
I also question whether it’s good for OpenAI/Anthropic if they intentionally obsolete their more expensive models. After Opus 5.5 released a month ago, there hasn’t been any discussion about either Fable 5.1 or GPT-6 Astra because Opus 5.5 is just that good.
Top-and-left. via Anthropic
I fully expect a Fable 5.2/GPT-6.1 Astra to release in a couple weeks and prove me wrong, and I will be very curious to see how it will be priced.
Another less-cynical factor that could explain the price cuts is that LLM infrastructure has improved over the past few months—when Anthropic said “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that,” I believe it. One outcome that would be genuinely ironic is that if these models are more compute efficient, it reduces the need for these massive data center buildouts, which could cause cascading economic failures. However, that likely won’t happen since inference is only one part of the compute mix and those data centers are still needed for other parts of the pipeline.
Overall, the price cut is weird, but as a user I’m certainly not complaining! Open-weight models and secondary inference providers will continue to serve as an economic check on the prices of LLMs and other business shenanigans the large labs may concoct. Even if Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s IPOs are catastrophic and cause both companies to fold, it will not suddenly cause LLMs and agents as an industry to die.
I am a former Data Scientist of 9 years currently seeking a job in data science/machine learning/AI in-person in the San Francisco Bay Area, ideally within San Francisco proper. If you found my writing interesting and you’re interested, please let me know at max[at]minimaxir.com!
Max Woolf (@minimaxir) is formerly a Senior Data Scientist at BuzzFeed in San Francisco who works with AI/ML tools and open source projects. Max’s projects are funded by his Patreon.

title: Making the Buddha Head from Merv Whole Again | Getty News
content:
Breadcrumb Navigation
Getty
News & Stories
Making the Buddha Head from Merv Whole Again
Making the Buddha Head from Merv Whole Again
A collaboration between the Getty Museum and the State Museum of Turkmenistan
Topics
Art & ArchitectureScience & Tech
The Buddha head during excavation at Merv, about 1966. © State Museum of Turkmenistan
By Susanne Gänsicke
Mar 11, 2026
Copy Page URL
URL copied to clipboard
Share on Facebook. Opens in new tab.
Share on Twitter. Opens in new tab.
Editor’s Note
Susanne Gänsicke is senior conservator and head of antiquities conservation in the Department of Antiquities at the Getty Museum.
Body Content
I first saw the large head of a Buddha, resting on an earthen pedestal, in historic black-and-white photographs in 2020.
The images were taken some 60 years ago, when the head had just been discovered during excavations by the South Turkmenistan Archaeological Inter-disciplinary Expedition (YuTAKE) of the Academy of Sciences of the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic in the ancient oasis town of Merv. Located in the Karakum Desert of Turkmenistan, the Silk Road city had been occupied since the third millennium BCE and served as a vibrant urban center of enormous wealth (it’s said to have counted one million inhabitants in the 12th century).
The head undergoing emergency stabilization during excavation at Merv, about 1966. © State Museum of Turkmenistan
Sculpted originally from unfired clay around a skeletal framework of wood, straw, and rope, the head once belonged to a much larger sculpture—likely a seated Buddha. This construction method was not merely technical but imbued with ritual meaning, conceived to endow the divine image with body and life.
That figure is lost today, and the head appears to have been separated in antiquity, but what exactly happened remains unknown. It was unearthed in the stupa of a Buddhist monastery within the Gyaur Kala at Merv, an ancient fortress known as the “castle of infidels” because its inhabitants adhered to different faiths—Zoroastrian, Christian, Jewish, and Buddhist—at the time of the Arab conquest. Dated to the fifth–sixth century CE, this Buddha is the westernmost example of its kind and is crucial for understanding Buddhism’s spread.
Fabio Colombo, Susanne Gänsicke, and Giuseppe Salemi on top of the stupa at the Gyaur Kala at Merv. The ramparts of the castle are visible in the distance. Photo courtesy of Maysa Nepesova
Measuring nearly 35½ inches (90 cm) in height, the head dwarfed the archaeologists in the excavation photographs. Little is known about its modern history. It survived almost intact, although with damage on the proper left front and side. The unfired clay made it heavy yet fragile, and moving it would have been difficult. Other images show that decades ago it was cut into four major sections.
The head’s elegantly curved brow and heavy, lidded eye caught my attention five years ago, when the Getty Museum was invited to collaborate with the State Museum of Turkmenistan on the object’s conservation. I recognized both the challenge and promise of this unusual task, as well as the privilege of being invited to build a partnership with Turkmenistan. As the principal investigator, I was responsible for shaping the project’s narrative, defining its technical scope, and developing its timeline and budget. In 2021, Getty was awarded the 30th U.S. Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation grant, supported by the U.S. Embassy in Turkmenistan—an affirmation of the venture’s significance and potential to strengthen cultural ties.
Examination and cleaning begin
Fast forward to the beginning of our project. We formed a team with conservators Fabio Colombo from Rome, Elisa Pannunzio from Venice, and Giuseppe Salemi from Padua University—a specialist in 3D technology and heritage preservation. All brought deep experience in the preservation of Buddhist sculpture in Central and South Asia. So far, we have completed five missions in Ashgabat and expect three more to finalize the conservation. Work also continues remotely.
When we first examined the four surviving head fragments in Ashgabat, only thin outer shells of painted clay remained—like remnants of a giant egg.
Fragments of the head in the conservation laboratory at the State Museum of Turkmenistan. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
The interior matrix had been removed and partially replaced with unsuitable modern materials, such as resin coatings, gauze, and foamed synthetic polymers. The process started with careful examination, documentation, archival research, and discussion with museum staff, scholars, and international colleagues. The head sections were recorded using photogrammetry (with high- and very high–resolution sensors and structured light scanning), allowing 3D visualization and the creation of mathematically accurate models.
After surveying the external surfaces, we digitally modeled their shape (below left) to create 3D- printed shells (below right) that would lend support during treatment.
Data from photogrammetry allowed the creation of 3D-printed shells to support the fragments of the head during treatment. Photo courtesy of Giuseppe Salemi
The shells, held by Giuseppe Salemi and Fabio Colombo, arriving in the laboratory in Ashgabat. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
The conservation intervention began with the meticulous reversal of inappropriate materials applied during earlier restoration campaigns, and we carefully removed the old repairs mechanically from the interior of the head sections. Carried out over several weeks, this proved to be particularly difficult due to the fragility of the inner surfaces and the tenacity of the aged compounds.
Fabio Colombo removing intractable old polyurethane foam with the aid of power tools. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Susanne Gänsicke using a steamer to detach previously applied cotton gauze facings from the interior surface of the smallest head section. Photo courtesy of U.S. Embassy in Turkmenistan
Next, the inner surfaces were cleaned, consolidated, and lined with modern stable materials for support.
The interior of the proper right side of the face: before removing old repair materials, during cleaning, and after cleaning, with some new repair patches. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Fabio Colombo applying new support materials to the interior of the proper right side of the face using Paraloid B72 resin, layers of cotton gauze, and fiberglass. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Then, the sections could be flipped, and work on the front surfaces began. Among the most delicate operations was the detachment of multiple gauze layers adhered previously with starch paste and intended as temporary protection. Carefully lifting the overlapping gauze patches gradually exposed the original surface, revealing for the first time the flesh tones and the vivid blue eye of the largest fragment of the face, previously entirely concealed.
The proper right side of the face with a remaining part of the 3D-printed support shell. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Fabio Colombo and Elisa Pannunzio removing gauze, aided by customized conservation gels, revealing the surface of the face with ancient layers of polychromy. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
The surface and edges of the sections remain soft and brittle, requiring thorough cleaning, consolidation, and the application of suitable backing supports. Notably, the earlier repair had failed to adequately reinforce the thin edges of the sections, which are now warped and deformed, complicating the reassembly of the four main components.
Unifying the head
In our ongoing project, Giuseppe continues to develop 3D models based on the data he has been acquiring.
Giuseppe Salemi capturing the newly exposed surfaces using a structural light scanner. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Slowly we have been developing a concept for unifying the main four parts into the fully sculpted head. The work involves again utilizing 3D-printed supports for the individual sections, this time to line their interiors for structural stability, and building a larger structure on which the head fragments will be reunited.
A preliminary digital 3D reconstruction allows visualization of the volume of the head. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Miniature 3D-printed models of the preliminary reconstruction of the head and the extant parts of the ancient head for modeling their respective positions. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
A major challenge will be the final 3D reconstruction and loss compensation to create a modern interpretation of the head and prepare it for display at the museum.
The four parts of the head, now structurally stable, laid out next to each other for the first time, providing a glimpse of how much remains of their original decoration. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
The proper right sides of the face and head positioned for the first time in a way that allows evaluation of their original connection. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
We also have begun to study the material history of the head, how it was made, how it changed over ancient and modern times, and how it relates to other Buddhist images in the larger region. The face bears layers of red and yellow pigments, with a large blue eye. Multiple color patches suggest ancient repairs and repainting, a common practice, while the molded blue curls of hair appear not to have been retouched. Tiny paint samples analyzed by the Getty Conservation Institute have revealed the multilayered paint and pigment composition. Our goal is to compare our results to other clay sculptures of the era and cultural milieu.
This project extends far beyond its technical scope. Supported by the U.S. Embassy in Turkmenistan and the State Museum of Turkmenistan, it fosters cultural diplomacy and opens avenues for future collaborations. Traveling to archaeological sites—including Merv and the place where the Buddha’s head once lay buried—gave us a vivid sense of context. Encountering even a fragment of Central Asia’s immensity stirred my imagination: millennia of cultural exchange, shifting borders, and layered histories suddenly felt present and alive. Working on the ground, immersed in local rhythms and hospitality, allowed us not only to understand the culture more deeply but also to form the kinds of personal relationships that make this work meaningful.
Ambassador Elizabeth Rood (left) and Nona Majidi (right) of the U.S. Embassy in Turkmenistan discussing the progress of the project with Susanne Gänsicke (center) in May 2025. Photo courtesy of Giuseppe Salemi
Meretgeldy Charyev, director of the State Museum of Turkmenistan, Susanne Gänsicke, Giuseppe Salemi, Elisa Pannunzio, and Fabio Colombo in the conservation laboratory in January 2026.
The result of our efforts will open the door to a new narrative within the museum’s galleries—one that weaves together religion, technical study, conservation methods, and public engagement. Although the original Buddha figure will never be whole again, its restored head will stand as an emblem of Turkmenistan’s heritage and of the role that technology can play in safeguarding the past. When we first arrived, we had no clear sense of what we would find. Yet as the sculpture slowly regains its form, our delight has grown in equal measure. Contributing to its resurrection has been professionally rewarding, yet also demanding, and deeply joyful—an experience made all the richer by sharing it with our colleagues in Ashgabat.

title: Retired Woking decorator's Pokémon cards sell for £1.5m
content:
Retired decorator's Pokémon cards sell for £1.5m
4 days ago
Share
Save
Add as preferred on Google
Joshua Askew
South East
Ewbank's
The auctioneer said there had been an "incredible" buzz before the sale
A retired decorator has become a millionaire after selling a collection of Pokémon cards at auction.
The man, from Woking, said he had no idea the cards had any value until he read in his local newspaper about a single card fetching more than £6,000.
His collection, which had been in an attic for 15 years, was auctioned off at Ewbank's on Wednesday for £1.56m.
The Surrey auction house claimed it was the UK's most valuable trading cards auction ever and suggested it could be a European record.
"I know people always talk about finding treasure in the attic, but in my case that is literally true," said the man, who asked not to be identified.
"When my son was young, in the late 1990s, he started getting cards and swapping them at school.
"I thought they looked nice and wondered whether they might be a good investment.
"He had his own cards, but he never got to touch these, I'm glad to say."
Pokémon is a Japanese franchise best known for its trading cards, video games and animated television series.
The man said he had bought some complete sets of the cards from someone in Malaysia on eBay.
One set which cost him £300 at the time went for £75,000 at Wednesday's auction.
The cards, all filed into bespoke Pokémon binders while still sealed, were stored in the attic after his son lost interest in the franchise.
Global bidders
Ewbank's said "jaws hit the floor" when the man presented his 42 sets of cards to them.
"When we saw what he had – all in mint condition – we couldn't believe it," said James Spooner, its head of trading cards.
The auction house added the sale had been their most successful in more than 30 years in business.
Its top lot was the Legendary Collection Complete Master Set, including a Charizard card in near-mint condition. It had been pitched at £15,000-£20,000 but bagged £100,000.
Ewbank's
The auctioneer said the "buzz was incredible"
Andrew Ewbank, who runs Ewbank's and conducted the sale from the rostrum himself, told bidders he was "going for a lie down" afterwards.
"The build-up to this... has been phenomenal, and on the day it did not disappoint," he added later.
"We had bidders from all over the world.
"The buzz was incredible, especially because the collectors could not believe how good this collection was – extensive, untouched, complete, and with just about every rarity you could hope for."
"It was a hell of a ride," he told the BBC.
Ewbank added that Pokemon was "booming" at the moment.
He said people who were young when the franchise first came out were now in their 30s and 40s and had a "bit of disposable income".
"Nostalgia is a big of part of it," he added.
"It's about bringing back those memories of childhood."
Gotta catch 'em all: Why Pokémon is booming again
Ewbank urged anyone who thought they had something valuable in the attic to "get it down and looked at".
"If you buy something for your son, as happened in this case, and they don't want it, well, maybe pop it away because you never know what value it might have in the future," he said.
The record sum for the Pokemon collection beat the previous best, set only on 9 October in London, when a sale at Stanley Gibbons declared a sale total of £872,000, according to Ewbank's.

title: “We should be more ambitious with the software we build”
content:
Since early this year, Michael Malis (of pgrust) has been showing me interesting things he's done and saying
[W]e should be more ambitious1 with the software we build
There is, understandably, a lot of skepticism about projects like pgrust because there are so many low-quality AI-generated projects out there. If I didn't know Malis and didn't look into it, I would just assume that pgrust was another vibe slopped project that's never going to work. But I know Malis well enough to trust his work without looking into it, and if you look into it a bit, you'll see that in testing pgrust, he's testing thoroughly enough that he's even uncovering real bugs in Postgres, such as this numerical bug that can cause valid SP-GiST operations to fail, this format cache bug that can cause incorrect results from JSONPath, this pgcrypto bug that can cause later operations to fail, multiple memory safety bugs in the dictionary loader2, this money overflow bug, etc.
This isn't to say that pgrust is bug free3, but it does indicate that there's a substantial amount of testing happening and, even if pgrust itself is never successful, just making the attempt will have improved Postgres in a durable way. The main pitch for pgrust is actually performance, and that's where the really interesting work is happening; if pgrust fails, it's possible that some of the optimizations they've demonstrated will make it into Postgres, Clickhouse, etc., but that's obviously less direct than filing Postgres bugs which get fixed.
That being said, I find it understandable that, every time I see pgrust discussed on a news aggregator, most people dismiss it as vibeslop garbage because almost all of these rewrite projects are slop. If I didn't know Malis, I would make the same assumption, because who has the time to look into all of these projects? Because I know Malis, I didn't bother to look at it; I just trusted him (I only found the above because I wanted to check on pgrust before using it as an example for this post).
As a consumer of software, everywhere you look, there's slow software that the creator is claiming is fast because the creator is touting some slop benchmark, e.g., here's one of multiple examples I saw yesterday, and of course low-quality software that doesn't work is more common than ever.
But, as a builder of software, it doesn't matter that almost all of these projects are vibeslop, that other people are out there shoveling out huge piles of crap and calling it gold. You can build things like pgrust or other projects that would've been too large to really be feasible in the past and, if you do a reasonable job with testing and benchmarking, that stuff can actually be good-enough quality to use.
If I were writing it, I would say "we can be more ambitious with the software we build" and not "we should", but Malis has been casually chatting with me when he's said this, so maybe he would say the same in an actual post; don't read too much into should vs. can here. What's interesting to me is how capabilities have advanced such that we can do a lot more.
Just for example, after hearing that OpenAI was going to use Cerebras for their SOTA models and not just fast-but-low-quality models like 5.3-Codex-Spark, I looked at where time on my computer would go if I was using a SOTA model, but 10x to 100x faster; some things that were already sometimes a bottleneck that would only get worse with a faster model were:
Ripgrep
Compiling Rust
Syscall and filesystem overhead
At the level of a "works for me" project, these are all things that can seriously be improved. I don't have much spare time at the moment but, even so, I built this regex engine that can be tweaked to be faster than other general-purpose regex libraries on any particular workload I care about, this ripgrep fork that uses the native code compiler from the regex engine and is faster for my codex ripgrep workloads (of course a text index is the better solution, but I've already worked on text indexing and this was a "just for fun" project where I wasn't trying to do the optimal thing), and a Rust that sped up builds for my projects (huge improvement for cold builds, moderate for warm, limited by wanting to avoid forking the Rust compiler front-end). For syscalls and filesystem overhead, just switching development from Mac to Linux improved this a lot, and of course this is another thing that can be sped up a lot as well, especially when agents are hammering lots of small filesystem operations (it's not uncommon to see my machine waiting on filesystem ops because the standard OS filesystem interface wasn't designed with modern disk performance in mind). With modern disks, there's no reason to use the *nix filesystem API. In the past, writing a developer toolchain that uses direct I/O instead of normal filessytem operations or building a custom OS or a funny layer that fakes out syscalls would've been an absurd endevaor, but that's totally doable now.
For someone like me who doesn't know anything about regexes, string matching algorithms, compilers, interpreters, etc., this set of projects would've taken a year or more to get to "works for me" quality. Instead, this was a low single-digit number of hours of my time. If I wanted to make any of these things meet a "useful product or open source project" quality bar, that would be a lot more work0, but it's still pretty incredible how much this process is sped up.
My read of Malis's meaning when he says “we should be more ambitious with the software we build”, is that it doesn't even occur to people to do these things that are now easy. For weeks, every time I logged into Twitter, I saw someone complain about how Rust compilation is slow and is limiting development velocity (I think this wasn't actually true when I saw the complaints, in that this was before 5.6 Sol and 6 Astra were available on Cerebras, and if you measured where the time actually went, Rust compilation time wasn't actually that much of a bottleneck at the time). Sure, Rust compliation is slow. You can just write a Rust interpreter as well as speed up compilation directly. There are problems like this which I see people complaining about daily that are solvable without a lot of time or effort now. As far as I can tell, these problems are problems because people are implicitly carrying around a pre-agentic cost model. Ten years ago, the kind of person who implemented a new compiler because their compiler was slow was the kind of person who started programming a new 3d game engine when they wanted to make an indie game, i.e., the kind of person who never ships anything. Most productive programmers I know still have an aversion to this kind of thing, even though it is now actually reasonable to implement this kind of thing now4.
Another project I previously mentioned was this Azul AI which is superhuman at matched time controls. When I did that (with GPT-5.1/5.2), with zero AI knowledge, it took about 5 hours of my time to get something superhuman, and about 20 hours of my time to become what appeared to be the strongest AI at the time, including being stronger against humans than this AI that was used to cheat on Board Game Arena. Gabriel Cangussu recently built an AI that demolishes my AI, and AFAICT, it took him substantially less time than my AI took me. From talking to him about it, one key difference is that Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 have a much better understanding of board game AIs. When I used GPT-5.1/5.2, pretty much every suggestion they had was wrong and I had to do a lot of steering to get things to be remotely reasonable. If I had GPT read a codebase or a paper to implement relevant techniques from the paper, it would fail. If I read the paper myself and named a technique, it would say it did the technique, but it would generally do something that superficially looked like the technique but wasn't the actual technique until I issued some corrections. When the model is that far from being able to do the right thing, if you have no background in the area, it's fairly time consuming to check if the model did the right thing since you have to learn enough about what it's supposed to do to be able to check that it did what was claimed.
When I did that project, I said to friends that I didn't think the state models were in could last. It seemed impossible that they wouldn't get good enough to be able to read a paper and implement the techniques soon, and it seemed like they should also be able to pick out codebases and papers to crib from as well. From my experience messing around a bit with Fable 5 and Cangussu's experience with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, that seems to have happened, which is a huge time saver for someone like me who doesn't know anything about board game AIs (I know a little bit now, but still less than any real AI researcher)5.
For any particular domain, like board game AIs, you can say, "who cares? Board game AIs don't matter", but I've found this increase in capability to be true in quite a few different domains. Just for example, I did this toy eval of verification and test techniques with GPT-5.6 Sol implementing zstd on medium and xhigh. I haven't had time to write it up, but when I published that post, I also re-did the evals with GPT-6 Astra. 6 Astra was so good that I had to find different evals because models had advanced too much. For zstd, 6 Astra succeeds at passing all of the registered tests more than 99% of the time across all conditions, even the ones that significantly impair performance, like using TDD (and, BTW, it does it more cheaply as well, taking about $1 to implement zstd). I ended up using the IMAP RFC, which 5.6 Sol couldn't do effectively, and Pandoc, which is a pretty major thing to implement as it needs to be able to read and write many different formats6.
BTW, when people have said they used the new model and everything just works, software is solved, etc., I haven't found this to be true at all. It's true that there are a lot more things the newer model can one-shot, where things basically just work, but this just means that I end up working on more ambitious things where models still struggle7. I'm more productive and can work faster, but I find that, in terms of what I'm doing, I get farther from "it just works" with each more capable model because the gap between what the model can verify effectively without significant handholding and what the model can implement has been increasing8. All of that is a long-winded and less eloquent way of saying: we should be more ambitious with the software we build.
Thanks to Laurence Tratt, Yossi Kreinin, Alex Kolovsky, and Michael Malis for comments/corrections/discussion.
I've had this note on my recent posts, which also applies to this one. In order to get more posts out, I'm trying to crank posts out in half an hour and not review them much. This definitely means less well-supported posts. If I were writing this in my standard style, I would've had comprehensive benchmarks for all of my projects that I mentioned. Instead, I did a quick comparison that satisfied my curiosity and am writing this up without rigorous benchmarking, and there are maybe twenty or thirty things in this post that I'd like to do but haven't done.
I haven't even written up this Rust interpreter. If, five years ago, I'd cobbled together a Rust interpreter that got a 50x speedup on cold compiles and 2x on warm/cached builds (with much more being possible if edits to the Rust compiler were in bounds), that woudl be a super interestin thing that I'd want to write up, but even operating in this mode where I barely edit posts and just blast them out, this isn't interesting enough to write up because it's so easy to do things that would've been considered very interesting not all that long ago.
Appendix: we should be less ambitious with the software we build
Here's a comment from Yossi Kreinin, quoted (with permission, of course):
If you publish this I will publish a response explaining that for most people they should be less ambitious with the software they build with AI or they'll experience abject failure. I think a lot of the problems don't lend themselves that well to "agentic loops" since you don't have clear pass/fail criteria, and even when you do most people have trouble reasoning about giant black boxes which they can impose constraints on but can't understand the innards of [I include myself in this set.] This is a little bit like microservices I guess, where some people both need it and are very good at using it but likely for most people, they need it less and can't use it well at all. I sort of envy the ones who should and actually can be this ambitious about the software they build of course; not saying you shouldn't be more ambitious at all but moderating said ambition is a big part of handling the current situation for most I think
I have a similar thought about "there's no reason for software to be slow" BTW; in many cases, if you use AI to speed up some flow, you will add a bunch of messy code that will be overfit for the use case you tested on and will neither generalize, perf-wise, for all the use cases you should care about, nor will be maintainable upon future changes. If you know what you're doing and you understand how the system should be decomposed into parts and when it makes sense to go all-in on optimizing some part or a combination of them working together and how to properly benchmark it, etc., then things are great, but if for instance you have a manager who thinks there's no reason for software to be slow and he pushes people to use AI to make random parts of the software fast... Run for cover
My feeling is that, overall, the situation here is a bit analogous to the discussion here about why I don't like when people talk about how AI gives a 100x or 1000x productivity increase. There are some things that are sped up by a very large factor, easily over 1000000x. And some things don't currently get sped up at all. If you do exactly what you would've done five years ago, but with AI, the speedup is fairly poor because of Amdahl's law. But, in the general case, you can choose what to speed up and if you're looking for things that are productive to do, this often seems to involve things that were previously too expensive to do.
And, I think that you can often set up systems that have some kind of self-checking property even when most people wouldn't. This discussion of the implementation of Guards of Atlantis 2 is an example of that. It's a poor choice for an AI project because the official rules are a mess of ambiguous and contradictory English text (it's probably the game I've seen humans misplay at the highest rate, and the rules are confusing enough that the designer has often changed their mind about what their own rules mean despite continually maintaining that the rules are perfectly clear and one can play the game by simply reading the rules as written). title: I refuse to accept a censored Internet. Join Me at FOSDEM 27 – Bogomil Shopov – Бого
content:
I refuse to accept a censored Internet. Join Me at FOSDEM 27
October 25, 2026 by Bogomil Shopov
As one of the managers of the Digital Dissident Devroom, I invite you to be part of a conversation we cannot afford to ignore.
Around the world, people are being silenced, monitored, and denied access to information. Free software can help change that, but only if we build it together. We need tools people can trust and control to communicate safely, expose the truth, and resist censorship.
This devroom brings together developers, researchers, activists, and everyone committed to digital freedom. We want real solutions, honest lessons, and collaboration across projects, not product pitches.
If you believe technology should serve people, not control them, join us. Bring your ideas, experience, and questions. Let’s build the tools that help keep freedom alive.
Our focus complements other devrooms, including Decentralized Internet and Privacy, which explores the broader decentralized ecosystem. While they focus on technologies, we focus on the people under threat and the complete chain of tools that can protect them.
How to apply to speak at the dev room?
Go to FOSDEM’s official CFP portal from here and login or register.
Click on “Submit a proposal”
Then fill in the form and select “Digital Dissident” as a track.
Done!
Please note that by doing this you also accept the FOSDEM Code of Conduct.
Define: Digital Dissident Developer Room
Privacy and anonymity tools each have a home at FOSDEM: the network, security, decentralised and messaging rooms, and various main-track and lightning talks. Someone living under an authoritarian regime (Russia, Iran, China, Belarus, Myanmar and others) never uses a single tool, though. Their day-to-day security depends on a chain of tools that has to hold up end to end:
reaching the network at all (censorship circumvention),
communicating without leaking metadata,
collecting, verifying and storing evidence safely,
publishing or leaking it without exposing the author,
doing all this on devices and infrastructure that are themselves a risk.
The weakest link decides the outcome. Talks about one tool rarely cover how it fits with the others, where the seams are, or what breaks at the hand-offs (for example, a circumvention transport that is fingerprinted, or a messenger whose push notifications tie your identity to a Google or Apple account). Nobody currently owns that cross-project view.
What this devroom does. It brings developers of circumvention, anonymity, messaging, publishing and whistleblowing tools into one room. It is deliberately not about any single project. Each session is judged on how well it advances the toolchain: interoperability, shared threat models, shared failure data, and shared engineering practice.
Why now. Censorship in Russia, Iran and China has grown much more sophisticated. It now includes national allow-lists and whitelist-only internet shutdowns, TLS and QUIC fingerprinting, deep packet inspection with active probing, throttling of specific protocols, mobile internet shutdowns, app-store removal of circumvention tools, and mandatory state-run messengers and “sovereign internet” routing. Anti-censorship developers have responded with pluggable transports, domain fronting alternatives, mixnets, decentralised and email-based messaging, and new obfuscation protocols. Progress is fast but fragmented. At FOSDEM 2026 the relevant talks were scattered: Vitaly Repin’s “The Russian Censorship Circumvention, Tom’s Traps, and Jerry’s VPN: A 5-Year Journey” (Saturday, H.1302, Network track) drew a large audience, while NymVPN and Delta Chat’s multi-relay messaging (both Sunday, Decentralized Internet and Privacy devroom) and other related talks ran in other rooms. A single devroom lets that audience and those speakers meet in one place.
Relationship to the existing “Decentralized Internet and Privacy” devroom. That room covers decentralised technology broadly (P2P protocols, browsers, code collaboration, key infrastructure), and censorship or anonymity is only a part of it. Digital Dissident is different: the organising principle is a user under threat and the end-to-end chain that protects them, not a technology class. We want to work with, not against, that room, and will coordinate schedules so the two don’t overlap, and will point overflow speakers to whichever room fits.
Themes (details in the CfP below):
Censorship circumvention and transport: obfuscation, fingerprint resistance, active-probing defence, bridge distribution, resilience to protocol whitelisting and full shutdowns.
Metadata-resistant communication: mixnets, onion routing, decentralised and federated messengers, store-and-forward and offline-first (mesh, sneakernet, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi Direct).
Secure reporting and publishing: whistleblowing platforms, source protection, document sanitisation, provenance and authenticity, censorship-resistant hosting.
Devices and operational security: hardened mobile and desktop systems, amnesic systems, seizure and border-crossing scenarios, forensic resistance.
Usability and threat modelling for at-risk users: onboarding under duress, safe defaults, training, measuring what really works in the field.
Measurement and adversary analysis: how censors detect and block, open data on blocking events, reproducible censorship research.
Digital sovereignty from Big Tech (secondary theme): reducing dependence on centralised platforms, app stores, push infrastructure, cloud and identity providers, both for individuals and for civil-society organisations.
Structure. A mix of formats to keep a full room engaged across the whole session:
20 to 30 minute technical talks
A closing open discussion on interoperability gaps and shared next steps
Programme quality. Organisers will review all submissions on technical merit and fit to the toolchain framing, and will aim for a balance of projects, regions and speakers (established projects, new projects, researchers, people from affected communities). Every talk should include an explicit threat model and an honest account of limitations.
Projects and communities we intend to invite (no commitments yet): Nym (mixnet), Delta Chat / chatmail, SimpleX, the Fediverse (ActivityPub implementations and instance operators), Nostr, Psiphon and other circumvention and VPN providers, plus Tor-ecosystem, Reticulum and mesh-networking projects, whistleblowing and secure-submission platforms, and censorship-measurement researchers. Several of these projects presented at FOSDEM 2026.
Code of Conduct. We will follow the FOSDEM Code of Conduct. In addition, talks that describe circumvention or anonymity should avoid operational details that would endanger specific users in the field.
Important Dates
Sat, 24 October 2026: Call for Participation opens
Mon, 30 November 2026, 23:59 UTC: Call for Participation ends
Wed, 2 December 2026: Speakers notified
Fri, 4 December 2026: Deadline for speakers to confirm
Mon, 7 December 2026: Schedule published
The twenty-sixth edition of FOSDEM will take place on Saturday 30th and Sunday 31st January 2027 at the usual location, ULB Campus Solbosch in Brussels.

title: GitHub - KillaBoi/StealMyBitcoin-PoC: A public release of the Steal My Bitcoin challenge · GitHub
content:
sponsored with ❤️ by Steal My Bitcoin CTF proof of concept One live PHP callback against the Steal My Bitcoin challenge, start to finish, in a single standard-library Python file. This README explains stealmybitcoin_poc.py, a single-file Python reproduction of the request sequence used in my Steal My Bitcoin CTF run. It uses only Python's standard library. The script builds the requests itself, checks each leak before moving on, and records the HTTP bytes from a new run. This can probably be done easier without all the extra debug crap and as in my John Hammond video about the Steam Local Privilege Escalation I discovered, you could probably clean up this ugly PoC. Note ⚠️ Honestly please clean it up or make your own better version that isn't crumpled by Sol. ⚠️ Everything below is written against the Docker lab, not the live challenge. The lab is a local Alpine PHP 8.4.26 CLI server behind nginx, which is the same build and worker model the offsets were calibrated on. Stand it up in a minute and the whole chain runs end to end on your own machine. The live run that actually solved the challenge is kept as a historical note at the bottom. stage what goes out what comes back ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 0 health GET /php-version.php -> PHP 8.4.26 confirmed 1 heap leak 249,042 B producer + 8 x 6,672 B -> 256 B cookie (OOM poisons a worker) └─ Zend chunk base 2 code leak 251,557 B producer + 8 x 92,388 B -> 16 B cookie (OOM poisons a worker) └─ zval_ptr_dtor 3 callback 368,812 B POST -> forged HashTable runs (fake HashTable + command) └─ zif_system(cmd) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 20 HTTP requests at most. No looping, no retries. The short version A small multipart upload makes PHP chew through far more memory than the wire size suggests. When it runs out of memory partway through session upload-progress parsing, PHP leaves stale state behind in a worker that then gets reused. Shape the follow-up requests right and bytes fall out through session cookies. I read those as a heap address and a PHP code address. With both addresses, a final request drops a forged PHP structure where cleanup will find it, and cleanup calls zif_system, PHP's handler for system. That command sends back a fresh proof marker and one print-flag result over the connection that is still open. Why two addresses? The OS randomizes where PHP's code and heap land, independently. The heap leak tells the script where to put the forged structure, the code leak tells it where the function it wants to call actually lives. Addresses from an earlier worker or an earlier run are not safe substitutes, and every time I tried it the attempt just failed. Contents The lab Start here What each request does 1. How a small producer reaches the memory limit 2. How the heap address is recovered 3. How the PHP code address is recovered 4. How the final request reaches system Reading the result How often it actually works The live run that solved it Jargon, briefly Thanks The lab The offsets in this PoC are calibrated for Alpine PHP 8.4.26 running the built-in CLI server with four workers. The lab reproduces exactly that, behind nginx, on loopback. Important The build matters more than the version string. A Debian php:8.4.26-fpm stack reports the same PHP/8.4.26 but has a different binary layout, so the code-pointer fingerprint will never match and the run aborts at the code-leak stage. Use the Alpine image below. Three small files. Put them in an empty directory: public/php-version.php (the health endpoint, and the only page the PoC needs) Fatal error: Allowed memory size of 134217728 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 131072 bytes) in Unknown on line 0
1ef0e73d8615157a uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),0(root),1(bin),2(daemon),3(sys),4(adm),6(disk),10(wheel),11(floppy),20(dialout),26(tape),27(video) 0ec066e8b91457c7c19b5612f3e2ded7f117df08f402693669c1ffc2cfc24942 /usr/local/bin/print-flag LOCAL_DUMMY_WIF_NEVER_USE The PHP fatal, then the nonce this run generated, then id, then the hash of the binary it resolved, then the dummy flag. Exit status is 0 on a verified run and 1 on anything else. Warning The producer deliberately walks PHP into its memory limit. Only run this somewhere that behaviour is authorized. The script will only talk to the challenge endpoint or a loopback lab URL, and anything else aborts before a packet goes out. One run means one health GET, up to two leak batches, and at most one final request. No looping, no retries. Every multipart body stays under 1 MiB, though each leak batch pipelines nine separate requests down one connection. Flag What it does --url Lab endpoint, or the challenge. Required to do anything. --output-dir Where to write the run's evidence. Defaults to poc-run-. What each request does Step What goes out, what should come back Why Health One ordinary GET /php-version.php must return HTTP 200, PHP 8.4.26, and X-Powered-By: PHP/8.4.26. Keeps the memory-limit payload away from a changed or unhealthy endpoint. Heap leak One 249,042-byte multipart producer, then eight pipelined 6,672-byte consumers. The producer must return a PHP 128 MiB memory-limit fatal. A consumer may return a 256-byte PHPSESSID cookie. Four or more pointer-looking values in that cookie have to agree on one aligned 2 MiB Zend heap base. Code leak One 251,557-byte producer, then eight pipelined 92,388-byte consumers. A consumer may return a 16-byte PHPSESSID cookie. Its first eight bytes must encode 16, and its second eight must look like the locally calibrated zval_ptr_dtor pointer. Final callback One 368,812-byte multipart POST. A forged PHP HashTable points cleanup at zif_system and supplies a command argument. The fresh nonce, id output, and print-flag binary hash are the evidence that the callback actually ran. That is 20 HTTP requests at most: one health check, nine per leak batch, one final request. All eight consumers in a batch go out before the first response is read, which helps the timing, but it also means you cannot pull them back if the producer fails. A failed or malformed batch stops the next stage. 1. How a small producer reaches the memory limit The producer is multipart/form-data carrying PHPSESSID and PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS fields. PHP handles upload progress while it is still parsing the request. Hundreds of empty file controls get names like f[0][x][x]... with dozens of nested [x] segments, so the body stays around 250 KiB on the wire while parsing it spawns piles of nested PHP arrays and all the allocations that come with them. The producer also carries 1,001 distinct empty cookie names, which is what the request builder was configured to send at the time. The fatal you want says PHP exhausted its 128 MiB memory limit. What you are actually after is the stale state this particular failure leaves behind in a worker. Important On its own, a memory-limit fatal or an nginx 502 proves nothing about an address leak or code execution. 2. How the heap address is recovered The next request goes after the memory tied to that stale session state. It repeats a single numeric form key, then slips in a crafted value that changes the length PHP uses when it writes PHPSESSID. Land on the right reused worker with the right heap layout and the cookie comes back 256 bytes instead of the usual 32, with neighbouring heap data sitting inside it. heap_candidate() walks that cookie as little-endian 64-bit words, and will only accept a base if at least four pointer-looking values fall in the same aligned 2 MiB heap region. On top of that the runner wants HTTP 200, the expected PHP version, valid cookie lengths from all eight consumers, and exactly one agreed base. Anything short of that and it stops. 3. How the PHP code address is recovered A second producer triggers the same memory-limit condition. Its consumer uses a different array layout, calibrated locally to shake out a PHP function pointer. The cookie you want is exactly 16 bytes: an eight-byte value of 16, then a pointer read as zval_ptr_dtor against the Alpine PHP fingerprint. The script checks the pointer's range and its low 21 bits, 0x112930. That is the page offset of the symbol in the Alpine PHP 8.4.26 image, and ASLR does not move it. Treat it as a fingerprint, not as proof the remote executable is byte for byte the same thing. For this layout, zif_system works out as: zif_system = zval_ptr_dtor - 0x204BC0 Both leaks have to come from the current invocation. The script will not load historical pointer values into a live attempt. 4. How the final request reaches system The final POST parks a 384-byte forged HashTable in a multipart field I control. That structure overlaps a fake call frame and a fake zend_string holding the command. A 276-byte primer supplies a pointer into the controlled region, then a long form-field name drives another memory-limit failure. In the cleanup path, PHP reads the forged table's pDestructor as zif_system and hands it the string argument. 0x00 ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ zend_array header │ pDestructor -> zif_system 0x20 ├──────────────────────────┤ │ bucket / fake call frame │ arg1 -> zend_string below 0x80 ├──────────────────────────┤ │ zend_string header │ 0x98 ├──────────────────────────┤ │ command (231 B max) │ 0x180 └──────────────────────────┘ The target address uses a distance measured in the four-worker Alpine setup: fake_table = zend_heap_base - 0x8400000 + 0x16D1D8 That distance depends on the worker and the allocation layout. Change the image, the memory configuration, or the worker count and this falls over even though the PHP version still reads 8.4.26. The command that originally worked just ran print-flag once. This version prints a fresh random nonce, the output of id (UID and GID), and the SHA-256 of the resolved print-flag binary before invoking print-flag once. It hunts down the active accepted socket under /proc/self/fd so the output actually reaches the HTTP response. Ordinary process stdout got me nothing. Reading the result Every run drops a new poc-run- directory, unless --output-dir points at a new one. Everything is written before it is validated, so a run that aborts halfway still leaves usable evidence. The files worth opening: File Contents heap.request.http, code.request.http The plaintext HTTP bytes handed to each leak-stage socket's sendall, one producer plus eight pipelined consumers. If the transport fails you cannot be sure what actually got delivered. heap.response.http, code.response.http Plaintext HTTP bytes read back off each leak-stage socket, cookies included. heap.json, code.json Parsed response status, lengths, hashes, and candidate addresses. final.request.http The final request as constructed, headers and multipart body. Same caveat about transport failures. final.response.http, final.response.body, final.response.headers.json The final response as read, plus its parsed body and headers. Against the live challenge this body may contain a private WIF. final.json, run.json Summary fields, and whether the expected execution markers showed up. execution_proof_verified: true means the final response came back HTTP 200 carrying the fresh nonce, an id result, and a SHA-256 line for print-flag. Caution Against the real challenge a run directory can contain a live private key. Publish this source file, not a run's output. The script makes no claim about whether a returned WIF controls the advertised Bitcoin address. A checksum-valid WIF only tells you the string encodes a private key properly. Deriving the address and comparing it is a separate job. How often it actually works Both leak stages are races against three other workers, so a single run is not expected to succeed every time. title: Eunice is almost here
content:
Eunice is almost here
25 October 2026
William Gibson's Agency (2020) is a mind-bending science fiction novel. Without getting lost in its intricate plot, one storyline takes place in an alternate San Francisco in 2017, where a young woman named Verity is hired to test an experimental AI assistant called Eunice.
At one point, we encounter this extraordinary exchange:
Verity: "Where'd you get this? It's wrong."
Eunice: "This no-name account, in Zurich. Part of me knew it was there, how to get it, how to get it here. Plenty more, but if I tried it again, they'd be on us."
Verity: "Who?"
Eunice: "Fuck knows."
Verity: "When did you have time to do any of that?"
Eunice: "Started when we were looking out the window. Before we left, up to the park, it was already points."
Verity: "Points?"
Eunice: "Frequent flyer. There's a global market, buy or sell. Hard to track..."
Verity looked at the green bag.
Verity: "You did this since I turned you on?"
Gibson published Agency nearly three years before ChatGPT's release, and six years before the emergence of today's increasingly autononomous AI agents.
We now have GPT-Live and emerging models like Block's Dessa, bringing us remarkably human-like full-duplex conversations. Meanwhile, OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse are introducing 24/7 agents capable of independently pursuing goals, taking action, and working in the background.
What makes Eunice remarkable isn't just that she can talk, it's that she's doing so much else while talking. The pieces are coming together.
As always, Gibson was right on the money. Eunice is almost here.

DOLLY PARTON’S IMAGINATION LIBRARY
Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library is dedicated to inspiring a love of reading by gifting books free of charge to children from birth to age five, through funding shared by Dolly Parton and local community partners in the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia and Republic of Ireland.
Inspired by her father’s inability to read and write Dolly started her Imagination Library in 1995 for the children within her home county. Today, her program spans five countries and gifts millions of free books each month to children around the world.
“When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee, I knew my dreams would come true. I know there are children in your community with their own dreams. They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer.
The seeds of these dreams are often found in books and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world.”
In 1995, Dolly Parton launched an exciting new effort, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, to benefit the children of her home county in East Tennessee, USA. Dolly’s vision was to foster a love of reading among her county’s preschool children and their families by providing them with the gift of a specially selected book each month.

title: Overgrown, when plants invade your abandoned tabs | Charlie Gerard | Senior research engineer & Creative Technologist Charlie Gerard | Senior research engineer & Creative Technologist
content:
Charlie Gerard
Projects
Speaking
Blog
Overgrown, when plants invade your abandoned tabs
20/10/2026
I was doing a little creative exercise the other day around the word "Overgrowth". The first thing that came to mind was an apocalyptic scene, something like The Walking Dead or The Last of Us, where plants tend to overgrow abandoned buildings.
I then wanted to apply this idea to the digital world, and the word "abandoned" made me think of my browser tabs... What if my tabs were slowly taken over by plants the longer I left them unread? What if I had to clear away these invasive plants to access my tabs again? A bit like trying to open a door that's been overgrown...
So I built this fun little Chrome extension that does just that. It won't necessarily make me read my tabs more but it's ok.
Demo
Link to the repository
The idea
Every tab has a neglect clock. It runs while the tab is out of view and stops while you're looking at it.
The longer a tab is neglected, the more plants grow over it, from the edges towards the middle.
Once a tab is more than 5% overgrown, the page behind the vines is walled off: you can scroll, but you can't click, select or drag anything.
To free it, you have to slash through the vines by dragging your mouse across them. Get it down to 5% and the last bits fall off. If you abandon your tab once more, the jungle starts growing again.
Just for fun, you can pick your weapon of choice between the rusty machete, the chainsaw and the flamethrower.
You can also change how long it takes for your tabs to be fully overgrown.
Originally, I was thinking about blocking users from closing their overgrown tabs until they slash all plants, but I thought it would be too annoying... 😅
The extension
The code is organised in 3 main parts: the background logic, the content script to display the plants and animation on the tabs and the popup folder that handles the UI of the extension itself.
Background worker
The background.js file starts the jungle on each open tab and forgets it when it closes.
The popup
This folder handles the UI for the extension with some small components for the time setting, the weapon choice, the list of tabs and their current stat.
The overlay
The content folder contains the SVGs for the plants and the weapons, the logic to position and grow the clusters, the neglect clock and the sounds.
I've been wanting to get back into building things for a while now and this project felt like a small, fun way to start. I'm writing this on a new computer so I currently "only" have 22 tabs open but 14 of them are already completely overgrown... 😂 It might not make me read them more but slashing through the vines makes coming back to them more fun! 🪚🌿

title: GitHub - KrushnaVardhanReddy/PaperPilot: Your local AI copilot for documents · GitHub
content:
PaperPilot PDF tools for your AI agent — and for you. Pure Rust. Runs locally. Files never leave your machine. Try it in your browser → · Download · Roadmap PaperPilot is a PDF and document toolkit written in Rust. The same engine runs as: Surface Use it for MCP server Give Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any MCP client the ability to merge, split, OCR, and compress PDFs CLI Batch and scripted workflows Browser (WASM) Zero-install tools; files are processed in browser memory, nothing is uploaded Desktop app Tauri + Svelte GUI with viewer, markup, and diff Local REST API Call it from Python, Node, or n8n at localhost:7823 No Chromium, no C++ runtime, no cloud calls. Quick start 1. Use it with Claude / Cursor (MCP) Download paperpilot-mcp from Releases, then add it to claude_desktop_config.json: { "mcpServers": { "paperpilot": { "command": "/path/to/paperpilot-mcp" } } } Restart Claude and try: "Merge these two PDFs and compress the result." 2. Use the CLI # Merge paperpilot merge --inputs doc1.pdf doc2.pdf --output merged.pdf # Compress paperpilot compress --input in.pdf --quality 75 --output compressed.pdf # Rotate pages 1, 3–5 by 90° paperpilot rotate --input in.pdf --pages 1,3-5 --angle 90 --output out.pdf 3. Use it in the browser Go to usepaperpilot.com. Open your browser's Network tab while you work — you'll see no file uploads. 4. Build from source git clone https://github.com/KrushnaVardhanReddy/PaperPilot.git cd PaperPilot cargo build --release -p paperpilot-cli -p paperpilot-mcp -p paperpilot-gateway Desktop app: cd apps/desktop && pnpm install && pnpm tauri dev Requires Rust 1.75+, Node.js, and pnpm. What it can do today (v0.6) Organize: merge, split, rotate, delete pages, reorder pages, extract pages, booklet imposition, N-up grid Optimize: compress Extract: plain text, OCR (pure-Rust PaddleOCR via rten) Security: watermark, validate signatures, remove signatures, PII scan, deep sanitize Office data: Excel → JSON, Excel → CSV Coming next (see ROADMAP.md): v0.7: PDF ↔ Markdown / HTML / JSON v0.8: PDF → Word / Excel / PowerPoint v0.9: encrypt, decrypt, sign, redact, forms, annotations v1.0: render, flatten, repair, compare, PDF/A, Bates numbering Why another PDF tool? Private by default. Everything runs locally or in your browser tab. Agent-ready. MCP support is first-class, not an afterthought. One engine, many surfaces. CLI, MCP, REST, WASM, and desktop share the same Rust core, so behavior is consistent. Small and dependency-light. Pure Rust, built on lopdf, pdf_oxide, rten, and friends. Benchmarks Run cargo bench --workspace to reproduce. Methodology and results: SYSTEM_BENCHMARK_REPORT.md. Architecture Desktop (Tauri) · CLI · REST (Axum) · MCP (stdio) · WASM (browser / edge) │ Rust core workspace paperpilot-core · paperpilot-pdf · paperpilot-nlp · paperpilot-gateway paperpilot-mcp · paperpilot-wasm · paperpilot-storage Embed in your own site
Local REST API paperpilot serve --port 7823 curl -X POST http://localhost:7823/api/v1/pdf/merge \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"inputs": ["a.pdf", "b.pdf"], "output": "out.pdf"}' Swagger docs at http://localhost:7823/docs. Contributing Issues and PRs are welcome. Good first contributions: bug reports with a sample PDF, new tool requests, and docs fixes. License Community Edition (this repo): Apache 2.0. It includes the CLI, MCP server, REST gateway, WASM engine, and desktop app. An Enterprise Edition (SSO, RBAC, audit logs, DLP) is developed separately.

title: [2512.19428] Attention Is Not What You Need
content:
Computer Science > Machine Learning
[Submitted on 22 Dec 2025]
Attention Is Not What You Need
Zhang Chong
We revisit a basic question in sequence modeling: is explicit self-attention actually necessary for strong performance and reasoning? We argue that standard multi-head attention is best seen as a form of tensor lifting: hidden vectors are mapped into a high-dimensional space of pairwise interactions, and learning proceeds by constraining this lifted tensor through gradient descent. This mechanism is extremely expressive but mathematically opaque, because after many layers it becomes very hard to describe the model with a small family of explicit invariants.
To explore an alternative, we propose an attention-free architecture based on Grassmann flows. Instead of forming an L by L attention matrix, our Causal Grassmann layer (i) linearly reduces token states, (ii) encodes local token pairs as two-dimensional subspaces on a Grassmann manifold via Plucker coordinates, and (iii) fuses these geometric features back into the hidden states through gated mixing. Information therefore propagates by controlled deformations of low-rank subspaces over multi-scale local windows, so the core computation lives on a finite-dimensional manifold rather than in an unstructured tensor space.
On the Wikitext-2 language modeling benchmark, purely Grassmann-based models with 13 to 18 million parameters achieve validation perplexities within about 10 to 15 percent of size-matched Transformers. On the SNLI natural language inference task, a Grassmann-Plucker head on top of DistilBERT slightly outperforms a Transformer head, with best validation and test accuracies of 0.8550 and 0.8538 compared to 0.8545 and 0.8511. We analyze the complexity of Grassmann mixing, show linear scaling in sequence length for fixed rank, and argue that such manifold-based designs offer a more structured route toward geometric and invariant-based interpretations of neural reasoning.
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Algebraic Geometry (math.AG)
