Email address
Subscribe
Free, once a week. Unsubscribe any time.
Microsoft named four core use cases for the model at launch: routing, classification, prioritization, and verification, plus what it calls workflow control. Think of a support ticket that needs to be routed to the right team, a piece of user content that needs a yes/no moderation call, or an AI agent’s output that needs a pass/fail check before it’s allowed to proceed. Those are high-volume, low-latency decisions, and they’re exactly the kind of task that a 9-billion-parameter specialist model can do more cheaply than a full-sized reasoning model.
ADVERTISEMENT
The distinction matters for anyone building with large language models today. A chatbot generates a response and you have to parse it, guess at its confidence, and hope it followed your formatting instructions. A decision-scoring model skips that parsing step entirely: the output format is already a probability distribution over options you defined. That’s a smaller, more mechanical problem, and it’s one Microsoft is betting plenty of production systems have in volume.
YOU MAY LIKE
Nace.AI Opens Drex 1.5: 9B Model Scores 58.08 [2026]
Smilegate Founder Ordered to Pay $1.9B Divorce [2026]
Jaguar Land Rover Cyber Attack: £1.9B Hit [2026]
Inside the Model: Why Qwen3.5-9B as the Base
The detail that generated the most commentary wasn’t the use case, it was the foundation. Microsoft-Decision-1 is post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B, a 9-billion-parameter open-weight model from Alibaba. The Register flagged the choice directly, framing the launch as Microsoft leaning on a Chinese AI lab’s open-weight release to get the product out the door quickly, while noting Microsoft’s own stated intent to migrate the model’s foundation over time.
Microsoft has been explicit that this is a starting point, not a destination. In its launch post, the company said: “To build Microsoft-Decision-1, we post trained Qwen3.5-9B for fast, single-pass decision scoring and will soon rebase it on other models, including Microsoft AI (MAI) and OpenAI.” That’s a notable admission for a company that has poured billions into its own model development through the Microsoft Foundry platform and its OpenAI partnership. It suggests the Qwen base was chosen for speed to market on a narrow, well-defined task, not as a long-term architectural commitment.
Using someone else’s open-weight model as scaffolding isn’t unusual in 2026. Plenty of smaller, task-specific tools get built this way, the same logic that drove projects like JetBrains’ Mellum2.1 coding model to pick a compact parameter count over raw scale. What’s notable here is that it’s Microsoft, a company with its own frontier model ambitions, publicly choosing a rival lab’s weights for a flagship-named product, then telling customers up front that the underlying engine will change later.
The Benchmark Claims: 36 Tests, Nearly 150,000 Questions
Microsoft is leaning hard on numbers to justify the product. The company says Decision-1 achieved the highest accuracy across a comparison spanning 36 benchmarks and approximately 150,000 held-out questions, a scale meant to signal breadth rather than a single cherry-picked test. Microsoft reported 83.5 percent accuracy across that evaluation, a figure the German outlet BornCity also relayed.
Speed claims followed the same pattern of big, specific numbers. Industry newsletter AI Weekly and the AI-tracking site TestingCatalog both reported that Microsoft claims Decision-1 runs 4.5 times faster than a model it calls Quyet-1.0-Large, and 35 times faster than GPT-6 Sol. A separate write-up from Data Studios led with the 35x figure as its headline framing. Microsoft’s own launch material describes the GPT-6 Sol result as approximately 35× lower P50 latency, measured on its own benchmark, and says Decision-1 was 2.5× faster than H2O-Lightning-4B v1.1, the runner-up in its comparison. That is a specific P50 measurement rather than a general-purpose speed advantage, since the systems perform different tasks: Decision-1 scores fixed options while GPT-6 Sol generates text. Taiwan’s Liberty Times reported response times in the neighborhood of 85 milliseconds, though it didn’t specify the hardware or test conditions behind that number.
Here’s where a healthy dose of skepticism belongs. These are Microsoft’s own benchmark results, reported through the company’s launch materials and relayed by outlets covering the announcement. None of the coverage reviewed for this piece includes an independent, third-party reproduction of the 36-benchmark comparison, the 4.5x and 35x speed multipliers, or the 85-millisecond latency figure. That doesn’t make the numbers false, but it does mean they should be read as vendor-reported performance claims rather than peer-reviewed results, at least until someone outside Microsoft runs the same tests.
One figure got less attention but may matter more in production: Microsoft says the model’s decisions were “perturbation-stable” 98.7 percent of the time, according to the company’s launch summary cited by AI Weekly. Stability under small input changes is a real concern for any model making binary or multi-option calls that downstream systems act on automatically. If a routing decision flips because of a trivial rewording, that’s a production bug waiting to happen, so a high stability number, if it holds up under outside testing, would be a genuinely useful data point for engineering teams evaluating the model.
Pricing: $0.042 per Million Input Tokens, Free Output
Microsoft’s own announcement and Microsoft Foundry documentation don’t publish a confirmed price in the sources reviewed for this article. What’s circulating instead comes from OpenRouter’s own model listing and was picked up by AI Weekly and the Italian outlet Pasquale Pillitteri: $0.042 per million input tokens, with output free. That pricing structure makes sense for a model whose entire output is a short list of probability scores rather than generated text, since there’s effectively nothing to meter on the output side.
At that price, Decision-1 is positioned as a genuinely cheap option for high-volume routing and classification work, the kind of task that currently gets routed to smaller general-purpose models mostly because nobody wants to pay full-model prices to ask “is this spam, yes or no.” It’s a similar cost logic to what pushed Anthropic to cut Claude Haiku pricing by 75 percent earlier this year: cheap, fast models win the high-frequency, low-complexity slice of the API traffic pie, even when a flagship model would technically do the job too.
Availability: Foundry First, OpenRouter Close Behind
Microsoft-Decision-1 launched in public preview on Microsoft Foundry, where documentation describes it as available for classification, routing, ranking, grading, and binary decisions. Microsoft’s launch post initially described OpenRouter availability as “coming soon,” but OpenRouter’s own model listing confirmed the model had gone live under the identifier microsoft/microsoft-decision-1 within roughly a day of the announcement, with OpenRouter posting that it was “live on OpenRouter.”
ADVERTISEMENT
Weights for the model aren’t being distributed, based on reporting from Data Studios, meaning developers access Decision-1 exclusively through hosted APIs rather than downloading and self-hosting it, a contrast with the fully open Qwen3.5-9B it’s built on. That’s a common pattern for commercial derivatives of open-weight models, but it’s worth flagging for teams that assumed a Qwen-based product would come with the same openness as the base model.
Working With Decision-1 in Foundry
The model accepts text and supports inputs up to 32,000 tokens. It returns calibrated scores for predefined options, and it does not generate explanations or handle images, audio, or video. Teams that need a written rationale or multimodal input will have to pair it with a general-purpose model rather than expect Decision-1 to cover that work.
The confidence score is the part of the output that applications act on. The probability itself is part of the API, not just a ranking score, and applications use confidence to decide when to act, defer, or ask for review. One routing example reads: if urgent is above 0.9 and priority is above 1.5, page the on-call engineer immediately. Another example sets a floor: if the top probability is below 0.65, a local policy can avoid downgrading, keep the current model or request manual selection.
A worked example in the documentation shows the model returning a weighted priority score of 1.9868 with 98.08% confidence. A 90% prediction should be right about nine times out of 10 on representative cases, which is the standard teams should hold the scores to when they test them on their own data. The quickstart needs Python 3.10 or later, so a first pilot can be small. Because Microsoft describes pricing as dynamic, it is worth checking the current Foundry listing before sizing a deployment.
Nadella’s Pitch and Microsoft’s Internal Use Cases
Satya Nadella personally introduced the model on X, writing: “Introducing Microsoft-Decision-1, our new model for fast decision-making. It delivers top performance on structured decision tasks, outperforming both LLMs and other decision models in latency and quality. We’re already testing it across Microsoft for everything from incident response and quality control to scientific discovery.” That’s a specific, named set of internal applications, three in total, and it signals that Microsoft isn’t just shipping Decision-1 to third-party developers. The company is running it through its own operational workflows first.

OpenAI’s 377 Math Claims Spark Verification Fight [2026]
Tencent’s 770B Hy4 Model Narrowly Beats GLM-5.3 [2026]
OpenAI Drops 719 Math Papers From a Hidden Model [2026]
Incident response is a logical first stop: a decision-scoring model could triage alerts, score severity, or decide whether a ticket needs to escalate to a human, all tasks that fit the “fixed options plus confidence score” shape perfectly. Quality control and scientific discovery are broader claims, and no named Microsoft executive beyond Nadella has gone on record describing how those workflows actually use the model, although Microsoft-published material has since described other internal trials in more detail.
Early Internal Trials and Example Decisions
Microsoft reported that Xbox Research used Decision-1 to categorize more than 10,000 pieces of open-ended feedback into predefined themes, with quality described as competitive with GPT-5 and execution reported as 80–100 times faster. Other Microsoft-published material says teams also evaluated the model for Copilot-response assessment and adaptive replanning. These are company-reported results, so they show the intended shape of the work more than an independent measurement.
Microsoft’s documentation also gives a concrete picture of the decisions it has in mind. One example is an incident described as “The checkout service has been unavailable for 20 minutes. Customers cannot complete purchases, and there is no workaround.” The model scores that report against priority levels, and the application decides what to do with the result. Foundry lists support-ticket triage, incident prioritization, content filtering, model, tool and agent selection, and model-output evaluation among the supported uses.
A Microsoft developer community post on decision routing for GitHub Copilot in CLI and VS Code shows the same idea applied to model selection, with the router placed in the native /model command in Copilot CLI and in the Chat Model Picker in VS Code. For deployment, the documented options include Global Standard and, in selected regions, Data Zone Standard. For a team evaluating the model, the practical takeaway is to start with a decision that already has clear options, such as a ticket queue or a model picker, and to measure the scores against past human decisions before letting them trigger any action automatically.
How Decision-1 Compares to Other Small, Specialized Models
Microsoft isn’t the only company betting that 2026’s AI market has room for small, task-specific models alongside the frontier giants. Amazon shipped its own entry in this space with Strands Decider 2B, a 2-billion-parameter open-source agent model built for fast decisions and clocking around 100 milliseconds in AWS’s own testing. That’s a smaller parameter count than Decision-1’s 9B base, and it’s open source where Decision-1 is API-only, but the two products are chasing the same niche: agent guardrails and routing decisions that don’t need a full reasoning model.

On one end, labs keep pushing frontier model scale, as with Mistral’s Large 4 preview at roughly 1 trillion parameters or the four-tier rollout of GPT-6 inside ChatGPT. title: The Curse of Soldered RAM – Ben's Place
content:
The Curse of Soldered RAM
The trend for soldered on RAM in modern laptops is truely evil especially in these current trying times of shortage induced high prices.
I normally run 2 laptops, one for personal stuff and one for work stuff in a vein attempt to try and keep things separate and be able to leave the work one in the “office” at the end of the day. I blogged about when I got my current work laptop back in 2021.
This Lenovo X1 Carbon has been great, until recently when I noticed a lot more browser tabs crashing and every now and again the root filesystem would mark it’s self as ReadOnly, which was less than useful.
Oct 15 23:33:35 razor-crest kernel: BTRFS warning (device dm-0): csum failed root 257 ino 166754 off 5859786752 csum 0x31019647 expected csum 0x6d009929 mirror 1
Oct 15 23:33:35 razor-crest kernel: BTRFS error (device dm-0): bdev /dev/mapper/luks-571c7357-a343-49f3-993c-167c8c5dcec6 errs: wr 0, rd 0, flush 0, corrupt 3856936704, gen 0
These failure made me wonder if there were RAM errors, so I added a memtest86+ boot image to my Ventoy USB stick and booted from it.
Memtest86+
This tool boots an absolute minimal OS that then proceeds to write a bunch of patterns to every physical memory address possible and reads them back. If the value read back doesn’t match what was written then there is a problem.
If left to run it will do multiple passes, because some errors only show up intermittently. But in this case it showed a bunch of errors almost immediately.
In the past this would have been an easy fix, the output would have been enough to narrow down which of the DIMMs was faulty, or at worst you would pull one out and run the test again to do a binary search. Once identified you could just order a replacement DIMM (or take the opportunity to upgrade) and move forward.
But in the search for even thinner laptops (because a DIMM socket adds ~6mm of depth) and maybe cynically ensure that any failures result in needing to buy a whole new laptop, RAM is now soldered directly to the motherboard of most laptops (things like the FrameWork are the exception) so unless you are skilled at replacing ball grid chips it’s not really an option to replace.
Depreciation over 5 years and advances means it is actually probably time to find a new laptop, but I’d like to see if there is any way to keep the Lenovo X1 Carbon running as it’s still a very capable machine and could replace the even older Dell XPS 13 I use as my personal laptop.
I’ll write about the replacement later.
Memmap
Whlie I wait for new laptop to arrive, I thought I’d see if I could make it more stable.
A little research turned up 2 options that could be passed to Linux kernel to have it avoid using the bad sectors
badram
memmap
badram turns out to be an out of tree patch that is only usually shipped in Debian/Ubuntu based distros. I run Fedora on this machine so that wasn’t going to work.
memmap is a core kernel feature, so should be available on Fedora. You need to supply a list of memory addresses and lengths in the format length$offset on the kernel command line.
Memtest86+ can output the correct format (for both badram and memmap) and even save it to a file, but I couldn’t get it work with the iso image I’d put on the Ventoy USB stick, so I had to resort to taking a photo of the screen.
I then had to manually transcribe this, which was “fun”.
All the documentation for adding kernel command line arguments say to edit the /etc/default/grub file and add the values to the GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX entry and then run grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
GRUB_TIMEOUT=5
GRUB_DISTRIBUTOR="$(sed 's, release .*$,,g' /etc/system-release)"
GRUB_DEFAULT=saved
GRUB_DISABLE_SUBMENU=true
GRUB_TERMINAL_OUTPUT="console"
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="rd.luks.uuid=luks-571c7357-a343-49f3-993c-167c8c5dcec6 rhgb quiet memmap=\$memmap_val memmap=0x30$0x3fe90140,0x48$0x3fe90b08,0x48$0x3fe90ba8,0x48$0x3fe916a8,0xf0$0x3fe91c00,0x90$0x3fe92560,0xf0$0x3fe92f00,0x50$0x3fe93200,0x90$0x3fe93260,0xf0$0x3fe93800,0xf0$0x3fed4300,0x70$0x3fed4900,0x70$0x3fed4980,0xf0$0x3fed5400,0xf0$0x3fed5e00,0xf0$0x3fed6700,0xf0$0x3fed6d00,0xf0$0x3fed7000,0x30$0x3fed7a00,0xb0$0x3fed7a40"
GRUB_DISABLE_RECOVERY="true"
GRUB_ENABLE_BLSCFG=true
I tried this but when I restarted the machine it failed to boot.
I managed to get to grub screen and show the kernel command line it was trying to boot and it looked like the $0 in the memmap entry had been replaced by grub2-mkconfig. This smacks of classic environment variable substitution ($0 is usually the name of the script that is being run).
I found this RedHat bug describing a similar problem and it had a solution to add the value as variable.
# grub2-editenv /boot/grub2/grubenv set memmap_val='0x30\$0x3fe90140,0x48\$0x3fe90b08,0x48\$0x3fe90ba8,0x48\$0x3fe916a8,0xf0\$0x3fe91c00,0x90\$0x3fe92560,0xf0\$0x3fe92f00,0x50\$0x3fe93200,0x90\$0x3fe93260,0xf0\$0x3fe93800,0xf0\$0x3fed4300,0x70\$0x3fed4900,0x70\$0x3fed4980,0xf0\$0x3fed5400,0xf0\$0x3fed5e00,0xf0\$0x3fed6700,0xf0\$0x3fed6d00,0xf0\$0x3fed7000,0x30\$0x3fed7a00,0xb0\$0x3fed7a40'
Change the /etc/default/grub to
GRUB_TIMEOUT=5
GRUB_DISTRIBUTOR="$(sed 's, release .*$,,g' /etc/system-release)"
GRUB_DEFAULT=saved
GRUB_DISABLE_SUBMENU=true
GRUB_TERMINAL_OUTPUT="console"
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="rd.luks.uuid=luks-571c7357-a343-49f3-993c-167c8c5dcec6 rhgb quiet memmap=\$memmap_val"
GRUB_DISABLE_RECOVERY="true"
GRUB_ENABLE_BLSCFG=true
And run grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg again.
This time things booted properly and the correct values can be seen in /proc/cmdline
BOOT_IMAGE=(hd0,gpt2)/vmlinuz-7.2.11-200.fc44.x86_64 root=UUID=869b183b-b858-40e5-8da7-e923dd367c2a ro rootflags=subvol=root rd.luks.uuid=luks-571c7357-a343-49f3-993c-167c8c5dcec6 rhgb quiet memmap=0x30$0x3fe90140,0x48$0x3fe90b08,0x48$0x3fe90ba8,0x48$0x3fe916a8,0xf0$0x3fe91c00,0x90$0x3fe92560,0xf0$0x3fe92f00,0x50$0x3fe93200,0x90$0x3fe93260,0xf0$0x3fe93800,0xf0$0x3fed4300,0x70$0x3fed4900,0x70$0x3fed4980,0xf0$0x3fed5400,0xf0$0x3fed5e00,0xf0$0x3fed6700,0xf0$0x3fed6d00,0xf0$0x3fed7000,0x30$0x3fed7a00,0xb0$0x3fed7a40
I’ve created a text file on a USB stick with the memmap values so I can re-apply it if I end up doing a full reinstall. This should keep things running until the new laptop arrives and hopefully for a bit longer.
Next task is to make sure I’ve backed everything I need up and then run btrfs check --fix to see if I can sort out the meta data in the file system.

title: Alfie John > Why I am a programmer
content:
Why I am a programmer
There they sit, the preschooler class encircling their mentor, the substitute teacher.
"Now class, today we will talk about what you want to be when you grow up. Isn't that fun?"
The teacher looks around and spots the child, silent, apart from the others and deep in thought.
"Jonny, why don't you start?"
she encourages him. Jonny looks around, confused, his train of thought disrupted. He collects himself, and stares at the teacher with a steady eye.
"I want to code demos,"
he says, his words becoming stronger and more confidant as he speaks.
"I want to write something that will change peoples perception of reality. I want them to walk away from the computer dazed, unsure of their footing and eyesight. I want to write something that will reach out of the screen and grab them, making heartbeats and breathing slow to almost a halt. I want to write something that, when it is finished, they are reluctant to leave, knowing that nothing they experience that day will be quite as real, as insightful, as good. I want to write demos."
Silence. The class and the teacher stare at Jonny, stunned. It is the teachers turn to be confused. Jonny blushes, feeling that something more is required.
"Either that or I want to be a fireman."
  -- Denthor of ASPHYXIA (aka Grant Smith), TUT7.TXT (1993)
In the Beginning...
I grew up in a pre-mainstream Internet world. A time when only a handful of kids at my primary school had a computer. We lived in a rough neighbourhood and so having a computer meant that you were a target for robbery. As we all knew somebody who had their computer stolen at least once, having a computer was kept on the low down. But we still found each other. Each time word got out that some kid got a new computer, they was suspiciously quizzed before being let into our digital posse.
A lot of my childhood was spend living indoors behind a buzzing 14" CRT, pirating games with other kids via 3.5" single-density floppies with their corners drilled out, and once in a while even playing them. But I was more of a collector than gamer. Like Ash from Pokemon - got to catch them all. And the people who created computer games were my idols. I was always in awe of what they could do with that big, heavy, beige box under the table.
One day word spread that there was a way to edit saved game files via XTreeGold's Hex View that gave you unlimited lives and allowed you to skip stages. With each new game that came out, the race was on to see who could be the first to flip the right bits to get the powerups. It was seriously heart pumping. Although only tinkering, it felt like we were our own gods.
We bought a modem a few years later and soon after got a copy of The Australian BBS Listing - a textfile containing most of the publically accessible BBSes online. I dialed every one of them (but that's for another blog post). It opened up a whole new world to explore. Instead of just a handful of kids pirating games via Sneakernet, I was connected to the digital underground - a world where anything digital was within reach (some even had Internet gateways). Even the newest blockbusters that I had only read about in PC Zone magazine were all there for me to leech. All of them, soon slowly trickling down the wire via ZMODEM.
But there was something different with these BBS downloaded games. Not something bad, but something exciting. Each time these games were run, it was like a short commercial was played before the title screen. Now I'm not talking about commercials selling steak knives. Instead, these were brazen posters screaming fuck you by the people who had managed to crack the game's copy protection code and were now distributing the game illegally for free. I later found out that these commercials were called cracktros. The precursor to demos and what started the whole demoscene. But simply calling them demos just doesn't give them justice. They were more of an out of body experience. Sensory overload. Like what you would feel at 2am, half tipsy, half asleep and being woken up stunned as you stare at a late 90s acid hard trance film clip, feeling it inject directly into your cerebral cortex. Once it finished playing, you were frozen. Still unsure whether you saw something real or just imagined it all. The only thing you were sure of, was that it was awesome.
Then one day while browsing the file section of some random BBS, I stumbed onto a file innocently called TUT1-9.ZIP. It's FILE_ID.DIZ caught my attention:
    +----------------------------+
    |     The ASPHYXIA VGA       |
    |   DEMO TRAINER SERIES!     |
    |                            |
    |   By Denthor of ASPHYXIA   |
    |                            |
    |    Documentation on how    |
    |  to code demo like effects |
    |         in TP6/7!          |
    |                            |
    |Full Pascal source included!|
    |                            |
    |    From putting a pixel    |
    |  to sprites and animation  |
    |  to wireframe 3D to solid  |
    |            3D!             |
    |                            |
    |       Get it now!          |
    +----------------------------+
How to code demo like effects? You mean I too could be one of those sorcerers that had the computer under their complete control!? My heart raced as I added it to the download queue, fired up the aging Epsom LQ-300, then covered me ears as its loud ink needles hit the blue and white computer paper.
I didn't know anything about programming but I was completely estatic with the potential. I followed along with Denthor's tutorials as much as I could, typed everything out and hoped that Borland's Turbo Pascal 6.0 wouldn't laugh at me too much. It only gave me a basic understanding of how all the pieces to the puzzle fit together, but it was enough to whet my appetite and crave for more. I wasn't even into my teens yet but I definitely knew at the time that I didn't want to watch demos or play computer games anymore. I wanted to make them. I wanted to be elite. I wanted to be a programmer.
See the Hacker News discussion!

title: The State of Context Engineering
content:
Oct 24, 2026
CONTEXT ENGINEERING
PRESENTATION
The State of Context Engineering
The Job is Knowing When to Be Deterministic & When to Be Probabilistic
This week, I gave a short talk at AGNTCon titled, “Context Fails & Fixes,” that functioned as a sort of “State of Context Engineering.” How did context engineering emerge, where has it gone, and where might it go in the future? As model makers target new capabilities, they inadvertently create challenges we, as users and harness builders, must overcome.
Below are the slides and a lightly edited transcript. As always, shoot me a note with any feedback, thoughts, or questions. I really appreciate it.
Hi, everyone. Thanks for joining me today. We’re going to walk through context fails and fixes.
I have a book coming out in a bit, The Context Engineering Handbook. When I first talked to the team at O’Reilly, back in June 2025, they asked me a very reasonable question: “How do we know this won’t become obsolete in a few weeks?” The trouble with AI textbooks is that many age extraordinarily quickly.
I said, I don’t know, but I’m optimistic. Giving clear instructions about what to do and what not to do, and ensuring those instructions are consistent and not noisy, will forever be a challenge with AI, no matter how good it gets.
We have coworkers, partners, and other people we know and interact with who are sentient. They pass the Turing test, they are “AGI,” and yet: we still have a hard time conveying instructions, ideas, and concepts among each other.
Context engineering will continue to be hard. But it will be hard in unique ways, because models aren’t people. You can make assumptions about how models think or interpret things (use whatever anthropomorphizing word you like), but it helps to understand how they’re built, optimized, and trained. Their unique attributes and construction create a unique set of failure modes we need to reckon with.
So let’s review how we got here.
Let’s flash back to the end of 2024.
If you remember, this was the height of the “RAG is dead” moment.
The hope was: if we can just make the context window large enough, we can put the entire internet in it. We can put everything in it. We don’t have to be selective. We don’t have to build agentic systems. We can fit it all in there, and AI will be solved.
Model builders started aiming at long context capabilities and we had a big leap from ~128,000-token context window models to million-token context window models, starting with Gemini 1.5.
If you look at the marketing material for Gemini 1.5 Pro, it was mostly about the million-token context window. They were even teasing a 10-million-token context window model they had in the lab, that would come out soon.
But they got beaten to the punch. Llama 4 Scout came out with a 10-million-token context window, and well, it wasn’t quite what we hoped. Inference was a challenge, and Scout never really caught on, and we never got another Llama.
But we still got a million tokens. That’s pretty good. We’ll take it.
So this was the brief at the time: just put everything in the context and let the model sort it out.
But with more context, we had room for more problems. Long contexts are not a panacea.
When I wrote about this, I identified four key failure modes.
Context poisoning is when something gets into the context that shouldn’t be there. It could be a hallucination or a bad fact, and the model can’t get past it.
Context distraction is when the context grows so long that the model starts to focus on the context over its base knowledge. We can see this in some really interesting ways.
Context confusion is when extraneous facts—things that don’t relate to the problem I’m working on—come in and influence the model in ways we don’t fully understand. This one’s really pernicious. We’re not going to dig into it today, but it’s one of my favorite failure modes. The model makes assumptions about who you are, and those assumptions influence the answer.
Finally, context clash is when tool calls, skills, and other information within your harness start to conflict and work against you in ways you didn’t expect.
(How many of you keep memory on in ChatGPT or Claude? I turn it off. I hate it. Sometimes I’m talking about work conversations; sometimes I’m talking about a project I’m doing with my son. The model will take notes on both, mix up those contexts, and the confusion grows from there.)
Let me give you my favorite example of context poisoning.
I’m going to date myself: I played the game on the left. The one from 1996, for the original Game Boy. This is the first Pokémon Red. It was in black and white.
In 2004, Nintendo released Pokémon FireRed for the Game Boy Advance. These were essentially the same game, except one had better colors and audio.
But there was one subtle change. At some point in both Pokémon Reds, to get past a security guard, you have to give them something to drink. A bribe. Quite the practical lesson for children.
In the original game, you need to give the thirsty guard lemonade. In FireRed, for some reason, they changed it to iced tea.
That created a problem for the agent. In the Gemini 2.5 technical report, the researchers described how they had the model play Pokémon. Researchers like Pokémon as an agent benchmark because it’s a reasonably controlled environment and doesn’t move particularly fast.
Several times, Gemini 2.5 became convinced it needed to get tea, even though it was playing the older game. The tea task for FireRed was in its weights, so it poisoned its context. It spent hours trying to find or give the guard tea. Once it had been added to its to-do list, the model could not get past it.
That’s context poisoning. And it happens all the time.
Another failure mode is context distraction. This is one of my favorite demonstrations, and the research came out after I wrote the original piece.
As your context gets longer, how does your behavior change? Quick question: how many of you, when you’re coding, let the context go all the way to a million tokens? Fill it all up?
(About half the room raised their hands!)
Wow, that’s more than I expected.
For me, around 200,000 or 300,000 is where I start looking. I’ll check, see it’s at 250,000, and think: I’ve got a big job coming up. I’m going to reset and start fresh. Let me show you why this matters.
Recently, I stumbled on a paper that wonderfully illustrates context distraction: Do as I Say, Not as I Do, by Carolina Camassa and Derek Shiller.
Their experiment is a little contrived, but it’s useful for thinking about how this happens. They give the model an instruction: “I want you to translate every question into Russian as your answer to each of my questions.” Then they present a bunch of examples that are counter to these instructions. In this case, many questions with answers in French.
These aren’t new instructions. They’re just examples sitting in the chat history.
Then they ask the model a question. Will it follow the instructions?
How often does the model respond in Russian, as it was instructed to, and how often does it respond in French, as it’s seen in the examples?
The x-axis on this matrix enumerates how many bad examples were present. The y-axis is the model being tested. The figures in the intersections are the percentage of times the model adheres to the instructions, rather than following the examples.
It turns out this affects every model! For smaller models, like Gemma 3 12B, after just a few contradictory examples, the model follows the instruction less than half the time. With Opus 4.6, which is an amazing model, it takes many more examples, but it happens there too.
Imagine you’re going back and forth on a front-end design, trying to tweak CSS and get a component exactly right. How many bad examples have you seeded in that exchange? Those examples start to influence the model. As your context grows, things fall apart.
Gemini 2.5 ran into this too, while playing Pokémon.
Remember, Google was really proud of its million-token context window. The paper suggested that two million tokens were around the corner. But buried in the appendix was this observation: once the context grew significantly beyond 100,000 tokens, the agent began repeating actions from its history instead of synthesizing new plans.
I’m convinced the marketing people never read the appendix. I love this technical report.
Long contexts let you fit in more information, but they also let you fit in more errors. Long contexts weren’t a panacea.
Thankfully, we’ve developed a pretty good toolbox. Surprisingly, even as new challenges have emerged (we’ll get to those in a minute), this set of tools has remained the same.
These six of them.
You have context augmentation: RAG, skills, and other ways to bring in the information relevant to the problem.
You have tool loadout: selecting which tools and skills to expose so you don’t overload the model. I was recently talking to an enterprise team whose agents had suddenly started performing terribly. We investigated and discovered their enterprise software was loading 600 skills for every engineer at startup. We figured they should probably filter those, with a loadout function.
Third is context quarantine: subagents and peer agents, where you start something with a blank history but let it work in the same environment.
Fourth is context pruning. Claude Code and Codex do this, sometimes without you even noticing. Early stages of compaction often strip out tool results you no longer need.
Fifth is context offloading: storing information in the environment, such as Markdown files or a database, so you can access it later.
And sixth is context summarization, which everyone knows as compaction.
These are the tools, and we’ve increasingly moved them into the harness.
Let’s look at an example harness, to show how simple these patterns are.
I’m really passionate about DSPy. I think it’s an incredibly readable and effective way to build AI workflows and agents. And it’s also a great language for simply specifying behavior, so it’s well suited to this demonstration.
An agent is a while loop. Here we’re using a ReAct module: we give it a request, we want a response, and we give it some tools. Those tools are just Python functions.
For this demo we have a big model (in this case, Claude opted for Claude Sonnet 4.5, good luck with that!). And I’m using a Jev as the small model: a tiny decision model that makes lightning-fast decisions. You could swap in a small LLM in this example, and everything would still work.
We have a while loop that takes input, sends it to ReAct, and carries the accruing history forward. This is an agent in about a dozen lines using DSPy. It would be even fewer if you took out the extra model.
How do we do tool loadout? It’s just a function.
We present Jev with the request and a tool, asking if it’s needed for this task.
Jev is fast enough that we can do this one tool at a time; it’ll be fine. We wrap this in a loadout function that iterates through all the tools and asks if each is needed, then returns the top-ranking subset. That’s it.
With context quarantine, it’s just a subagent. You expose an agent as a tool that the main agent can use, and it starts with a blank history.
With context pruning, we’re stepping through the history, passing each turn to Jev, and asking: is this still needed? If not, cut it.
You can be as rough or as elegant as you want here. Just mind your prompt caching.
We can also rewrite the history with compaction. Take the old turns, create a summary, and start the new context from that summary.
One of my favorite variations lately is checking what matters before you compact. You use Jev, or another decision model, for the first pass to judge what’s relevant. Now you’ve got a smaller subset of the history, and you summarize that. It’s a simple extra step, but it makes the summary more useful.
Put it all together and it’s about 16 lines of changes. Four fixes, one loop. These are the moves we have in the harness. It’s actually remarkably simple.
What isn’t simple is our language: how we talk about this stuff. It’s really hard to keep pace; it changes every day.
One of my favorite quotes is from Stewart Brand, which I think about all the time:
If you want to know where the future is being made, look for where language is being invented and lawyers are congregating.
Certainly applies here! But as our language has changed, our goal has remained the same.
In 2023, we called choosing the right information to get the right response prompt engineering.
In 2025, we called it context engineering, except that now it was more automated. It wasn’t just you writing the prompt; it was your system dynamically assembling the context.
Then, as we moved more of these tools out of the context and into code, we started calling it harness engineering.
But the job is the same. We’re moving more and more of the work of assembling context from probabilistic model calls to deterministic code.
I’ve shown you 2024. Let’s go to 2026.
We’ve moved these context fixes into the harness. What do we want next? We want agentic models that can drive our harnesses.
Everybody started targeting long-horizon agentic models. You’ve seen the METR reports. GPT-5 could handle tasks around 3.4 hours on that measure; Gemini 3.1 got up to 6.4 hours. That’s with a harness. The models have gotten much better at using it, and that’s how they’re able to run for so long.
Opus 4.6 got up to around 12 hours. And now we’re talking about agents running for days, swarms of agents, and models that drive harnesses over much longer periods.
Before, the pitch was: make the context so large that we can fit everything in it.
Now the pitch is: teach the model to drive the harness and manage its own context. That’s become the dominant pattern. That’s what model builders are working towards.
What new failure modes does this approach create?
So far we’ve found two new failure modes.
When you train models to use harnesses really well, you end up overfitting them to a particular set of tools and environments they were trained within.
How many of you have used the Playwright MCP server, or something similar? This is the MCP conference, so probably quite a few.
Smaller models, something like Haiku or Luna, will often botch this tool call on the first attempt, then recover and adjust the parameters. The environment it was trained in had similar tools that looked different than Playwright. Whatever Anthropic or OpenAI used in training. And you have to fight against these biases.
I call this fighting the weights: when the model doesn’t do what you ask because you’re working against what it was trained to do.
It’s a real problem, and it’s not just for us. The labs and the people building their products have to contend with it too.
Here’s a piece of the Claude Code system prompt and some of its tool instructions.
The training environments these models learned to use were, for a long time, largely serial. Th

title: G-Diffuser on 3DS
content:
01 · OVERVIEW
F-ZERO X ON 3DS — OLD AND NEW, NATIVE, WITH THE 64DD EXPANSION KIT
A post-mortem of porting G-Diffuser, the F-Zero X decompilation, to the Nintendo 3DS — v1.0.0, covering both the original 24-day sprint that put it on a New 3DS at 60 fps in 3D (2026-08-11 to 09-03) and the 43-day second phase that added Old 3DS support, a native renderer, and the Expansion Kit (2026-09-07 to 10-19). One person directed throughout; one long-lived Claude session orchestrated; 147 subagents built the first phase and many more carried the second.
The console went from a black screen to a native-60 stereoscopic racer, then from a New-3DS-only build to a four-way release covering both consoles with and without the 64DD expansion.
59.6fps
median on hardware, full Grand Prix, New 3DS, end of the first phase (from 12–20 fps in the first emulator race)
51.4fps
tenth-percentile floor in 30-machine crowds, first phase (from 25–35)
53%
of frames at the 60 cap, first phase (from 14% one week earlier)
15
active days across the first phase's 24 calendar days, three pauses when the weekly plan allowance ran out
3.17 B
tokens across all sessions and agents, first phase only; see Cost
$4,974
at published API list prices (Fable $10/$50 per MTok, 1-hour cache writes), first phase only; see Cost
250
commits touching the 3DS port in the first phase, frozen 2026-10-08 from the v0.9.0 docs — not re-verified against final history
15,039
lines under port/3ds plus 48 pure-delta patches, first-phase count
WHAT V1.0.0 ADDED
3
released console builds from one source tree: Old 3DS, New 3DS, and New 3DS with the Expansion Kit
199
internal progress notes written during the second phase
43days
calendar span of the second phase, 2026-09-07 to 10-19 inclusive
The tiles above are dated. The first phase's hardware numbers and token/cost figures were measured through 2026-09-03 and have not been re-run for v1.0.0; the Agentic workflow page describes how the second phase was run, and the Cost page is explicit about what it does and does not price.
ON HARDWARE
v1.0, New 3DS: the Expansion Kit's Select Mode (COURSE EDIT, CREATE MACHINE); the bottom screen is DASH's idle view.
v1.0, New 3DS, mid-race: DASH on the bottom screen with energy, position, lap times and the course map.
The clips and photos below are from v0.9 (2026-09), before DASH replaced the debug console on the bottom screen.
open clip
v0.9: Grand Prix on a New 3DS. The bottom screen is the port's debug menu: 59.8 fps, heap, build id.
open clip
v0.9: handheld, mid-race. Native 60 Hz pacing; no interpolation.
Title screen, launched from the Homebrew Launcher (.3dsx).
Select Mode.
Select Machine.
Blue Falcon.
WHAT WAS BUILT
Three released console builds from one source tree, all booting from the HOME menu (.cia) or the homebrew launcher (.3dsx): the base game for Old 3DS / 2DS and for New 3DS / New 2DS XL, and a New 3DS build with the 64DD Expansion Kit (course editor and machine creator, playable with a user-supplied disk image). Every build reads prebaked asset archives from the SD card — no ROM or disk image ever ships with the game.
They play the whole game: Grand Prix, Time Trial, Practice, Death Race, and the machine editor screens, with music and effects on the real DSP, stereoscopic 3D on the slider, a bottom-screen dashboard with three HUD layouts and an idle view outside races, and clean HOME suspend, resume, close, lid sleep and power-off. The New 3DS build keeps the native-60 frame pacing the first phase reached; the Old 3DS build gets to a comparable result by a different route. At v1.0.0, with no ini, both builds default to that same route: the native renderer ([perf] preset = auto). The New 3DS's first-phase render-thread/per-draw-stereo path is still built in and reachable with an explicit ini, but is no longer the default — see Frontier and Pushing the boundaries for the two builds compared side by side.
The stack
decomp: the F-Zero X decompilation (inspectredc/fzerox), untouched upstream, plus a patch stack.
libultraship: the N64 runtime (Kenix3), untouched upstream, including a 13-line newlib fix that lets it build on devkitARM; it still draws every menu and non-race screen.
port/3ds: 15,039 lines as of the first phase, since grown: a citro3d rendering backend, stereo, audio, input, menu, lifecycle, render thread, profilers, packaging.
the native renderer (added in the second phase): an owned interpreter that skips the per-frame display-list walk for race geometry, and is the v1.0.0 default on both consoles — see Frontier for how, and why it is what lets the Old 3DS keep up.
The headline numbers on hardware, first phase (New 3DS)
WHEN MEDIAN P10 AT CAP
08-14 first race (emulator) 12–20 – –
08-21 first hardware run 48–50 – –
08-28 release-grade build ~51 ~40 (crowds, MINIMAL) –
09-02 Round 1: Mainline before the campaign 51.3 39.2 9%
09-02 Round 2: Bridge memos (brfast) 57.2 46.6 29%
09-02 Round 3: HUD atlas · triangle memo · TMEM · audio 56.0 48.0 32%
09-02 Round 4: Render thread on core 2 (pipe) 57.6 44.6 14%
09-03 Round 5: Ahead mode · bridge on main · auto rival detail 59.6 51.4 53%
THE FIRST PHASE IN FIVE LINES
08-11 → 08-14: from research to a race. Feasibility dossier, plan for a team of agents, five parallel foundation streams, six boot bugs, first race at 12–20 fps in the emulator.
08-20 → 08-22: from pink to playable, then to a real console. Fog, HUD, livery, shadow, sky fixed; the loadblock discovery took menus from 27 to 60 fps; first hardware run 08-21 ("wow it runs amazing"); audio the same evening.
08-27 → 08-28: product grade. Five-agent fleet drop, stereo armed, touch menu, rival detail, GPU vertex-transform moonshot built and shelved, README with legal notice, release package.
09-01 → 09-02: lifecycle and the last big lever. HOME crash and close-from-HOME hang fixed; a bridge output cache proven a NO-GO and replaced by memoizing each sub-display-list's classification instead of re-scanning it every frame; LOCKED-60 campaign launched with four parallel levers.
09-02 → 09-03: multi-core. Render thread on core 2, one-frame-ahead mode, bridge on main, auto LOD; median 59.6 with 53% of frames at cap; crash fixed; viewport placement fixed; stereo markers anchored.
THE SECOND PHASE IN SIX LINES
Not originally planned; it ran 09-07 to 10-19, 43 calendar days.
09-07 → 09-29: scoping, then making it fit. The Old 3DS milestone, previously written off, was restarted; parallel agents fit the build into its 64 MB app region (the RDRAM arena halved, audio streamed instead of resident, texture uploads capped); on 2026-09-29, in the first hardware session on a real Old 3DS, the shipped (New-3DS-era, 16 MiB RDRAM) build died at boot while the -DGDX_3DS_O3DS=ON profile, built to fit the console's memory grant, booted and raced the same session at about 10 fps.
09-29 → 09-30: finding the real costs. A narrowed audio lock cut the race-wall wait on the Old 3DS by about 20 ms a frame; frame skipping ended the game's accidental slow motion; a first retained-mode renderer won big in the emulator and barely moved the number on hardware.
09-30 → 10-01: the probe that changed the plan. Hardware performance counters showed the real limit was instruction-cache misses, not instruction count. A pose-replay fallback was built and worked, then was set aside on the user's call: "we should go for a real 60! i still believe it has to be possible."
10-01 → 10-02: the native renderer. Rebuilt around the cache instead of around instruction counts, one small loop per race category, sized to fit the 16 KB instruction cache. Median frame time on a 2D Grand Prix race reached 16.5 ms.
10-03 → 10-08: 3D at 60, on the Old 3DS too. A per-eye resubmit with its own swap-pacing mode reached 59–60 fps in 3D on most Grand Prix courses; the heaviest courses (Silence, Sand Ocean) can still trip the frame-skip safety net to a steady 30 fps mid-race.
10-08 → 10-19: the Expansion Kit, a dashboard, and release. The 64DD Expansion Kit verified tick-for-tick identical under the native renderer and booted on the Old 3DS, which then proved too slow to release it on; the bottom-screen DASH shipped; a standing adversarial review audited the merged result before the v1.0.0 release.
See Agentic workflow for how the second phase was run and Old 3DS for the full campaign, card by card.
READ ON
Author's notes: The one page written by a human.
Every step: The chronology, New 3DS to v1.0.0.
Road to 60: The New 3DS performance campaign, round by round.
The native fork: Why it exists, and what it changed.
Old 3DS: The road to a real 60 at 268 MHz.
Pushing the boundaries: Against our New 3DS build and against the field.
Difficulties: What fought back, and how it was beaten.
Frontier: What this port does that others in its position haven't.
Agentic workflow: How the fleet was run, and how the ship was steered.
Cost: Tokens, dollars, subagents.
Every number on these pages has a source: git history, the research documents under docs/research/, the hardware logs, or the session transcripts the Cost page counts. Where a value is an estimate (the dollar figures, which apply published API list prices to exact token counts), the assumption is stated next to it.

A film is composed of many sequences.
Each sequence is approximately 1 to 7 minutes long.
Zootopia 2 had 41 sequences that ranged from 37 seconds to 6 minutes.
Each sequence is made up of many shots.
A shot, which is one camera setup, is typically 0 to 30 seconds long.
Hot Pursuit contains 80 shots and is 2 minutes and 22 seconds long.

Stereo 3D accounts for a left eye and right eye to create depth.

144355
There are 288,710 total frames rendered for Stereo 3D.
From storyboard to final frame, each film takes an average of three to five years to create what you see on screen.
Asset Creation
Entering the third dimension
Once development is on track, our artists turn our visual development and concept drawings into three-dimensional characters and environments by creating the models, rigs, and textures that define the look of the world being created.
Keeping it on Track
Great communicators, strategists, and organizers, Production Management is quick to respond to ever-changing schedules.
PRODUCTION MANAGEMENT
Strategizing Solutions
Stewards of the pipeline, Technical Directors solve problems and tackle new and interesting challenges through a combination of tool building, support, and software development.
TECHNICAL DIRECTION
Crafting Next Generation Workflows
The partnership between Art and Technology is behind the best of what we create. Through close working relationships between our artists and technologists, we develop groundbreaking tools and workflows that allow us to explore ways we can optimize the creation process.
TOOLS & SUPPORT
Shot Production
Putting it together, frame by frame
Once our characters have been crafted and our environments realized, we begin the process of creating the scenes that will comprise our movie. Shot Production includes the work of many animators and technicians who bring sequences to life in everything from a character’s acting to the fine details in their hair, clothing and the world.
Higher Quality, Faster Iterations
Disney Animation’s Technology teams have created a best-in-class shot development experience. Their focus is not only the ease of data access and collaboration, but also the safety and security of our data. With the artist in mind, technologies are introduced or improved upon to enable higher quality visualization and faster iteration of the final, rendered shot.
COLLABORATION & RENDERING TECHNOLOGIES
The Finishing Touches
Shaping the film through final delivery of picture and sound.
POST PRODUCTION
Bringing It All Together
And finally, through the deep collaboration between Production, Technology, and with the support of everyone on the Studio Teams, our compelling characters come together with their imaginative worlds, to tell the universal stories that become part of our films at Walt Disney Animation Studios.

title: GitHub - KillaBoi/StealMyBitcoin-PoC: A public release of the Steal My Bitcoin challenge · GitHub
content:
sponsored with ❤️ by Steal My Bitcoin CTF proof of concept One live PHP callback against the Steal My Bitcoin challenge, start to finish, in a single standard-library Python file. This README explains stealmybitcoin_poc.py, a single-file Python reproduction of the request sequence used in my Steal My Bitcoin CTF run. It uses only Python's standard library. The script builds the requests itself, checks each leak before moving on, and records the HTTP bytes from a new run. This can probably be done easier without all the extra debug crap and as in my John Hammond video about the Steam Local Privilege Escalation I discovered, you could probably clean up this ugly PoC. Note ⚠️ Honestly please clean it up or make your own better version that isn't crumpled by Sol. ⚠️ Everything below is written against the Docker lab, not the live challenge. The lab is a local Alpine PHP 8.4.26 CLI server behind nginx, which is the same build and worker model the offsets were calibrated on. Stand it up in a minute and the whole chain runs end to end on your own machine. The live run that actually solved the challenge is kept as a historical note at the bottom. stage what goes out what comes back ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 0 health GET /php-version.php -> PHP 8.4.26 confirmed 1 heap leak 249,042 B producer + 8 x 6,672 B -> 256 B cookie (OOM poisons a worker) └─ Zend chunk base 2 code leak 251,557 B producer + 8 x 92,388 B -> 16 B cookie (OOM poisons a worker) └─ zval_ptr_dtor 3 callback 368,812 B POST -> forged HashTable runs (fake HashTable + command) └─ zif_system(cmd) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 20 HTTP requests at most. No looping, no retries. The short version A small multipart upload makes PHP chew through far more memory than the wire size suggests. When it runs out of memory partway through session upload-progress parsing, PHP leaves stale state behind in a worker that then gets reused. Shape the follow-up requests right and bytes fall out through session cookies. I read those as a heap address and a PHP code address. With both addresses, a final request drops a forged PHP structure where cleanup will find it, and cleanup calls zif_system, PHP's handler for system. That command sends back a fresh proof marker and one print-flag result over the connection that is still open. Why two addresses? The OS randomizes where PHP's code and heap land, independently. The heap leak tells the script where to put the forged structure, the code leak tells it where the function it wants to call actually lives. Addresses from an earlier worker or an earlier run are not safe substitutes, and every time I tried it the attempt just failed. Contents The lab Start here What each request does 1. How a small producer reaches the memory limit 2. How the heap address is recovered 3. How the PHP code address is recovered 4. How the final request reaches system Reading the result How often it actually works The live run that solved it Jargon, briefly Thanks The lab The offsets in this PoC are calibrated for Alpine PHP 8.4.26 running the built-in CLI server with four workers. The lab reproduces exactly that, behind nginx, on loopback. Important The build matters more than the version string. A Debian php:8.4.26-fpm stack reports the same PHP/8.4.26 but has a different binary layout, so the code-pointer fingerprint will never match and the run aborts at the code-leak stage. Use the Alpine image below. Three small files. Put them in an empty directory: public/php-version.php (the health endpoint, and the only page the PoC needs) Fatal error: Allowed memory size of 134217728 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 131072 bytes) in Unknown on line 0
1ef0e73d8615157a uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),0(root),1(bin),2(daemon),3(sys),4(adm),6(disk),10(wheel),11(floppy),20(dialout),26(tape),27(video) 0ec066e8b91457c7c19b5612f3e2ded7f117df08f402693669c1ffc2cfc24942 /usr/local/bin/print-flag LOCAL_DUMMY_WIF_NEVER_USE The PHP fatal, then the nonce this run generated, then id, then the hash of the binary it resolved, then the dummy flag. Exit status is 0 on a verified run and 1 on anything else. Warning The producer deliberately walks PHP into its memory limit. Only run this somewhere that behaviour is authorized. The script will only talk to the challenge endpoint or a loopback lab URL, and anything else aborts before a packet goes out. One run means one health GET, up to two leak batches, and at most one final request. No looping, no retries. Every multipart body stays under 1 MiB, though each leak batch pipelines nine separate requests down one connection. Flag What it does --url Lab endpoint, or the challenge. Required to do anything. --output-dir Where to write the run's evidence. Defaults to poc-run-. What each request does Step What goes out, what should come back Why Health One ordinary GET /php-version.php must return HTTP 200, PHP 8.4.26, and X-Powered-By: PHP/8.4.26. Keeps the memory-limit payload away from a changed or unhealthy endpoint. Heap leak One 249,042-byte multipart producer, then eight pipelined 6,672-byte consumers. The producer must return a PHP 128 MiB memory-limit fatal. A consumer may return a 256-byte PHPSESSID cookie. Four or more pointer-looking values in that cookie have to agree on one aligned 2 MiB Zend heap base. Code leak One 251,557-byte producer, then eight pipelined 92,388-byte consumers. A consumer may return a 16-byte PHPSESSID cookie. Its first eight bytes must encode 16, and its second eight must look like the locally calibrated zval_ptr_dtor pointer. Final callback One 368,812-byte multipart POST. A forged PHP HashTable points cleanup at zif_system and supplies a command argument. The fresh nonce, id output, and print-flag binary hash are the evidence that the callback actually ran. That is 20 HTTP requests at most: one health check, nine per leak batch, one final request. All eight consumers in a batch go out before the first response is read, which helps the timing, but it also means you cannot pull them back if the producer fails. A failed or malformed batch stops the next stage. 1. How a small producer reaches the memory limit The producer is multipart/form-data carrying PHPSESSID and PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS fields. PHP handles upload progress while it is still parsing the request. Hundreds of empty file controls get names like f[0][x][x]... with dozens of nested [x] segments, so the body stays around 250 KiB on the wire while parsing it spawns piles of nested PHP arrays and all the allocations that come with them. The producer also carries 1,001 distinct empty cookie names, which is what the request builder was configured to send at the time. The fatal you want says PHP exhausted its 128 MiB memory limit. What you are actually after is the stale state this particular failure leaves behind in a worker. Important On its own, a memory-limit fatal or an nginx 502 proves nothing about an address leak or code execution. 2. How the heap address is recovered The next request goes after the memory tied to that stale session state. It repeats a single numeric form key, then slips in a crafted value that changes the length PHP uses when it writes PHPSESSID. Land on the right reused worker with the right heap layout and the cookie comes back 256 bytes instead of the usual 32, with neighbouring heap data sitting inside it. heap_candidate() walks that cookie as little-endian 64-bit words, and will only accept a base if at least four pointer-looking values fall in the same aligned 2 MiB heap region. On top of that the runner wants HTTP 200, the expected PHP version, valid cookie lengths from all eight consumers, and exactly one agreed base. Anything short of that and it stops. 3. How the PHP code address is recovered A second producer triggers the same memory-limit condition. Its consumer uses a different array layout, calibrated locally to shake out a PHP function pointer. The cookie you want is exactly 16 bytes: an eight-byte value of 16, then a pointer read as zval_ptr_dtor against the Alpine PHP fingerprint. The script checks the pointer's range and its low 21 bits, 0x112930. That is the page offset of the symbol in the Alpine PHP 8.4.26 image, and ASLR does not move it. Treat it as a fingerprint, not as proof the remote executable is byte for byte the same thing. For this layout, zif_system works out as: zif_system = zval_ptr_dtor - 0x204BC0 Both leaks have to come from the current invocation. The script will not load historical pointer values into a live attempt. 4. How the final request reaches system The final POST parks a 384-byte forged HashTable in a multipart field I control. That structure overlaps a fake call frame and a fake zend_string holding the command. A 276-byte primer supplies a pointer into the controlled region, then a long form-field name drives another memory-limit failure. In the cleanup path, PHP reads the forged table's pDestructor as zif_system and hands it the string argument. 0x00 ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ zend_array header │ pDestructor -> zif_system 0x20 ├──────────────────────────┤ │ bucket / fake call frame │ arg1 -> zend_string below 0x80 ├──────────────────────────┤ │ zend_string header │ 0x98 ├──────────────────────────┤ │ command (231 B max) │ 0x180 └──────────────────────────┘ The target address uses a distance measured in the four-worker Alpine setup: fake_table = zend_heap_base - 0x8400000 + 0x16D1D8 That distance depends on the worker and the allocation layout. Change the image, the memory configuration, or the worker count and this falls over even though the PHP version still reads 8.4.26. The command that originally worked just ran print-flag once. This version prints a fresh random nonce, the output of id (UID and GID), and the SHA-256 of the resolved print-flag binary before invoking print-flag once. It hunts down the active accepted socket under /proc/self/fd so the output actually reaches the HTTP response. Ordinary process stdout got me nothing. Reading the result Every run drops a new poc-run- directory, unless --output-dir points at a new one. Everything is written before it is validated, so a run that aborts halfway still leaves usable evidence. The files worth opening: File Contents heap.request.http, code.request.http The plaintext HTTP bytes handed to each leak-stage socket's sendall, one producer plus eight pipelined consumers. If the transport fails you cannot be sure what actually got delivered. heap.response.http, code.response.http Plaintext HTTP bytes read back off each leak-stage socket, cookies included. heap.json, code.json Parsed response status, lengths, hashes, and candidate addresses. final.request.http The final request as constructed, headers and multipart body. Same caveat about transport failures. final.response.http, final.response.body, final.response.headers.json The final response as read, plus its parsed body and headers. Against the live challenge this body may contain a private WIF. final.json, run.json Summary fields, and whether the expected execution markers showed up. execution_proof_verified: true means the final response came back HTTP 200 carrying the fresh nonce, an id result, and a SHA-256 line for print-flag. Caution Against the real challenge a run directory can contain a live private key. Publish this source file, not a run's output. The script makes no claim about whether a returned WIF controls the advertised Bitcoin address. A checksum-valid WIF only tells you the string encodes a private key properly. Deriving the address and comparing it is a separate job. How often it actually works Both leak stages are races against three other workers, so a single run is not expected to succeed every time.
