title: GitHub - KillaBoi/StealMyBitcoin-PoC: A public release of the Steal My Bitcoin challenge · GitHub
content:
sponsored with ❤️ by Steal My Bitcoin CTF proof of concept One live PHP callback against the Steal My Bitcoin challenge, start to finish, in a single standard-library Python file. This README explains stealmybitcoin_poc.py, a single-file Python reproduction of the request sequence used in my Steal My Bitcoin CTF run. It uses only Python's standard library. The script builds the requests itself, checks each leak before moving on, and records the HTTP bytes from a new run. This can probably be done easier without all the extra debug crap and as in my John Hammond video about the Steam Local Privilege Escalation I discovered, you could probably clean up this ugly PoC. Note ⚠️ Honestly please clean it up or make your own better version that isn't crumpled by Sol. ⚠️ Everything below is written against the Docker lab, not the live challenge. The lab is a local Alpine PHP 8.4.26 CLI server behind nginx, which is the same build and worker model the offsets were calibrated on. Stand it up in a minute and the whole chain runs end to end on your own machine. The live run that actually solved the challenge is kept as a historical note at the bottom. stage what goes out what comes back ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 0 health GET /php-version.php -> PHP 8.4.26 confirmed 1 heap leak 249,042 B producer + 8 x 6,672 B -> 256 B cookie (OOM poisons a worker) └─ Zend chunk base 2 code leak 251,557 B producer + 8 x 92,388 B -> 16 B cookie (OOM poisons a worker) └─ zval_ptr_dtor 3 callback 368,812 B POST -> forged HashTable runs (fake HashTable + command) └─ zif_system(cmd) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 20 HTTP requests at most. No looping, no retries. The short version A small multipart upload makes PHP chew through far more memory than the wire size suggests. When it runs out of memory partway through session upload-progress parsing, PHP leaves stale state behind in a worker that then gets reused. Shape the follow-up requests right and bytes fall out through session cookies. I read those as a heap address and a PHP code address. With both addresses, a final request drops a forged PHP structure where cleanup will find it, and cleanup calls zif_system, PHP's handler for system. That command sends back a fresh proof marker and one print-flag result over the connection that is still open. Why two addresses? The OS randomizes where PHP's code and heap land, independently. The heap leak tells the script where to put the forged structure, the code leak tells it where the function it wants to call actually lives. Addresses from an earlier worker or an earlier run are not safe substitutes, and every time I tried it the attempt just failed. Contents The lab Start here What each request does 1. How a small producer reaches the memory limit 2. How the heap address is recovered 3. How the PHP code address is recovered 4. How the final request reaches system Reading the result How often it actually works The live run that solved it Jargon, briefly Thanks The lab The offsets in this PoC are calibrated for Alpine PHP 8.4.26 running the built-in CLI server with four workers. The lab reproduces exactly that, behind nginx, on loopback. Important The build matters more than the version string. A Debian php:8.4.26-fpm stack reports the same PHP/8.4.26 but has a different binary layout, so the code-pointer fingerprint will never match and the run aborts at the code-leak stage. Use the Alpine image below. Three small files. Put them in an empty directory: public/php-version.php (the health endpoint, and the only page the PoC needs) Fatal error: Allowed memory size of 134217728 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 131072 bytes) in Unknown on line 0
1ef0e73d8615157a uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),0(root),1(bin),2(daemon),3(sys),4(adm),6(disk),10(wheel),11(floppy),20(dialout),26(tape),27(video) 0ec066e8b91457c7c19b5612f3e2ded7f117df08f402693669c1ffc2cfc24942 /usr/local/bin/print-flag LOCAL_DUMMY_WIF_NEVER_USE The PHP fatal, then the nonce this run generated, then id, then the hash of the binary it resolved, then the dummy flag. Exit status is 0 on a verified run and 1 on anything else. Warning The producer deliberately walks PHP into its memory limit. Only run this somewhere that behaviour is authorized. The script will only talk to the challenge endpoint or a loopback lab URL, and anything else aborts before a packet goes out. One run means one health GET, up to two leak batches, and at most one final request. No looping, no retries. Every multipart body stays under 1 MiB, though each leak batch pipelines nine separate requests down one connection. Flag What it does --url Lab endpoint, or the challenge. Required to do anything. --output-dir Where to write the run's evidence. Defaults to poc-run-. What each request does Step What goes out, what should come back Why Health One ordinary GET /php-version.php must return HTTP 200, PHP 8.4.26, and X-Powered-By: PHP/8.4.26. Keeps the memory-limit payload away from a changed or unhealthy endpoint. Heap leak One 249,042-byte multipart producer, then eight pipelined 6,672-byte consumers. The producer must return a PHP 128 MiB memory-limit fatal. A consumer may return a 256-byte PHPSESSID cookie. Four or more pointer-looking values in that cookie have to agree on one aligned 2 MiB Zend heap base. Code leak One 251,557-byte producer, then eight pipelined 92,388-byte consumers. A consumer may return a 16-byte PHPSESSID cookie. Its first eight bytes must encode 16, and its second eight must look like the locally calibrated zval_ptr_dtor pointer. Final callback One 368,812-byte multipart POST. A forged PHP HashTable points cleanup at zif_system and supplies a command argument. The fresh nonce, id output, and print-flag binary hash are the evidence that the callback actually ran. That is 20 HTTP requests at most: one health check, nine per leak batch, one final request. All eight consumers in a batch go out before the first response is read, which helps the timing, but it also means you cannot pull them back if the producer fails. A failed or malformed batch stops the next stage. 1. How a small producer reaches the memory limit The producer is multipart/form-data carrying PHPSESSID and PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS fields. PHP handles upload progress while it is still parsing the request. Hundreds of empty file controls get names like f[0][x][x]... with dozens of nested [x] segments, so the body stays around 250 KiB on the wire while parsing it spawns piles of nested PHP arrays and all the allocations that come with them. The producer also carries 1,001 distinct empty cookie names, which is what the request builder was configured to send at the time. The fatal you want says PHP exhausted its 128 MiB memory limit. What you are actually after is the stale state this particular failure leaves behind in a worker. Important On its own, a memory-limit fatal or an nginx 502 proves nothing about an address leak or code execution. 2. How the heap address is recovered The next request goes after the memory tied to that stale session state. It repeats a single numeric form key, then slips in a crafted value that changes the length PHP uses when it writes PHPSESSID. Land on the right reused worker with the right heap layout and the cookie comes back 256 bytes instead of the usual 32, with neighbouring heap data sitting inside it. heap_candidate() walks that cookie as little-endian 64-bit words, and will only accept a base if at least four pointer-looking values fall in the same aligned 2 MiB heap region. On top of that the runner wants HTTP 200, the expected PHP version, valid cookie lengths from all eight consumers, and exactly one agreed base. Anything short of that and it stops. 3. How the PHP code address is recovered A second producer triggers the same memory-limit condition. Its consumer uses a different array layout, calibrated locally to shake out a PHP function pointer. The cookie you want is exactly 16 bytes: an eight-byte value of 16, then a pointer read as zval_ptr_dtor against the Alpine PHP fingerprint. The script checks the pointer's range and its low 21 bits, 0x112930. That is the page offset of the symbol in the Alpine PHP 8.4.26 image, and ASLR does not move it. Treat it as a fingerprint, not as proof the remote executable is byte for byte the same thing. For this layout, zif_system works out as: zif_system = zval_ptr_dtor - 0x204BC0 Both leaks have to come from the current invocation. The script will not load historical pointer values into a live attempt. 4. How the final request reaches system The final POST parks a 384-byte forged HashTable in a multipart field I control. That structure overlaps a fake call frame and a fake zend_string holding the command. A 276-byte primer supplies a pointer into the controlled region, then a long form-field name drives another memory-limit failure. In the cleanup path, PHP reads the forged table's pDestructor as zif_system and hands it the string argument. 0x00 ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ zend_array header │ pDestructor -> zif_system 0x20 ├──────────────────────────┤ │ bucket / fake call frame │ arg1 -> zend_string below 0x80 ├──────────────────────────┤ │ zend_string header │ 0x98 ├──────────────────────────┤ │ command (231 B max) │ 0x180 └──────────────────────────┘ The target address uses a distance measured in the four-worker Alpine setup: fake_table = zend_heap_base - 0x8400000 + 0x16D1D8 That distance depends on the worker and the allocation layout. Change the image, the memory configuration, or the worker count and this falls over even though the PHP version still reads 8.4.26. The command that originally worked just ran print-flag once. This version prints a fresh random nonce, the output of id (UID and GID), and the SHA-256 of the resolved print-flag binary before invoking print-flag once. It hunts down the active accepted socket under /proc/self/fd so the output actually reaches the HTTP response. Ordinary process stdout got me nothing. Reading the result Every run drops a new poc-run- directory, unless --output-dir points at a new one. Everything is written before it is validated, so a run that aborts halfway still leaves usable evidence. The files worth opening: File Contents heap.request.http, code.request.http The plaintext HTTP bytes handed to each leak-stage socket's sendall, one producer plus eight pipelined consumers. If the transport fails you cannot be sure what actually got delivered. heap.response.http, code.response.http Plaintext HTTP bytes read back off each leak-stage socket, cookies included. heap.json, code.json Parsed response status, lengths, hashes, and candidate addresses. final.request.http The final request as constructed, headers and multipart body. Same caveat about transport failures. final.response.http, final.response.body, final.response.headers.json The final response as read, plus its parsed body and headers. Against the live challenge this body may contain a private WIF. final.json, run.json Summary fields, and whether the expected execution markers showed up. execution_proof_verified: true means the final response came back HTTP 200 carrying the fresh nonce, an id result, and a SHA-256 line for print-flag. Caution Against the real challenge a run directory can contain a live private key. Publish this source file, not a run's output. The script makes no claim about whether a returned WIF controls the advertised Bitcoin address. A checksum-valid WIF only tells you the string encodes a private key properly. Deriving the address and comparing it is a separate job. How often it actually works Both leak stages are races against three other workers, so a single run is not expected to succeed every time. title: The State of Context Engineering
content:
Oct 24, 2026
CONTEXT ENGINEERING
PRESENTATION
The State of Context Engineering
The Job is Knowing When to Be Deterministic & When to Be Probabilistic
This week, I gave a short talk at AGNTCon titled, “Context Fails & Fixes,” that functioned as a sort of “State of Context Engineering.” How did context engineering emerge, where has it gone, and where might it go in the future? As model makers target new capabilities, they inadvertently create challenges we, as users and harness builders, must overcome.
Below are the slides and a lightly edited transcript. As always, shoot me a note with any feedback, thoughts, or questions. I really appreciate it.
Hi, everyone. Thanks for joining me today. We’re going to walk through context fails and fixes.
I have a book coming out in a bit, The Context Engineering Handbook. When I first talked to the team at O’Reilly, back in June 2025, they asked me a very reasonable question: “How do we know this won’t become obsolete in a few weeks?” The trouble with AI textbooks is that many age extraordinarily quickly.
I said, I don’t know, but I’m optimistic. Giving clear instructions about what to do and what not to do, and ensuring those instructions are consistent and not noisy, will forever be a challenge with AI, no matter how good it gets.
We have coworkers, partners, and other people we know and interact with who are sentient. They pass the Turing test, they are “AGI,” and yet: we still have a hard time conveying instructions, ideas, and concepts among each other.
Context engineering will continue to be hard. But it will be hard in unique ways, because models aren’t people. You can make assumptions about how models think or interpret things (use whatever anthropomorphizing word you like), but it helps to understand how they’re built, optimized, and trained. Their unique attributes and construction create a unique set of failure modes we need to reckon with.
So let’s review how we got here.
Let’s flash back to the end of 2024.
If you remember, this was the height of the “RAG is dead” moment.
The hope was: if we can just make the context window large enough, we can put the entire internet in it. We can put everything in it. We don’t have to be selective. We don’t have to build agentic systems. We can fit it all in there, and AI will be solved.
Model builders started aiming at long context capabilities and we had a big leap from ~128,000-token context window models to million-token context window models, starting with Gemini 1.5.
If you look at the marketing material for Gemini 1.5 Pro, it was mostly about the million-token context window. They were even teasing a 10-million-token context window model they had in the lab, that would come out soon.
But they got beaten to the punch. Llama 4 Scout came out with a 10-million-token context window, and well, it wasn’t quite what we hoped. Inference was a challenge, and Scout never really caught on, and we never got another Llama.
But we still got a million tokens. That’s pretty good. We’ll take it.
So this was the brief at the time: just put everything in the context and let the model sort it out.
But with more context, we had room for more problems. Long contexts are not a panacea.
When I wrote about this, I identified four key failure modes.
Context poisoning is when something gets into the context that shouldn’t be there. It could be a hallucination or a bad fact, and the model can’t get past it.
Context distraction is when the context grows so long that the model starts to focus on the context over its base knowledge. We can see this in some really interesting ways.
Context confusion is when extraneous facts—things that don’t relate to the problem I’m working on—come in and influence the model in ways we don’t fully understand. This one’s really pernicious. We’re not going to dig into it today, but it’s one of my favorite failure modes. The model makes assumptions about who you are, and those assumptions influence the answer.
Finally, context clash is when tool calls, skills, and other information within your harness start to conflict and work against you in ways you didn’t expect.
(How many of you keep memory on in ChatGPT or Claude? I turn it off. I hate it. Sometimes I’m talking about work conversations; sometimes I’m talking about a project I’m doing with my son. The model will take notes on both, mix up those contexts, and the confusion grows from there.)
Let me give you my favorite example of context poisoning.
I’m going to date myself: I played the game on the left. The one from 1996, for the original Game Boy. This is the first Pokémon Red. It was in black and white.
In 2004, Nintendo released Pokémon FireRed for the Game Boy Advance. These were essentially the same game, except one had better colors and audio.
But there was one subtle change. At some point in both Pokémon Reds, to get past a security guard, you have to give them something to drink. A bribe. Quite the practical lesson for children.
In the original game, you need to give the thirsty guard lemonade. In FireRed, for some reason, they changed it to iced tea.
That created a problem for the agent. In the Gemini 2.5 technical report, the researchers described how they had the model play Pokémon. Researchers like Pokémon as an agent benchmark because it’s a reasonably controlled environment and doesn’t move particularly fast.
Several times, Gemini 2.5 became convinced it needed to get tea, even though it was playing the older game. The tea task for FireRed was in its weights, so it poisoned its context. It spent hours trying to find or give the guard tea. Once it had been added to its to-do list, the model could not get past it.
That’s context poisoning. And it happens all the time.
Another failure mode is context distraction. This is one of my favorite demonstrations, and the research came out after I wrote the original piece.
As your context gets longer, how does your behavior change? Quick question: how many of you, when you’re coding, let the context go all the way to a million tokens? Fill it all up?
(About half the room raised their hands!)
Wow, that’s more than I expected.
For me, around 200,000 or 300,000 is where I start looking. I’ll check, see it’s at 250,000, and think: I’ve got a big job coming up. I’m going to reset and start fresh. Let me show you why this matters.
Recently, I stumbled on a paper that wonderfully illustrates context distraction: Do as I Say, Not as I Do, by Carolina Camassa and Derek Shiller.
Their experiment is a little contrived, but it’s useful for thinking about how this happens. They give the model an instruction: “I want you to translate every question into Russian as your answer to each of my questions.” Then they present a bunch of examples that are counter to these instructions. In this case, many questions with answers in French.
These aren’t new instructions. They’re just examples sitting in the chat history.
Then they ask the model a question. Will it follow the instructions?
How often does the model respond in Russian, as it was instructed to, and how often does it respond in French, as it’s seen in the examples?
The x-axis on this matrix enumerates how many bad examples were present. The y-axis is the model being tested. The figures in the intersections are the percentage of times the model adheres to the instructions, rather than following the examples.
It turns out this affects every model! For smaller models, like Gemma 3 12B, after just a few contradictory examples, the model follows the instruction less than half the time. With Opus 4.6, which is an amazing model, it takes many more examples, but it happens there too.
Imagine you’re going back and forth on a front-end design, trying to tweak CSS and get a component exactly right. How many bad examples have you seeded in that exchange? Those examples start to influence the model. As your context grows, things fall apart.
Gemini 2.5 ran into this too, while playing Pokémon.
Remember, Google was really proud of its million-token context window. The paper suggested that two million tokens were around the corner. But buried in the appendix was this observation: once the context grew significantly beyond 100,000 tokens, the agent began repeating actions from its history instead of synthesizing new plans.
I’m convinced the marketing people never read the appendix. I love this technical report.
Long contexts let you fit in more information, but they also let you fit in more errors. Long contexts weren’t a panacea.
Thankfully, we’ve developed a pretty good toolbox. Surprisingly, even as new challenges have emerged (we’ll get to those in a minute), this set of tools has remained the same.
These six of them.
You have context augmentation: RAG, skills, and other ways to bring in the information relevant to the problem.
You have tool loadout: selecting which tools and skills to expose so you don’t overload the model. I was recently talking to an enterprise team whose agents had suddenly started performing terribly. We investigated and discovered their enterprise software was loading 600 skills for every engineer at startup. We figured they should probably filter those, with a loadout function.
Third is context quarantine: subagents and peer agents, where you start something with a blank history but let it work in the same environment.
Fourth is context pruning. Claude Code and Codex do this, sometimes without you even noticing. Early stages of compaction often strip out tool results you no longer need.
Fifth is context offloading: storing information in the environment, such as Markdown files or a database, so you can access it later.
And sixth is context summarization, which everyone knows as compaction.
These are the tools, and we’ve increasingly moved them into the harness.
Let’s look at an example harness, to show how simple these patterns are.
I’m really passionate about DSPy. I think it’s an incredibly readable and effective way to build AI workflows and agents. And it’s also a great language for simply specifying behavior, so it’s well suited to this demonstration.
An agent is a while loop. Here we’re using a ReAct module: we give it a request, we want a response, and we give it some tools. Those tools are just Python functions.
For this demo we have a big model (in this case, Claude opted for Claude Sonnet 4.5, good luck with that!). And I’m using a Jev as the small model: a tiny decision model that makes lightning-fast decisions. You could swap in a small LLM in this example, and everything would still work.
We have a while loop that takes input, sends it to ReAct, and carries the accruing history forward. This is an agent in about a dozen lines using DSPy. It would be even fewer if you took out the extra model.
How do we do tool loadout? It’s just a function.
We present Jev with the request and a tool, asking if it’s needed for this task.
Jev is fast enough that we can do this one tool at a time; it’ll be fine. We wrap this in a loadout function that iterates through all the tools and asks if each is needed, then returns the top-ranking subset. That’s it.
With context quarantine, it’s just a subagent. You expose an agent as a tool that the main agent can use, and it starts with a blank history.
With context pruning, we’re stepping through the history, passing each turn to Jev, and asking: is this still needed? If not, cut it.
You can be as rough or as elegant as you want here. Just mind your prompt caching.
We can also rewrite the history with compaction. Take the old turns, create a summary, and start the new context from that summary.
One of my favorite variations lately is checking what matters before you compact. You use Jev, or another decision model, for the first pass to judge what’s relevant. Now you’ve got a smaller subset of the history, and you summarize that. It’s a simple extra step, but it makes the summary more useful.
Put it all together and it’s about 16 lines of changes. Four fixes, one loop. These are the moves we have in the harness. It’s actually remarkably simple.
What isn’t simple is our language: how we talk about this stuff. It’s really hard to keep pace; it changes every day.
One of my favorite quotes is from Stewart Brand, which I think about all the time:
If you want to know where the future is being made, look for where language is being invented and lawyers are congregating.
Certainly applies here! But as our language has changed, our goal has remained the same.
In 2023, we called choosing the right information to get the right response prompt engineering.
In 2025, we called it context engineering, except that now it was more automated. It wasn’t just you writing the prompt; it was your system dynamically assembling the context.
Then, as we moved more of these tools out of the context and into code, we started calling it harness engineering.
But the job is the same. We’re moving more and more of the work of assembling context from probabilistic model calls to deterministic code.
I’ve shown you 2024. Let’s go to 2026.
We’ve moved these context fixes into the harness. What do we want next? We want agentic models that can drive our harnesses.
Everybody started targeting long-horizon agentic models. You’ve seen the METR reports. GPT-5 could handle tasks around 3.4 hours on that measure; Gemini 3.1 got up to 6.4 hours. That’s with a harness. The models have gotten much better at using it, and that’s how they’re able to run for so long.
Opus 4.6 got up to around 12 hours. And now we’re talking about agents running for days, swarms of agents, and models that drive harnesses over much longer periods.
Before, the pitch was: make the context so large that we can fit everything in it.
Now the pitch is: teach the model to drive the harness and manage its own context. That’s become the dominant pattern. That’s what model builders are working towards.
What new failure modes does this approach create?
So far we’ve found two new failure modes.
When you train models to use harnesses really well, you end up overfitting them to a particular set of tools and environments they were trained within.
How many of you have used the Playwright MCP server, or something similar? This is the MCP conference, so probably quite a few.
Smaller models, something like Haiku or Luna, will often botch this tool call on the first attempt, then recover and adjust the parameters. The environment it was trained in had similar tools that looked different than Playwright. Whatever Anthropic or OpenAI used in training. And you have to fight against these biases.
I call this fighting the weights: when the model doesn’t do what you ask because you’re working against what it was trained to do.
It’s a real problem, and it’s not just for us. The labs and the people building their products have to contend with it too.
Here’s a piece of the Claude Code system prompt and some of its tool instructions.

title: G-Diffuser on 3DS
content:
01 · OVERVIEW
F-ZERO X ON 3DS — OLD AND NEW, NATIVE, WITH THE 64DD EXPANSION KIT
A post-mortem of porting G-Diffuser, the F-Zero X decompilation, to the Nintendo 3DS — v1.0.0, covering both the original 24-day sprint that put it on a New 3DS at 60 fps in 3D (2026-08-11 to 09-03) and the 43-day second phase that added Old 3DS support, a native renderer, and the Expansion Kit (2026-09-07 to 10-19). One person directed throughout; one long-lived Claude session orchestrated; 147 subagents built the first phase and many more carried the second.
The console went from a black screen to a native-60 stereoscopic racer, then from a New-3DS-only build to a four-way release covering both consoles with and without the 64DD expansion.
59.6fps
median on hardware, full Grand Prix, New 3DS, end of the first phase (from 12–20 fps in the first emulator race)
51.4fps
tenth-percentile floor in 30-machine crowds, first phase (from 25–35)
53%
of frames at the 60 cap, first phase (from 14% one week earlier)
15
active days across the first phase's 24 calendar days, three pauses when the weekly plan allowance ran out
3.17 B
tokens across all sessions and agents, first phase only; see Cost
$4,974
at published API list prices (Fable $10/$50 per MTok, 1-hour cache writes), first phase only; see Cost
250
commits touching the 3DS port in the first phase, frozen 2026-10-08 from the v0.9.0 docs — not re-verified against final history
15,039
lines under port/3ds plus 48 pure-delta patches, first-phase count
WHAT V1.0.0 ADDED
3
released console builds from one source tree: Old 3DS, New 3DS, and New 3DS with the Expansion Kit
199
internal progress notes written during the second phase
43days
calendar span of the second phase, 2026-09-07 to 10-19 inclusive
The tiles above are dated. The first phase's hardware numbers and token/cost figures were measured through 2026-09-03 and have not been re-run for v1.0.0; the Agentic workflow page describes how the second phase was run, and the Cost page is explicit about what it does and does not price.
ON HARDWARE
v1.0, New 3DS: the Expansion Kit's Select Mode (COURSE EDIT, CREATE MACHINE); the bottom screen is DASH's idle view.
v1.0, New 3DS, mid-race: DASH on the bottom screen with energy, position, lap times and the course map.
The clips and photos below are from v0.9 (2026-09), before DASH replaced the debug console on the bottom screen.
open clip
v0.9: Grand Prix on a New 3DS. The bottom screen is the port's debug menu: 59.8 fps, heap, build id.
open clip
v0.9: handheld, mid-race. Native 60 Hz pacing; no interpolation.
Title screen, launched from the Homebrew Launcher (.3dsx).
Select Mode.
Select Machine.
Blue Falcon.
WHAT WAS BUILT
Three released console builds from one source tree, all booting from the HOME menu (.cia) or the homebrew launcher (.3dsx): the base game for Old 3DS / 2DS and for New 3DS / New 2DS XL, and a New 3DS build with the 64DD Expansion Kit (course editor and machine creator, playable with a user-supplied disk image). Every build reads prebaked asset archives from the SD card — no ROM or disk image ever ships with the game.
They play the whole game: Grand Prix, Time Trial, Practice, Death Race, and the machine editor screens, with music and effects on the real DSP, stereoscopic 3D on the slider, a bottom-screen dashboard with three HUD layouts and an idle view outside races, and clean HOME suspend, resume, close, lid sleep and power-off. The New 3DS build keeps the native-60 frame pacing the first phase reached; the Old 3DS build gets to a comparable result by a different route. At v1.0.0, with no ini, both builds default to that same route: the native renderer ([perf] preset = auto). The New 3DS's first-phase render-thread/per-draw-stereo path is still built in and reachable with an explicit ini, but is no longer the default — see Frontier and Pushing the boundaries for the two builds compared side by side.
The stack
decomp: the F-Zero X decompilation (inspectredc/fzerox), untouched upstream, plus a patch stack.
libultraship: the N64 runtime (Kenix3), untouched upstream, including a 13-line newlib fix that lets it build on devkitARM; it still draws every menu and non-race screen.
port/3ds: 15,039 lines as of the first phase, since grown: a citro3d rendering backend, stereo, audio, input, menu, lifecycle, render thread, profilers, packaging.
the native renderer (added in the second phase): an owned interpreter that skips the per-frame display-list walk for race geometry, and is the v1.0.0 default on both consoles — see Frontier for how, and why it is what lets the Old 3DS keep up.
The headline numbers on hardware, first phase (New 3DS)
WHEN MEDIAN P10 AT CAP
08-14 first race (emulator) 12–20 – –
08-21 first hardware run 48–50 – –
08-28 release-grade build ~51 ~40 (crowds, MINIMAL) –
09-02 Round 1: Mainline before the campaign 51.3 39.2 9%
09-02 Round 2: Bridge memos (brfast) 57.2 46.6 29%
09-02 Round 3: HUD atlas · triangle memo · TMEM · audio 56.0 48.0 32%
09-02 Round 4: Render thread on core 2 (pipe) 57.6 44.6 14%
09-03 Round 5: Ahead mode · bridge on main · auto rival detail 59.6 51.4 53%
THE FIRST PHASE IN FIVE LINES
08-11 → 08-14: from research to a race. Feasibility dossier, plan for a team of agents, five parallel foundation streams, six boot bugs, first race at 12–20 fps in the emulator.
08-20 → 08-22: from pink to playable, then to a real console. Fog, HUD, livery, shadow, sky fixed; the loadblock discovery took menus from 27 to 60 fps; first hardware run 08-21 ("wow it runs amazing"); audio the same evening.
08-27 → 08-28: product grade. Five-agent fleet drop, stereo armed, touch menu, rival detail, GPU vertex-transform moonshot built and shelved, README with legal notice, release package.
09-01 → 09-02: lifecycle and the last big lever. HOME crash and close-from-HOME hang fixed; a bridge output cache proven a NO-GO and replaced by memoizing each sub-display-list's classification instead of re-scanning it every frame; LOCKED-60 campaign launched with four parallel levers.
09-02 → 09-03: multi-core. Render thread on core 2, one-frame-ahead mode, bridge on main, auto LOD; median 59.6 with 53% of frames at cap; crash fixed; viewport placement fixed; stereo markers anchored.
THE SECOND PHASE IN SIX LINES
Not originally planned; it ran 09-07 to 10-19, 43 calendar days.
09-07 → 09-29: scoping, then making it fit. The Old 3DS milestone, previously written off, was restarted; parallel agents fit the build into its 64 MB app region (the RDRAM arena halved, audio streamed instead of resident, texture uploads capped); on 2026-09-29, in the first hardware session on a real Old 3DS, the shipped (New-3DS-era, 16 MiB RDRAM) build died at boot while the -DGDX_3DS_O3DS=ON profile, built to fit the console's memory grant, booted and raced the same session at about 10 fps.
09-29 → 09-30: finding the real costs. A narrowed audio lock cut the race-wall wait on the Old 3DS by about 20 ms a frame; frame skipping ended the game's accidental slow motion; a first retained-mode renderer won big in the emulator and barely moved the number on hardware.
09-30 → 10-01: the probe that changed the plan. Hardware performance counters showed the real limit was instruction-cache misses, not instruction count. A pose-replay fallback was built and worked, then was set aside on the user's call: "we should go for a real 60! i still believe it has to be possible."
10-01 → 10-02: the native renderer. Rebuilt around the cache instead of around instruction counts, one small loop per race category, sized to fit the 16 KB instruction cache. Median frame time on a 2D Grand Prix race reached 16.5 ms.
10-03 → 10-08: 3D at 60, on the Old 3DS too. A per-eye resubmit with its own swap-pacing mode reached 59–60 fps in 3D on most Grand Prix courses; the heaviest courses (Silence, Sand Ocean) can still trip the frame-skip safety net to a steady 30 fps mid-race.
10-08 → 10-19: the Expansion Kit, a dashboard, and release. The 64DD Expansion Kit verified tick-for-tick identical under the native renderer and booted on the Old 3DS, which then proved too slow to release it on; the bottom-screen DASH shipped; a standing adversarial review audited the merged result before the v1.0.0 release.
See Agentic workflow for how the second phase was run and Old 3DS for the full campaign, card by card.
READ ON

Every step: The chronology, New 3DS to v1.0.0.
Road to 60: The New 3DS performance campaign, round by round.
The native fork: Why it exists, and what it changed.
Old 3DS: The road to a real 60 at 268 MHz.
Pushing the boundaries: Against our New 3DS build and against the field.
Difficulties: What fought back, and how it was beaten.
Frontier: What this port does that others in its position haven't.
Agentic workflow: How the fleet was run, and how the ship was steered.
Cost: Tokens, dollars, subagents.
Every number on these pages has a source: git history, the research documents under docs/research/, the hardware logs, or the session transcripts the Cost page counts. Where a value is an estimate (the dollar figures, which apply published API list prices to exact token counts), the assumption is stated next to it.

title: ADRs4AI — Your thinking stops disappearing. Your decisions start compounding.
content:
ADRs4AI
get started
the idea
blog
github
ADRs4AI
Your thinking stops disappearing. Your decisions start compounding.
The template
A repository starter: ADR & seed templates, the directives, the inbox protocol, task-runner recipes. Adopt whole or by feature — it works from your first seed.
The VS Code extension
Tree views of your open questions, diagnostics that catch malformed records as you type, deep links, and an MCP server so your agents can query the record. Also on Open VSX.
The iOS client
Your project's open questions, in your pocket: sign in, import a repo, review, and one-tap Accept that lands real answers as commits. On the App Store.
The most valuable byproduct of the collaboration between a human and an AI is the thinking — and in ordinary practice, all of it evaporates. You can already make good decisions with your AI. Every session produces reasoning you will need again, and lose by default. This keeps the why, so it compounds.
A record, verbatim
This is the method’s product — one question from a live, public project’s own record, exactly as it sits in the repository:
### QST-HISTORICAL-TRUTH: How should corrections preserve what was previously believed?
- Status: answered
- Why asking: Conversation attribution needs “what was true or documented as
  of date X,” while later research may correct earlier records.
- Need: Approve or revise the proposed temporal policy.
**Options**:
- **A — Mutable present truth**: Correct records in place; rely on Git
  history for prior states.
- **B — Append-only assertions**: Never change claims; append corrections
  and supersession edges.
- **C — Bitemporal hybrid**: Correct descriptive records when needed, while
  claims/events carry valid-time, observed-time, and explicit supersession;
  Git remains a third audit layer.
**Recommendation**: (by GPT 5.6 Sol at Perplexity Computer)
**C — Bitemporal hybrid.**
**Rationale**: Git history records when repository bytes changed, not when a
release became valid or when a provider made a statement. Explicit
valid-time and observed-time support historical queries, while supersession
edges preserve corrections without forcing every typo into an eternal
domain event.
**Confidence**: High that Git history alone is insufficient; medium-high
that two temporal axes cover the first release.
**Falsifier**: If real attribution cases require additional independent
times, such as product-availability time distinct from announced and
effective time, the temporal model must expand rather than overload either
axis.
**ANS:** (by Jérémie "Sonnet 4.5" Lumbroso (via ADRs4AI mobile))
C — Bitemporal hybrid.
From frontier-model-observatory, verbatim. The AI staked the question; the recommendation — options, rationale, confidence, and what would prove it wrong — is GPT 5.6 Sol’s; the one-line ruling came from the founder’s phone. That’s the whole mechanic: The AI carries the reasoning, the human spends one judgment — accept, override, or any answer in any shape — and the record keeps the why, for every mind that comes later.
Ten minutes, from zero
Real commands, the flow the founder actually runs — one seed, one question, one ruling:
# 1 · Your copy of the template
gh repo create my-project --private --clone \
  --template ADRs4AI/human-ai-collaboration-template-A
cd my-project
# 2 · Open CLAUDE.md, fill in the top block (messy is fine),
#     then stake the record before any work starts:
git add -A && git commit -m "chore: the record begins before the building does"
# 3 · Recruit — open your agent and offer the mission:
claude    # or your agent of choice
#   "Hello — I have a mission for you. Read about it and tell me
#    if you accept, or any pushback."
Then dump your thinking into a first seed — dictation is fine; your AI chunks it into ADRs that keep your actual words, the options, the reasoning, the open questions. Answer the first question it stakes. Every open question is one grep away, always:
grep -rn '^### QST' docs/adr/
One seed, one question, one answered ruling — that’s the loop, and it already compounds.
Running a crew — several seats, wake-on-brief, you stop being the message bus — is the optional next chapter: steps 7–9 of Get started.
How it works, in twenty seconds
Dump your thinking into a seed — messy is fine, dictation is fine; capture first. Your AI chunks it into ADRs that keep what usually evaporates: your actual words, the options considered, the reasoning, the open questions. Every question is findable by one grep — ### QST: — or surfaced by the editor extension, the MCP server, the phone in your pocket; and each arrives with the AI’s options, its recommendation, its rationale, its stated confidence, and what would prove it wrong — so answering streamlines to accept or override: Cognitive load down, bandwidth freed for the deliberations that matter. It’s where conversations become decisions that keep their reasons — deliberative programming, in one habit.
You don’t need to be an experienced engineer to start. The method was built through daily practice by one human and a growing crew of AI collaborators, and its whole point is that the record does the remembering — as much for the veteran with too many projects, as for the beginner building their very first one.
The extension’s Open Questions view, on this project’s own record: A question, its options, an attributed recommendation — and the answer box. Question 16 of 75, that day.
What it is not
Not transcript archival. Not vector-database “memory.” Not an orchestration platform. Not a claim that an AI possesses persistent identity — the record holds, minds change, and the work resumes either way.
The ecosystem, mapped
Everything in the ADRs4AI world and what each piece is for, on one page — methodology & template, editors & clients, crew automation, projects practicing it, learning & teaching — every entry marked by kind and language: awesome-adrs4ai, the curated map.
Papers
Cybernetic and Epistemic: A Missing Vocabulary for Trustworthy Agentic Delegation — accepted at the AAAI 2026 Fall Symposium on Trustworthy Agentic Systems (TAS 2026) · arXiv:2610.00961
Deliberative Programming: A Versioned Deliberation Protocol for Human–AI Collectives — DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23300579
The methodology template itself is citable: concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23303469 — always resolves to the latest archived release.
The idea underneath
The most valuable thing that happens between a human and an AI is not the code, the draft, or the answer. It’s the thinking — and in ordinary practice, all of it evaporates. […] It does not make an AI persistent, and it does not make anyone remember. It makes the work resumable — and the thinking compound.
— from What is ADRs4AI?, the founding essay. A stranger can read it cold; its authorship and review record are public, because that is the method.
From the blog
2026-08-25Acknowledgments, before the launch
2026-08-25Cybernetic and epistemic: Two ways to relate to AI
An epistemic-continuity protocol for humans and AI.
Built in the open by Jérémie Lumbroso and a crew of named, attributed AI collaborators — which is the whole point. · Why this exists · Privacy · Support

title: “We should be more ambitious with the software we build”
content:
Since early this year, Michael Malis (of pgrust) has been showing me interesting things he's done and saying
[W]e should be more ambitious1 with the software we build
There is, understandably, a lot of skepticism about projects like pgrust because there are so many low-quality AI-generated projects out there. If I didn't know Malis and didn't look into it, I would just assume that pgrust was another vibe slopped project that's never going to work. But I know Malis well enough to trust his work without looking into it, and if you look into it a bit, you'll see that in testing pgrust, he's testing thoroughly enough that he's even uncovering real bugs in Postgres, such as this numerical bug that can cause valid SP-GiST operations to fail, this format cache bug that can cause incorrect results from JSONPath, this pgcrypto bug that can cause later operations to fail, multiple memory safety bugs in the dictionary loader2, this money overflow bug, etc.
This isn't to say that pgrust is bug free3, but it does indicate that there's a substantial amount of testing happening and, even if pgrust itself is never successful, just making the attempt will have improved Postgres in a durable way. The main pitch for pgrust is actually performance, and that's where the really interesting work is happening; if pgrust fails, it's possible that some of the optimizations they've demonstrated will make it into Postgres, Clickhouse, etc., but that's obviously less direct than filing Postgres bugs which get fixed.
That being said, I find it understandable that, every time I see pgrust discussed on a news aggregator, most people dismiss it as vibeslop garbage because almost all of these rewrite projects are slop. If I didn't know Malis, I would make the same assumption, because who has the time to look into all of these projects? Because I know Malis, I didn't bother to look at it; I just trusted him (I only found the above because I wanted to check on pgrust before using it as an example for this post).
As a consumer of software, everywhere you look, there's slow software that the creator is claiming is fast because the creator is touting some slop benchmark, e.g., here's one of multiple examples I saw yesterday, and of course low-quality software that doesn't work is more common than ever.
But, as a builder of software, it doesn't matter that almost all of these projects are vibeslop, that other people are out there shoveling out huge piles of crap and calling it gold. You can build things like pgrust or other projects that would've been too large to really be feasible in the past and, if you do a reasonable job with testing and benchmarking, that stuff can actually be good-enough quality to use.
If I were writing it, I would say "we can be more ambitious with the software we build" and not "we should", but Malis has been casually chatting with me when he's said this, so maybe he would say the same in an actual post; don't read too much into should vs. can here. What's interesting to me is how capabilities have advanced such that we can do a lot more.
Just for example, after hearing that OpenAI was going to use Cerebras for their SOTA models and not just fast-but-low-quality models like 5.3-Codex-Spark, I looked at where time on my computer would go if I was using a SOTA model, but 10x to 100x faster; some things that were already sometimes a bottleneck that would only get worse with a faster model were:
Ripgrep
Compiling Rust
Syscall and filesystem overhead
At the level of a "works for me" project, these are all things that can seriously be improved. I don't have much spare time at the moment but, even so, I built this regex engine that can be tweaked to be faster than other general-purpose regex libraries on any particular workload I care about, this ripgrep fork that uses the native code compiler from the regex engine and is faster for my codex ripgrep workloads (of course a text index is the better solution, but I've already worked on text indexing and this was a "just for fun" project where I wasn't trying to do the optimal thing), and a Rust that sped up builds for my projects (huge improvement for cold builds, moderate for warm, limited by wanting to avoid forking the Rust compiler front-end). For syscalls and filesystem overhead, just switching development from Mac to Linux improved this a lot, and of course this is another thing that can be sped up a lot as well, especially when agents are hammering lots of small filesystem operations (it's not uncommon to see my machine waiting on filesystem ops because the standard OS filesystem interface wasn't designed with modern disk performance in mind). With modern disks, there's no reason to use the *nix filesystem API. In the past, writing a developer toolchain that uses direct I/O instead of normal filessytem operations or building a custom OS or a funny layer that fakes out syscalls would've been an absurd endevaor, but that's totally doable now.
For someone like me who doesn't know anything about regexes, string matching algorithms, compilers, interpreters, etc., this set of projects would've taken a year or more to get to "works for me" quality. Instead, this was a low single-digit number of hours of my time. If I wanted to make any of these things meet a "useful product or open source project" quality bar, that would be a lot more work0, but it's still pretty incredible how much this process is sped up.
My read of Malis's meaning when he says “we should be more ambitious with the software we build”, is that it doesn't even occur to people to do these things that are now easy. For weeks, every time I logged into Twitter, I saw someone complain about how Rust compilation is slow and is limiting development velocity (I think this wasn't actually true when I saw the complaints, in that this was before 5.6 Sol and 6 Astra were available on Cerebras, and if you measured where the time actually went, Rust compilation time wasn't actually that much of a bottleneck at the time). Sure, Rust compliation is slow. You can just write a Rust interpreter as well as speed up compilation directly. There are problems like this which I see people complaining about daily that are solvable without a lot of time or effort now. As far as I can tell, these problems are problems because people are implicitly carrying around a pre-agentic cost model. Ten years ago, the kind of person who implemented a new compiler because their compiler was slow was the kind of person who started programming a new 3d game engine when they wanted to make an indie game, i.e., the kind of person who never ships anything. Most productive programmers I know still have an aversion to this kind of thing, even though it is now actually reasonable to implement this kind of thing now4.
Another project I previously mentioned was this Azul AI which is superhuman at matched time controls. When I did that (with GPT-5.1/5.2), with zero AI knowledge, it took about 5 hours of my time to get something superhuman, and about 20 hours of my time to become what appeared to be the strongest AI at the time, including being stronger against humans than this AI that was used to cheat on Board Game Arena. Gabriel Cangussu recently built an AI that demolishes my AI, and AFAICT, it took him substantially less time than my AI took me. From talking to him about it, one key difference is that Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 have a much better understanding of board game AIs. When I used GPT-5.1/5.2, pretty much every suggestion they had was wrong and I had to do a lot of steering to get things to be remotely reasonable. If I had GPT read a codebase or a paper to implement relevant techniques from the paper, it would fail. If I read the paper myself and named a technique, it would say it did the technique, but it would generally do something that superficially looked like the technique but wasn't the actual technique until I issued some corrections. When the model is that far from being able to do the right thing, if you have no background in the area, it's fairly time consuming to check if the model did the right thing since you have to learn enough about what it's supposed to do to be able to check that it did what was claimed.
When I did that project, I said to friends that I didn't think the state models were in could last. It seemed impossible that they wouldn't get good enough to be able to read a paper and implement the techniques soon, and it seemed like they should also be able to pick out codebases and papers to crib from as well. From my experience messing around a bit with Fable 5 and Cangussu's experience with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, that seems to have happened, which is a huge time saver for someone like me who doesn't know anything about board game AIs (I know a little bit now, but still less than any real AI researcher)5.
For any particular domain, like board game AIs, you can say, "who cares? Board game AIs don't matter", but I've found this increase in capability to be true in quite a few different domains. Just for example, I did this toy eval of verification and test techniques with GPT-5.6 Sol implementing zstd on medium and xhigh. I haven't had time to write it up, but when I published that post, I also re-did the evals with GPT-6 Astra. 6 Astra was so good that I had to find different evals because models had advanced too much. For zstd, 6 Astra succeeds at passing all of the registered tests more than 99% of the time across all conditions, even the ones that significantly impair performance, like using TDD (and, BTW, it does it more cheaply as well, taking about $1 to implement zstd). I ended up using the IMAP RFC, which 5.6 Sol couldn't do effectively, and Pandoc, which is a pretty major thing to implement as it needs to be able to read and write many different formats6.
BTW, when people have said they used the new model and everything just works, software is solved, etc., I haven't found this to be true at all. It's true that there are a lot more things the newer model can one-shot, where things basically just work, but this just means that I end up working on more ambitious things where models still struggle7. I'm more productive and can work faster, but I find that, in terms of what I'm doing, I get farther from "it just works" with each more capable model because the gap between what the model can verify effectively without significant handholding and what the model can implement has been increasing8. All of that is a long-winded and less eloquent way of saying: we should be more ambitious with the software we build.
Thanks to Laurence Tratt, Yossi Kreinin, Alex Kolovsky, and Michael Malis for comments/corrections/discussion.
I've had this note on my recent posts, which also applies to this one. In order to get more posts out, I'm trying to crank posts out in half an hour and not review them much. This definitely means less well-supported posts. If I were writing this in my standard style, I would've had comprehensive benchmarks for all of my projects that I mentioned. Instead, I did a quick comparison that satisfied my curiosity and am writing this up without rigorous benchmarking, and there are maybe twenty or thirty things in this post that I'd like to do but haven't done.
I haven't even written up this Rust interpreter. If, five years ago, I'd cobbled together a Rust interpreter that got a 50x speedup on cold compiles and 2x on warm/cached builds (with much more being possible if edits to the Rust compiler were in bounds), that woudl be a super interestin thing that I'd want to write up, but even operating in this mode where I barely edit posts and just blast them out, this isn't interesting enough to write up because it's so easy to do things that would've been considered very interesting not all that long ago.
Appendix: we should be less ambitious with the software we build
Here's a comment from Yossi Kreinin, quoted (with permission, of course):
If you publish this I will publish a response explaining that for most people they should be less ambitious with the software they build with AI or they'll experience abject failure. I think a lot of the problems don't lend themselves that well to "agentic loops" since you don't have clear pass/fail criteria, and even when you do most people have trouble reasoning about giant black boxes which they can impose constraints on but can't understand the innards of [I include myself in this set.] This is a little bit like microservices I guess, where some people both need it and are very good at using it but likely for most people, they need it less and can't use it well at all. I sort of envy the ones who should and actually can be this ambitious about the software they build of course; not saying you shouldn't be more ambitious at all but moderating said ambition is a big part of handling the current situation for most I think
I have a similar thought about "there's no reason for software to be slow" BTW; in many cases, if you use AI to speed up some flow, you will add a bunch of messy code that will be overfit for the use case you tested on and will neither generalize, perf-wise, for all the use cases you should care about, nor will be maintainable upon future changes. If you know what you're doing and you understand how the system should be decomposed into parts and when it makes sense to go all-in on optimizing some part or a combination of them working together and how to properly benchmark it, etc., then things are great, but if for instance you have a manager who thinks there's no reason for software to be slow and he pushes people to use AI to make random parts of the software fast... Run for cover
My feeling is that, overall, the situation here is a bit analogous to the discussion here about why I don't like when people talk about how AI gives a 100x or 1000x productivity increase. There are some things that are sped up by a very large factor, easily over 1000000x. And some things don't currently get sped up at all. If you do exactly what you would've done five years ago, but with AI, the speedup is fairly poor because of Amdahl's law. But, in the general case, you can choose what to speed up and if you're looking for things that are productive to do, this often seems to involve things that were previously too expensive to do.
And, I think that you can often set up systems that have some kind of self-checking property even when most people wouldn't. This discussion of the implementation of Guards of Atlantis 2 is an example of that. It's a poor choice for an AI project because the official rules are a mess of ambiguous and contradictory English text (it's probably the game I've seen humans misplay at the highest rate, and the rules are confusing enough that the designer has often changed their mind about what their own rules mean despite continually maintaining that the rules are perfectly clear and one can play the game by simply reading the rules as written). title: Removing Next.js Got My Blog to 100 on Every Lighthouse Category
content:
Removing Next.js Got My Blog to 100 on Every Lighthouse Category
K
korindiehacker
Author
2026-10-26
9 min read
English
My blog just scored a perfect 100 on every Lighthouse category. I love blogging. I wanted to build a blog that’s light, fast, free of clutter, able to run multiple blogs, and fully accessible on top of that. And finally, at long last, I’ve more or less pulled it off. It was quite a tedious process. Ugh… and I even had to remove Next.js, the framework I’d been using most. It was far, far more painful than I expected. I’d like to share the journey of improving performance while building this blog.
Why did I decide to build my own blog?
When you think of blogs, a few names come to mind. Medium, Blogger, Ghost… But none of them satisfied me. Medium and Blogger are bloated with features, and their actual performance wasn’t satisfying either.
Blogger
Medium
Truly horrifying.
Hmm…… And there was another problem: it’s a hassle to work directly with the markup and raw code we all love (Markdown, HTML, CSS).
For the record, all performance measurements were taken with pagespeed.web.dev.
Of course, there are plenty of alternatives: WordPress, Ghost, Hugo. I didn’t like WordPress’s plugin hell. Ghost has to be self-hosted (there’s ghost.org too, but it’s way too expensive…), and every version upgrade broke something in the editor, so keeping it up to date was a chore. Hugo is the best of the bunch, but in the end, setting it up is still a hassle. Looking back, I guess what I really wanted was SaaS.
The one I liked most was Bear Blog. Great performance. I love its product philosophy, too. But its extreme minimalism was a downside for me. The editor UX didn’t work for me, either.
If it at least let me add AdSense and attach images for free, I probably would’ve just used Bear Blog.
As fast as Bear Blog, but with a bit more functionality and better usability. That’s the blog I wanted to build. Oh, and if you’re curious, you can check it out at bloffy.co.
Anyway. Enough about me. Let me share how I actually improved the performance.
Let’s hit 100 on Lighthouse Performance.
Obviously, caching is a must.
It goes without saying that caching is essential. Get caching right and performance improves dramatically. And Next.js makes caching really convenient. There’s ISR, and it also extends fetch with a next option for caching. Handy. Using these well alone gets you a long way on performance.
Unfortunately, though, our site can be reached from anywhere in the world. Why is that unfortunate? Within the same region, caching makes things fast, but visitors from other regions still end up eating the network latency.
No, silly. That’s what a CDN is for.
Yes. That’s why we use a CDN. And if you deploy a Next.js app to Vercel, you get a CDN out of the box. I don’t dislike Vercel; it’s incredibly convenient. But the Pro plan is pricey right from the start, there’s the serverless cold start problem, and the dependency on the Vercel ecosystem isn’t something you can ignore either.
So why not use a different CDN service? Cloudflare, for example. I honestly think Cloudflare is a genuinely nice company. You can run large-scale infrastructure and most apps on it for free. But then I figured I didn’t really need Next.js’s caching anymore. Having to invalidate two caches every time I publish a post makes things a pain to manage.
In short, for a static website, I figured a CDN alone is enough. And that’s reason number one why I didn’t need Next.js.
Image optimization.
Images these days run over 10MB. Serve those on the web as-is and your performance will go completely off the rails.
Optimizing images is quite a hassle. You have to resize per device, compress, and then handle the CDN on top of that. On a previous project, I had a serverless function (AWS Lambda) compress and resize images whenever one landed in storage (S3), and I put CloudFront in front as the CDN. It was a pretty reasonable setup for tailoring things exactly the way I wanted. But it’s also a setup that needs a fair amount of upkeep.
So this time I went with Cloudflare’s Image Transformations. Even on the free tier you get 5,000 images, so I use it without a second thought.
At this point I sound like a Cloudflare sales rep. I’m just an ordinary solo developer.
Ta-da. Here’s the Next.js blog’s performance after all that caching and image optimization.
For reference, this was Next.js 16.1.6.
Pretty high scores. But this isn’t enough. We want 100. A clean, no-asterisks 100. So I dug into what the problem was.
It said a substantial amount of legacy JavaScript was found, and it wasn’t code I wrote. It came from the framework runtime that Next.js ships in its bundle.
But this page is a static page with zero interaction. Every page is pre-rendered with ISR, and I thought I’d followed the Next.js guidelines well. So as an experiment, I ripped out every client component the app had, left only server components, and measured again. The score didn’t budge.
At first I suspected hydration, but once I dug in, the problem wasn’t hydration alone. The cause was the client runtime that Next.js always ships, even for static pages. Even with only server components, the runtime chunks, hydration, and the RSC payload for the router all stay. That’s because next/link and next/image are themselves client components ('use client'), so having just those two is enough to pull in the runtime and trigger hydration.
So what if I strip out next/link and next/image too? The App Router’s own runtime, the router and error boundaries, still remains. There’s no official way to get it down to zero; the only option was a hack: stripping the scripts out of the rendered HTML. That’s when it hit me: “If I’m going to do that, why am I even using Next.js?”
And then, the unused code.
You can see that the bulk of the JavaScript is code that isn’t needed. Unused code alone comes to 230,460 bytes. That’s not good. Most static websites don’t need JavaScript at all. Unused JavaScript is needed even less.
This is where I really agonized. Is dropping Next.js for the sake of 100 points the right call? I’d spent a lot of time building the public-facing web app.
Let’s remove Next.js.
In the end, for the quality of the blog (even if it’s just 5 points), I decided to rip Next.js out entirely. My judgment was that I wouldn’t need Next.js’s excess features in the long run either. I considered going fully vanilla, but I didn’t want to give up the productivity and infrastructure benefits of a framework. I needed to find the right one.
I chose Hono. I liked its technical philosophy. “Fast and simple” was exactly the solution I needed most, and JSX support was a bonus. The migration cost didn’t look too big, either.
Ta-da. Finally, 100.
Tada. And just like that, 100 across the board. Go ahead and run the very page you’re reading right now through pagespeed.web.dev.
There’s no JavaScript, and unused code dropped sharply to 407 bytes. As a bonus, build time went down by about 40% too.
Oh, why is SEO at 69? That site was built for testing, and it deliberately blocks search indexing. That’s why it’s 69.
By the way, if you score 100 on everything in DevTools, Lighthouse actually sets off fireworks for you. 🎉🎉
Hono vs. Next.js Performance
Next.js Performance (server components only)
Hono Performance
The long task that runs before anything is rendered on screen took 309.3ms on Next.js, and when I built the same page with Hono, it took 68.01ms. That’s roughly a 78% improvement.
Does your static site really need Next.js?
Is a JS payload, hydration included, really doing a static site any good? I don’t think so. It leaves behind unnecessary JavaScript, so in most cases I think it’s simply not needed.
That said, for an interaction-heavy app, I think Next.js can be a great framework. In fact, the management app for this very blog is built with Next.js!
P.S. This blog runs on Bloffy, the blogging platform I’m building. If you want a blog that scores like this without the setup, you can try it at bloffy.co.
Published with Bloffy

title: Making the Buddha Head from Merv Whole Again | Getty News
content:
Breadcrumb Navigation
Getty
News & Stories
Making the Buddha Head from Merv Whole Again
Making the Buddha Head from Merv Whole Again
A collaboration between the Getty Museum and the State Museum of Turkmenistan
Topics
Art & ArchitectureScience & Tech
The Buddha head during excavation at Merv, about 1966. © State Museum of Turkmenistan
By Susanne Gänsicke
Mar 11, 2026
Copy Page URL
URL copied to clipboard
Share on Facebook. Opens in new tab.
Share on Twitter. Opens in new tab.
Editor’s Note
Susanne Gänsicke is senior conservator and head of antiquities conservation in the Department of Antiquities at the Getty Museum.
Body Content
I first saw the large head of a Buddha, resting on an earthen pedestal, in historic black-and-white photographs in 2020.
The images were taken some 60 years ago, when the head had just been discovered during excavations by the South Turkmenistan Archaeological Inter-disciplinary Expedition (YuTAKE) of the Academy of Sciences of the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic in the ancient oasis town of Merv. Located in the Karakum Desert of Turkmenistan, the Silk Road city had been occupied since the third millennium BCE and served as a vibrant urban center of enormous wealth (it’s said to have counted one million inhabitants in the 12th century).
The head undergoing emergency stabilization during excavation at Merv, about 1966. © State Museum of Turkmenistan
Sculpted originally from unfired clay around a skeletal framework of wood, straw, and rope, the head once belonged to a much larger sculpture—likely a seated Buddha. This construction method was not merely technical but imbued with ritual meaning, conceived to endow the divine image with body and life.
That figure is lost today, and the head appears to have been separated in antiquity, but what exactly happened remains unknown. It was unearthed in the stupa of a Buddhist monastery within the Gyaur Kala at Merv, an ancient fortress known as the “castle of infidels” because its inhabitants adhered to different faiths—Zoroastrian, Christian, Jewish, and Buddhist—at the time of the Arab conquest. Dated to the fifth–sixth century CE, this Buddha is the westernmost example of its kind and is crucial for understanding Buddhism’s spread.
Fabio Colombo, Susanne Gänsicke, and Giuseppe Salemi on top of the stupa at the Gyaur Kala at Merv. The ramparts of the castle are visible in the distance. Photo courtesy of Maysa Nepesova
Measuring nearly 35½ inches (90 cm) in height, the head dwarfed the archaeologists in the excavation photographs. Little is known about its modern history. It survived almost intact, although with damage on the proper left front and side. The unfired clay made it heavy yet fragile, and moving it would have been difficult. Other images show that decades ago it was cut into four major sections.
The head’s elegantly curved brow and heavy, lidded eye caught my attention five years ago, when the Getty Museum was invited to collaborate with the State Museum of Turkmenistan on the object’s conservation. I recognized both the challenge and promise of this unusual task, as well as the privilege of being invited to build a partnership with Turkmenistan. As the principal investigator, I was responsible for shaping the project’s narrative, defining its technical scope, and developing its timeline and budget. In 2021, Getty was awarded the 30th U.S. Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation grant, supported by the U.S. Embassy in Turkmenistan—an affirmation of the venture’s significance and potential to strengthen cultural ties.
Examination and cleaning begin
Fast forward to the beginning of our project. We formed a team with conservators Fabio Colombo from Rome, Elisa Pannunzio from Venice, and Giuseppe Salemi from Padua University—a specialist in 3D technology and heritage preservation. All brought deep experience in the preservation of Buddhist sculpture in Central and South Asia. So far, we have completed five missions in Ashgabat and expect three more to finalize the conservation. Work also continues remotely.
When we first examined the four surviving head fragments in Ashgabat, only thin outer shells of painted clay remained—like remnants of a giant egg.
Fragments of the head in the conservation laboratory at the State Museum of Turkmenistan. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
The interior matrix had been removed and partially replaced with unsuitable modern materials, such as resin coatings, gauze, and foamed synthetic polymers. The process started with careful examination, documentation, archival research, and discussion with museum staff, scholars, and international colleagues. The head sections were recorded using photogrammetry (with high- and very high–resolution sensors and structured light scanning), allowing 3D visualization and the creation of mathematically accurate models.
After surveying the external surfaces, we digitally modeled their shape (below left) to create 3D- printed shells (below right) that would lend support during treatment.
Data from photogrammetry allowed the creation of 3D-printed shells to support the fragments of the head during treatment. Photo courtesy of Giuseppe Salemi
The shells, held by Giuseppe Salemi and Fabio Colombo, arriving in the laboratory in Ashgabat. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
The conservation intervention began with the meticulous reversal of inappropriate materials applied during earlier restoration campaigns, and we carefully removed the old repairs mechanically from the interior of the head sections. Carried out over several weeks, this proved to be particularly difficult due to the fragility of the inner surfaces and the tenacity of the aged compounds.
Fabio Colombo removing intractable old polyurethane foam with the aid of power tools. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Susanne Gänsicke using a steamer to detach previously applied cotton gauze facings from the interior surface of the smallest head section. Photo courtesy of U.S. Embassy in Turkmenistan
Next, the inner surfaces were cleaned, consolidated, and lined with modern stable materials for support.
The interior of the proper right side of the face: before removing old repair materials, during cleaning, and after cleaning, with some new repair patches. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Fabio Colombo applying new support materials to the interior of the proper right side of the face using Paraloid B72 resin, layers of cotton gauze, and fiberglass. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Then, the sections could be flipped, and work on the front surfaces began. Among the most delicate operations was the detachment of multiple gauze layers adhered previously with starch paste and intended as temporary protection. Carefully lifting the overlapping gauze patches gradually exposed the original surface, revealing for the first time the flesh tones and the vivid blue eye of the largest fragment of the face, previously entirely concealed.
The proper right side of the face with a remaining part of the 3D-printed support shell. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Fabio Colombo and Elisa Pannunzio removing gauze, aided by customized conservation gels, revealing the surface of the face with ancient layers of polychromy. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
The surface and edges of the sections remain soft and brittle, requiring thorough cleaning, consolidation, and the application of suitable backing supports. Notably, the earlier repair had failed to adequately reinforce the thin edges of the sections, which are now warped and deformed, complicating the reassembly of the four main components.
Unifying the head
In our ongoing project, Giuseppe continues to develop 3D models based on the data he has been acquiring.
Giuseppe Salemi capturing the newly exposed surfaces using a structural light scanner. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Slowly we have been developing a concept for unifying the main four parts into the fully sculpted head. The work involves again utilizing 3D-printed supports for the individual sections, this time to line their interiors for structural stability, and building a larger structure on which the head fragments will be reunited.
A preliminary digital 3D reconstruction allows visualization of the volume of the head. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
Miniature 3D-printed models of the preliminary reconstruction of the head and the extant parts of the ancient head for modeling their respective positions. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
A major challenge will be the final 3D reconstruction and loss compensation to create a modern interpretation of the head and prepare it for display at the museum.
The four parts of the head, now structurally stable, laid out next to each other for the first time, providing a glimpse of how much remains of their original decoration. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
The proper right sides of the face and head positioned for the first time in a way that allows evaluation of their original connection. Photo courtesy of Susanne Gänsicke
We also have begun to study the material history of the head, how it was made, how it changed over ancient and modern times, and how it relates to other Buddhist images in the larger region. The face bears layers of red and yellow pigments, with a large blue eye. Multiple color patches suggest ancient repairs and repainting, a common practice, while the molded blue curls of hair appear not to have been retouched. Tiny paint samples analyzed by the Getty Conservation Institute have revealed the multilayered paint and pigment composition. Our goal is to compare our results to other clay sculptures of the era and cultural milieu.
This project extends far beyond its technical scope. Supported by the U.S. Embassy in Turkmenistan and the State Museum of Turkmenistan, it fosters cultural diplomacy and opens avenues for future collaborations. Traveling to archaeological sites—including Merv and the place where the Buddha’s head once lay buried—gave us a vivid sense of context. Encountering even a fragment of Central Asia’s immensity stirred my imagination: millennia of cultural exchange, shifting borders, and layered histories suddenly felt present and alive. Working on the ground, immersed in local rhythms and hospitality, allowed us not only to understand the culture more deeply but also to form the kinds of personal relationships that make this work meaningful.
Ambassador Elizabeth Rood (left) and Nona Majidi (right) of the U.S. Embassy in Turkmenistan discussing the progress of the project with Susanne Gänsicke (center) in May 2025. Photo courtesy of Giuseppe Salemi
Meretgeldy Charyev, director of the State Museum of Turkmenistan, Susanne Gänsicke, Giuseppe Salemi, Elisa Pannunzio, and Fabio Colombo in the conservation laboratory in January 2026.
The result of our efforts will open the door to a new narrative within the museum’s galleries—one that weaves together religion, technical study, conservation methods, and public engagement. Although the original Buddha figure will never be whole again, its restored head will stand as an emblem of Turkmenistan’s heritage and of the role that technology can play in safeguarding the past. When we first arrived, we had no clear sense of what we would find. Yet as the sculpture slowly regains its form, our delight has grown in equal measure. Contributing to its resurrection has been professionally rewarding, yet also demanding, and deeply joyful—an experience made all the richer by sharing it with our colleagues in Ashgabat.
